name: fast_image_resize
baseline: libvips 8.15.1 (single-threaded); also the Rust image 0.25.6 and resize 0.8.9 crates
workload: Single-threaded resize of a 4928x3279 image to 852x567 (RGB8, RGBA8 with alpha multiply/divide, L8) with Nearest, Box, Bilinear, Bicubic and Lanczos3 filters, criterion timings.
claimed_speedup: RGB8 Lanczos3: 13.52 ms (AVX2) vs libvips 17.31 ms, image 176.09 ms, resize 137.70 ms. RGB8 Bilinear: 3.55 ms vs libvips 5.58 ms. RGB8 Box: 2.65 ms vs libvips 61.51 ms. caveats: Does not compare against ImageMagick or stb_image_resize, so the named baselines of this category are not beaten directly; the closest incumbent measured is libvips, and the lead over it is small for RGB8 (Lanczos3 13.52 ms vs 17.31 ms, about 1.3x, derived from page data; libvips Nearest and Box differ more). libvips was run single-threaded via a Rust binding. workload: Single-thread parity benchmark at 512x512, 1024x1024 and 4096x4096: RGB to HSV conversion, box blur r=2 on RGB, Gaussian sigma 2, flips and morphology, in Mpix/s.
claimed_speedup: RGB to HSV: go-images 65.6 vs scikit-image 13.7 Mpix/s at 512x512 (4.81x), 4.71x at 1024x1024, 4.76x at 4096x4096. Box blur r=2 RGB: 2.64x, 1.78x, 2.29x. Flip horizontal 2.01x to 2.28x. Gaussian sigma 2: 1.02x to 1.26x. OpenCV on the same RGB to HSV test reaches 1,554 Mpix/s (about 24x faster than go-images, derived from page data).

name: kornia-rs (Image.resize and imgproc kernels, kornia-py)
baseline: OpenCV 4.13.0 cv2.resize (INTER_LANCZOS4) and Pillow 12.2.0 Image.resize (LANCZOS)
workload: Python bake-off on a 1080p RGB image, best-of-N minimum time per call with GC disabled (kornia-py/benchmarks/bake_off_pil_cv2.py and _bench.py): resize 1080p to 720p Lanczos, a resize matrix over bilinear, bicubic and lanczos for several shapes, and 13 image ops.
claimed_speedup: Resize 1080p->720p Lanczos: kornia 1.67 ms vs cv2 7.36 ms (4.4x) vs PIL 43.6 ms. Resize matrix (antialias=False vs OpenCV): 1080p->2160p bilinear 1.78 ms vs 9.80 ms (5.52x faster); 1080p->224x224 bilinear 0.25 ms vs 0.72 ms (2.84x); 1080p->540p bilinear 0.42 ms vs 0.82 ms (1.97x); 1080p->2160p bicubic 1.21x and lanczos 1.07x. Other ops: normalize 3.810 ms vs 67.76 ms (17.78x), ORB detect+compute 11.19 ms vs 45.51 ms. Score 9 wins, 4 ties, 0 losses over 13 ops; JPEG decode tied with OpenCV (39.64 ms vs 39.3 ms) and JPEG encode 0.94x.
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.93.0, release build with opt-level=2 (LLVM bug workaround for faer), NEON intrinsics, rayon; pyo3 0.28, Python 3.10.12, numpy 2.2.6, OpenCV 4.13.0, Pillow 12.2.0, albumentations 2.0.8; run at commit 07e52d7 on branch feat/gray-f32-neon (2026-06-20)
hardware: NVIDIA Jetson Orin (aarch64), Cortex-A78AE, 6 cores at 1.728 GHz max, LPDDR5, JetPack R36.4.3, Linux 5.15.148-tegra
stars_or_usage: 720 stars; crates.io crate kornia and PyPI package kornia-rs
tradeoffs: Aarch64 NEON fast paths come first and AVX2 exists only for some ops; rayon multithreading; Rust crate plus PyO3 Python wheels and kornia-cpp bindings; antialias=True matches PIL semantics and antialias=False matches OpenCV INTER_CUBIC and LANCZOS4 semantics (different work). Pillow-SIMD is not in the matrix because it is x86-only.
caveats: First-party numbers, one ARM machine, no x86 results, measured on a feature-branch commit. The bake-off script calls k_img.resize(1280, 720) with default settings while cv2 uses INTER_LANCZOS4; the doc says kornia's 'u8 fast-AA path' beats OpenCV 'at the same kernel', but an antialiased kernel and OpenCV's fixed 8-tap kernel are not identical work (the aa=False matrix wins by smaller margins, 1.07x-3.09x). kornia uses rayon across 6 cores while OpenCV thread settings are not stated for resize rows (the grayscale row says cv2 6T). Page itself marks several 1080p ops below its 2x target and says resize 1080p is noise-bound (1.81-2.03x run to run). JPEG decode and encode are ties because all three use libjpeg-turbo. The page's own note says an earlier ORB-versus-VPI figure was inflated by harness overhead. The kornia-rs README has no benchmarks and Albumentations issue #1584 only states the claim without numbers. A WebSearch snippet of arXiv 2501.13131 (page blocked, snippet only) reports JPEG decode on Apple M4 Max of 1034 images/s for kornia-rs vs 1016 for OpenCV and 775 for Pillow; the current ternaus/imread_benchmark README no longer ships results or lists kornia-rs, so that independent figure could not be verified. Tier A rests on public harness plus stated Rust version, opt-level and CPU model.

baseline: Magick.NET (ImageMagick) and ImageSharp; System.Drawing and SkiaSharp also measured
workload: Load a large JPEG or TIFF, shrink by 10 percent, sharpen, and save again (the scenario from the libvips 'Speed and memory use' page), run with BenchmarkDotNet under NativeAOT.
claimed_speedup: JPEG: NetVips 74.47 ms vs Magick.NET 1,626.85 ms (ratio 21.85), ImageSharp 366.95 ms (4.93), System.Drawing 1,185.58 ms (15.92), SkiaSharp 5,362.23 ms (72.01). TIFF: NetVips 49.80 ms vs Magick.NET 1,533.49 ms (30.79), ImageSharp 186.51 ms (3.75), System.Drawing 985.05 ms (19.78). README summary: 'around 26 times faster than Magick.NET and 4 times faster than ImageSharp'.
compiler_and_flags: BenchmarkDotNet v0.15.8, .NET SDK 10.0.101, .NET 10.0.1 NativeAOT, X64 RyuJIT x86-64-v4, 'dotnet run -c Release'; libvips 8.18.0, Magick.NET 14.10.1, ImageSharp 3.1.12, SkiaSharp 3.119.1, System.Drawing.Common 10.0.1
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7900 3.70GHz, 12 physical / 24 logical cores, Windows 11 25H2
tradeoffs: Needs the libvips native library (NuGet native packages exist for common platforms). Pipeline is demand-driven and streaming, so memory use is low. It is a binding, so the speed comes from libvips.
caveats: Binding of libvips, which is already catalogued (likely folds into libvips as a duplicate); the evidence is a new .NET-specific comparison against ImageMagick via Magick.NET. Benchmark is run by the binding's author (also a libvips maintainer). The scenario includes JPEG or TIFF decode and encode, not only resampling, and libvips uses multiple threads by default while the harness does not state a thread limit for the others. System.Drawing was run without the sharpen step because it lacks one (footnote on the page), which flatters System.Drawing. ImageSharp 3.1.12 is not OSI-licensed (footnote on the page). Single scenario, one machine.

name: stb-image-resize-opt
baseline: stb_image_resize2.h v2.18 (nothings/stb, compiled -O2)
workload: Resize throughput matrix (mixed suite, isolated AVX2 vs baseline kernels, uint8/uint16/float output, sRGB, half output, and a downstream consumer benchmark) comparing the fork's prebuilt library against stock upstream.
claimed_speedup: Mixed suite +36-38% geomean with held-out PGO (+32.8% without PGO); isolated AVX2 kernels +34.9% geomean (non-half); 1.2-1.7x per row for uint8/uint16/float; sRGB path 1.10-1.22x; half output 1.0x; downstream consumer benchmark 1.23x.
tradeoffs: Byte-identical output to upstream (README states a differential test of 8,284 cases on 3 dispatch paths). The resampler source is unchanged; the speedup comes from shipping a prebuilt static library with baseline and AVX2 variants chosen by CPUID at runtime, plus PGO. Header-only use gets only the baseline build. x86-64 gains only; aarch64 is a single scalar/NEON build. half output falls back to baseline.
caveats: Brand-new unofficial fork, not endorsed by the stb author, 0 stars, one day of history, so the claim has had no outside scrutiny. Part of the gain is compiler flags and PGO (-O3 and PGO against stock -O2), not algorithmic change. Reported figures are geomeans over the author's own matrix; results CSVs (results/summary.csv, kernels.csv, consumer.csv) were named in the README but not opened. Documents upstream quirks it does not fix (uninitialized read in uint16 WRAP BOX upsample).

name: tir (tiny image resize, in tinyexr)
baseline: stb_image_resize2 (successor of stb_image_resize, matched filter, float32 path); also tinyexr's own exr_resize_float
workload: Separable float32 resampling with a Mitchell (4-tap) filter on random data, 1-channel and 4-channel, shapes 960x640 to 1920x1280 (2x up), 1920x1280 to 960x640 (2x down) and 4096x2560 to 561x350 (7.3x down); output megapixels per second on one thread, about 0.3 s per measurement (tools/resize/tests/tir_bench.c).
claimed_speedup: README table (MP/s, one AVX2 core, Mitchell), tir AVX2 vs stb2 vs exr_v3. 4-channel: 2x up 295 / 266 / 135; 2x down 78 / 73 / 30; 7.3x down 7.6 / 6.4 / 2.2. 1-channel: 2x up 1218 / 1279 / 443; 2x down 334 / 365 / 92; 7.3x down 27.3 / 25.4 / 8.2. Author text: 'tir beats exr_resize_float 2-5x everywhere', 'against stb2 (matched filters) tir wins on every 4-channel case', 'within ~5% on 1-channel 2x cubic up/down'. Ratios vs stb2 (derived from page data): 4-channel 1.11x, 1.07x, 1.19x; 1-channel 7.3x down 1.07x, but 0.95x and 0.92x on the 2x cases (stb2 faster).
compiler_and_flags: Makefile target resize-bench: $(CC) (Makefile default CC ?= gcc, version not stated) -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -O2 -g, no -march or -mavx2 flag; tir picks AVX2+FMA at runtime. stb_image_resize2.h is added with make resize-bench STB=1 (-DTIR_BENCH_STB) after the user drops the header into tools/resize/tests/.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (Zen 2), one AVX2 core
stars_or_usage: 836 stars (tinyexr repository; tir lives in tools/resize)
tradeoffs: Pure C11 with a header that is safe to include from C++. Internal float32 filtering with u8, u16, f16 and f32 pixel I/O; runtime SSE2, SSE4.1 and AVX2+FMA dispatch, NEON at compile time, SVE behind a runtime gate. One arena allocation, streaming push_row/pull_row API with O(support) memory, optional C11-threads band parallelism with output identical to serial. HDR-aware (antiring, no clamping), normal-map and height-map modes, premultiplied-alpha filtering. Filters: box, triangle, B-spline, Gaussian, Mitchell, Catmull-Rom, Lanczos-2/3. Not a standalone repository: the code sits under tools/resize in the tinyexr tree (no dependency on the EXR codec for the library itself).
caveats: Margin over stb2 is small (about 7-19% on 4-channel) and stb2 is faster on the 1-channel 2x cases, so the honest claim is 'competitive with, and better on RGBA/HDR'; the 2-5x figure is against the project's own exr_resize_float. The benchmark uses float32 pixels, not the 8-bit RGBA path that stb_image_resize2 is usually tuned for. The Makefile builds without -mavx2, and stb_image_resize2 selects SIMD at compile time, so stb2 probably ran its SSE2 path while tir used runtime AVX2 dispatch; this could understate stb2. Lanczos3 row compares against 4-tap Catmull-Rom on the stb side and is excluded here. Author-run numbers on a single Zen 2 machine, compiler version not stated. tir is very new (first commit 2026-07-02, version 0.x), so the API may still change. Tier A rests on public benchmark code, Makefile flags and a named CPU; a verifier may prefer C if the unstated compiler version counts against it.

baseline: ImageMagick (6.8.9-9 and 6.9.7-4 in pillow-perf; 7.1.1 in the libvips Speed-and-memory-use benchmark)
workload: pillow-perf: resize of a 2560x1600 RGB image (bilinear/bicubic), Gaussian blur and a load/transpose/resize/blur cycle; libvips wiki: crop, 10 percent bilinear shrink and 3x3 sharpen of a 10000x10000 8-bit RGB tiled TIFF.
claimed_speedup: pillow-perf on Core i5-4430 (derived from page data): bicubic 2560x1600 to 320x200 takes 5.41 ms for OpenCV 4.1.2 vs 89.2 ms for ImageMagick 6.9.7-4 (16.5x); to 2048x1280 48.2 vs 222.93 ms (4.6x); to 5478x3424 bicubic 115.25 vs 1256.13 ms (10.9x) and bilinear 57.74 vs 1007.63 ms (17.5x); Gaussian blur radius 1 px 69.39 vs 675.34 ms (9.7x), 10 px 445.67 vs 1768.07 ms (4.0x), 30 px 1399.39 vs 4090.08 ms (2.9x). libvips wiki: whole pipeline 3.15 s for opencv 4.10 vs 4.41 s for magick 7.1.1 (1.4x, derived from page data). speedtest-resize (Core i7 3.4GHz, JPEG load, 150x100 thumbnail, save; via go-opencv): 0.110 s vs ImageMagick_resize 0.568 s (5.2x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated: pillow-perf uses the opencv-python binary wheel (OpenCV 4.1.2 in the results); the libvips wiki used the Ubuntu package (opencv 4.10).
hardware: pillow-perf: Intel Core i5-4430 @ 3.00GHz, Ubuntu 18.04.3 (also Xeon 8124M, EPYC 7571 and Core i5-8279U files in the same directory). libvips wiki: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3955WX 16-core, Ubuntu 25.04.
tradeoffs: Large dependency; BGR channel order; cv::resize with bilinear or bicubic does not apply an anti-aliasing filter on strong downscales (per the pillow-resize README), so output differs from convolution-based resamplers such as Pillow, libvips or ImageMagick; JPEG load is slower than ImageMagick in pillow-perf (47.89 vs 27.38 ms on the i5-4430).
caveats: Baseline versions are old (ImageMagick 6.x) in pillow-perf, and the suite is maintained by the Pillow and Pillow-SIMD authors. OpenCV bilinear and Lanczos3 cells are empty for the 320x200 and 2048x1280 targets; the Lanczos row for 5478x3424 is OpenCV Lanczos4 (439.03 ms) against ImageMagick Lanczos3 (1495.61 ms), so not like for like. The libvips pipeline is I/O dominated and the wiki itself says the test flatters libvips; OpenCV does not thread automatically there. vips-bench issue 8 points out that the benchmark programs use different resampling algorithms (affine bilinear in libvips, convolution resampling in Pillow, ImageMagick and others), so the pipelines are not strictly equivalent.
found_via: libvips wiki Speed-and-memory-use table (raw wiki page), pillow-perf result data docs/src/data/*.json and the speedtest-resize README, all reached from the starting query on resize shootouts.

name: OpenImageIO
baseline: ImageMagick 7.1.1 (magick, convert)
workload: libvips benchmark: load a 10000x10000 8-bit RGB tiled TIFF, crop 100 pixels off every edge, shrink 10 percent with bilinear interpolation, sharpen with a 3x3 convolution, save (oiiotool 2.5.18).
claimed_speedup: 3.46 s for oiio vs 4.41 s for magick and 4.44 s for convert (1.3x, derived from page data); the page's own 'times slower than libvips' column reads oiio 6.07 vs magick 7.74 and convert 7.79.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (Ubuntu packages).
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3955WX 16-core, Ubuntu 25.04 (run 12 Aug 2025)
stars_or_usage: 2.4k stars; VFX industry standard (Academy Software Foundation)
tradeoffs: Large dependency set; peak memory 2236.57 MB in this run, higher than ImageMagick (1500.52 MB) and libvips (94.28 MB).
caveats: Modest 1.3x margin on a trivial, I/O-dominated test that the wiki says flatters libvips. The wiki notes the test uses oiiotool, which 'may not be the best way to test the library'. Run by the libvips maintainer, who is the benchmark author (third party for OpenImageIO). vips-bench issue 8 points out that the benchmark programs use different resampling algorithms (affine bilinear in libvips, convolution resampling in Pillow, ImageMagick and others), so the pipelines are not strictly equivalent.
found_via: libvips wiki Speed-and-memory-use shootout table (oiio row), from the starting query on resize shootouts.

name: rez (pure Go and SIMD image resizer)
baseline: ImageMagick convert -resize; also nfnt/resize, disintegration/imaging, gift, bild and golang.org/x/image/draw
workload: Load 5616x3744 JPEG photos, scale each to a 150x100 thumbnail, write a JPEG, and report average time per file (third-party speedtest-resize shootout; load and save time is included).
claimed_speedup: Third-party scenario (3.4GHz Intel Core i7, Ubuntu 16.10): rez_bilinear 0.349 s per file vs ImageMagick_resize 0.568 s (about 1.6x faster, derived from page data), x_image_draw 0.370 s, imaging_box 0.439 s, gift_box 0.440 s, Nfnt_NearestNeighbor 0.447 s, bild_resize 0.515 s. Scenario by rez's author (3.3GHz Core i5, Windows 7): rez_bilinear 148 ms vs imaging_Box 243 ms and Nfnt_NearestNeighbor 233 ms. On the original Pentium T2390 1.86GHz run rez_bilinear took 2.913 s, slower than ImageMagick_resize at 2.316 s.
hardware: Several: Intel Pentium T2390 1.86GHz (Ubuntu 14.04), Intel Core i5 3.3GHz (Windows 7), Intel Core i7 3.4GHz (Ubuntu 16.10)
tradeoffs: Pure Go with AMD64 assembly horizontal and vertical scalers (asm/, hscalers_amd64.s, vscalers_amd64.s); resizes YCbCr, RGBA, NRGBA and Gray, supports chroma subsample conversion, interlaced-aware resize and parallel slices. The repo is archived (2024-05-19).
caveats: Old hardware and Go versions (2014 to 2016 era), no Go version or flags stated. The rez README carries no numbers; the evidence is a shootout by an independent author (speedtest-resize has no stated license). rez is slower than ImageMagick -resize in the first scenario, and ImageMagick -thumbnail with a jpeg:size hint (0.057 s in the i7 table) beats every Go library there, so the ImageMagick baseline here is a slow command line. The metric includes JPEG decode and encode.
found_via: GitHub: fawick/speedtest-resize README (surfaced by WebSearch 'Go image resize library benchmark faster than nfnt/resize disintegration/imaging SIMD github'); rez README opened separately

name: Skia
baseline: ImageMagick 6.8.9-9
workload: pillow-perf: resize of a 2560x1600 RGB image to 320x200 and 2048x1280 with bilinear and Lanczos filters (Skia 53, SSE2).
claimed_speedup: Xeon E5-2666 v3 (c4.large): 2560x1600 to 320x200 Lanczos 18.1 ms for Skia vs 127.67 ms for ImageMagick (7.1x, derived from page data); bilinear 6.41 vs 46.15 ms (7.2x); to 2048x1280 Lanczos 39.8 vs 276.76 ms (7.0x). Core i5-4258U: Lanczos 320x200 24.8 vs 156.8 ms (6.3x).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated ('Skia 53 SSE2' label only).
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2666 v3 @ 2.90GHz on Amazon EC2 c4.large, Ubuntu 16.04.1 (macbook.json: Intel Core i5-4258U @ 2.40GHz)
stars_or_usage: 11k stars (GitHub mirror of skia.googlesource.com); used in Chrome and Android
tradeoffs: Graphics library, not an image-processing toolbox; heavy build; the resize path measured is one SkBitmap scale call among many APIs.

found_via: pillow-perf result data docs/src/data/c4.large.json and macbook.json (competitor list skia-53), reached from the starting query on resize shootouts.

name: T-REZ (Go resizer on OpenCV and libjpeg-turbo)
baseline: ImageMagick convert -resize
workload: Load 5616x3744 JPEG photos, scale each to a 150x100 thumbnail, write a JPEG, and report average time per file (third-party speedtest-resize shootout).
claimed_speedup: Third-party scenario (3.4GHz Intel Core i7, Ubuntu 16.10): T-REZ 0.204 s per file vs ImageMagick_resize 0.568 s (about 2.8x faster, derived from page data). In the same table ImageMagick_thumbnail (0.057 s), vips (0.070 s), epeg (0.079 s), fastjpeg (0.082 s) and opencv (0.110 s) are all faster than T-REZ.
hardware: Intel Core i7 3.4GHz, Ubuntu 16.10
tradeoffs: Go program using cgo with OpenCV and libjpeg-turbo; strips IPTC, EXIF and ColorSync profile data; fit and fill modes, gravity, background color and JPEG quality option. Needs OpenCV and libjpeg installed.
caveats: Thin layer over OpenCV and libjpeg-turbo, so the speed is borrowed from those (OpenCV is already catalogued; a plain OpenCV run was faster in the same table). The T-REZ README has no baseline, only a 24-thread rate of about 700 resizes per second on a dual-socket Xeon (model 45) it calls illustrative. Evidence is one row of an older shootout, with no compiler or flags, against a slow ImageMagick command line. Last commit date not shown on the repo page (7 commits, copyright 2014).
found_via: GitHub: fawick/speedtest-resize README (T-REZ row); repo page opened separately

name: Albumentations
baseline: torchvision, Kornia, imgaug and AugLy (CPU image-augmentation transforms)
workload: uint8 images per second on one CPU thread for each transform (Resize, RandomResizedCrop, Hue, Saturation, Grayscale, Brightness, Contrast, ColorJitter and others), 2000 images, 5 runs per transform.
claimed_speedup: README table (images per second): Resize 3532 vs imgaug 2995, AugLy 1083, Kornia 645, torchvision 260 (1.18x over fastest other); RandomResizedCrop 4347 vs torchvision 837 (5.19x); ColorJitter 1020 vs AugLy 418 (2.44x); Hue 1944 vs Kornia 150 (12.98x); Saturation 1596 vs imgaug 495 (3.22x); Grayscale 32284 vs AugLy 6088 (5.30x); Brightness 11985 vs AugLy 2108 (5.68x); Contrast 12394 vs AugLy 1379 (8.99x). Not faster on Elastic (0.95x), LinearIllumination (0.68x) and PlasmaShadow (0.85x).
compiler_and_flags: Python 3.12.8; albumentations 2.0.4, augly 1.0.0, imgaug 0.4.0, kornia 0.8.0, torchvision 0.20.1; no compiler flags (Python)
hardware: macOS 15.1 arm64 (Apple silicon), 16 CPU cores; exact chip not stated; one thread per run
tradeoffs: Python library for deep-learning data augmentation; the repo is archived (2025-07-10) and development moved to AlbumentationsX, which is dual-licensed AGPL-3.0 or commercial. Operates on numpy uint8 images.
caveats: Augmentation transforms, not a general resampler or color-management library; the baselines are other augmentation libraries rather than ImageMagick or stb_image_resize. The speed is probably from the underlying OpenCV and NumPy kernels rather than a new resampling algorithm (not verified in code here). First-party README numbers from one macOS arm machine; the benchmark code lives in a separate repo that was not opened. Archived repo.
found_via: GitHub: README of albumentations-team/albumentations (checked as a Python image-augmentation library with resize and color transforms)

name: babl
baseline: Little CMS 2 (lcms2)
workload: Pixel format and colour space conversion (GIMP 2.10 and GEGL pipeline).
claimed_speedup: GIMP 2.10 release notes (snippet only): babl is 'up to 10 times faster than LCMS2 for the cases tested'. Disputed: a Little CMS blog post (snippet only) measured lcms2 3.59 s vs babl 6.36 s on 8-bit samples, i.e. lcms2 about 1.8x faster (derived from snippet).
stars_or_usage: 25 stars (read-only GitHub mirror of gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/babl); used by GIMP and GEGL
tradeoffs: Converts between pixel formats with runtime-optimised fast paths and caching; needs lcms2 for CMYK profiles (per search snippet); the GitHub page is a read-only mirror.
caveats: Snippet only: www.gimp.org release notes and littlecms.com are blocked here, so neither the 10x claim nor the rebuttal could be opened. The only independent measurement found contradicts the claim for 8-bit data. Keep as a flagged, low-confidence entry. The GitHub repo page was opened but carries no README claim.
found_via: WebSearch 'babl faster than lcms2 color conversion GEGL benchmark ICC' (GIMP 2.10 release notes and the Little CMS 'Babl throughput comparative' post).

name: BoofCV
baseline: OpenCV (opencv-python 4.5.1.48 pip wheel, CPU)
workload: SpeedTestCV example output on one large chessboard JPEG and one binary PNG: BoofCV 0.38-SNAPSHOT under JMH (avgt, 5 iterations, ms/op) against OpenCV Python calls timed by a script (ms per call). Operations: Gaussian blur radius 5, Sobel, local mean threshold radius 5, histogram, Canny edge chains, external contours, Shi-Tomasi corners, polar Hough lines.
claimed_speedup: Mixed result, ratios derived from page data (OpenCV ms divided by BoofCV ms, from the two readme example outputs). BoofCV faster: good features 38.313 ms vs 277.2 ms (7.2x), Hough polar 743.051 ms vs 3086.3 ms (4.2x), histogram 2.268 ms vs 7.0 ms (3.1x), external contour 47.055 ms vs 83.3 ms (1.8x), Sobel 8.010 ms vs 14.0 ms (1.7x). BoofCV slower: Gaussian blur 36.139 ms vs 12.1 ms (OpenCV 3.0x faster), Canny 142.658 ms vs 61.7 ms (OpenCV 2.3x faster), local mean threshold 20.495 ms vs 15.4 ms (OpenCV 1.3x faster). No OpenCV row for SIFT or SURF (SURF not in the pip wheel; SIFT skipped).
compiler_and_flags: BoofCV 0.38-SNAPSHOT (build.gradle), JDK 1.8 and JDK 11 said to give similar output, JMH 1.19; OpenCV side pinned to opencv-python 4.5.1.48 pre-built wheel by opencv/requirements.txt (rule 1 of the benchmark: pre-built binaries only). The OpenCV figures are on https://github.com/lessthanoptimal/SpeedTestCV/blob/master/opencv/readme.md
tradeoffs: Pure Java, runs on the JVM with JIT warm-up. Gaussian blur rounds results (OpenCV truncates with integer division) and RGB-to-gray is a plain average by default (OpenCV uses a weighted average), per the SpeedTestCV readme. Optional OpenCV interop through JavaCV.
caveats: Weak evidence for a catalogue entry in this category: the numbers are 'Example Output' blocks in two sub-readmes of the author's SpeedTestCV repo (no license shown, last commit 2022-07-28), not a published results table; hardware and CPU model are not stated (the BoofCV block says 'On my system'), and the two blocks may come from different runs or machines. BoofCV is timed with JMH (with warm-up), OpenCV with a hand-written Python loop (mean of 10 time.time() trials after gc.collect, one trial for the histogram, no warm-up) in benchmark.py; that loop has cv2.setNumThreads(0) commented out, so OpenCV runs multi-threaded as shipped. The OpenCV Canny row includes a findContours call to produce pixel chains, to match BoofCV's chain output, and the benchmark file itself lists TODOs. BoofCV 0.38-SNAPSHOT and OpenCV 4.5.1 are years old, current BoofCV and OpenCV releases are not retimed. The comparison is not a win overall: OpenCV is 2-3x faster on Gaussian blur and Canny. None of the rows is a colour conversion or resampler, so the assigned category fits only loosely (Gaussian blur and Sobel are the nearest). The author's fuller page, boofcv.org Performance:OpenCV:BoofCV (2012-era, referenced from a BoofCV mailing-list thread seen only as a search result), is blocked in this environment (EGRESS_BLOCKED) and was not read. A 2012 SURF paper by the BoofCV author (title only, not opened; arXiv blocked) reportedly compares SURF runtimes of several implementations; nothing from it is used here. Retier idea for a session with arXiv or boofcv.org access.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/lessthanoptimal/BoofCV README, then https://github.com/lessthanoptimal/SpeedTestCV and its boofcv/readme.md and opencv/readme.md

name: CompV
baseline: OpenCV (cv::resize bilinear; cvtColor CV_RGB2GRAY, CV_YUV2RGB_I420, CV_RGB2HSV)
workload: 10,000 iterations on a 1282x720 image of: RGB24 to grayscale, YUV420P to RGB24, RGB24 to HSV, and bilinear scaling to 1064x597, CompV (hand-written assembly, SSE/AVX, multithreaded) versus OpenCV.
claimed_speedup: RGB24->Gray 449 ms vs 3086 ms ('almost 7 times faster'); YUV420P->RGB24 968 ms vs 5919 ms ('6 times'); RGB24->HSV 2137 ms vs 15709 ms ('7 times'); bilinear scaling 1474 ms (mt, avx2) vs 4148 ms ('almost 3 times'), and 2645 ms (mt, plain c++) is still faster than OpenCV
hardware: Intel Core i7-4790K @ 4.00GHz (8 CPUs), Apple iMac15,1 running Windows 8 Pro 64-bit
stars_or_usage: 212 stars, 46 forks; code used in the vendor's commercial SDKs
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0 (copyleft, commercial use needs the vendor's licence); README says it is an R&D project with no documentation and is not intended for use by other companies; hand-written assembler and TBBMalloc/TCMalloc are part of the quoted results; large library with GPU back ends.
caveats: The only evidence is the committed result file, dated to a Windows 8 era machine; the OpenCV version, compiler and build flags are not stated and the benchmark driver was not located. The file itself notes CompV results use assembler plus TBBMalloc/TCMalloc. CompV single-thread AVX2 bilinear (5435 ms) is slower than OpenCV's multithreaded 4148 ms, and the bicubic scaling and bicubic rotation rows are marked 'Shame!!' (no CompV result). The README's headline 'up to 50 times faster than OpenCV' is not matched by any row of the result file (the largest ratio there is about 28x, on a feature matcher, and the colour and scaling rows are about 3-11x).
found_via: WebSearch 'FlatCV pure C image processing computer vision library benchmark faster than OpenCV' (result list), confirmed on GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/computer-vision?l=c%2B%2B&q=than+opencv, then README and speed_compare file read

name: CUDARGB2Y
baseline: OpenCV cv::cvtColor (CV_BGR2GRAY, CPU path as called in the repo's main.cpp)
workload: RGB to 8-bit grayscale conversion of one test.jpg: CUDA kernel time per call averaged over 2000 runs after 100 warm-ups, input already resident on the GPU as a texture object, versus cv::cvtColor on a host cv::Mat over 2000 runs; the harness checks pixels agree within 1.
claimed_speedup: 'Roughly 5x to 30x faster than OpenCV's implementation, depending on your card.' (README and main.cpp header; no per-card numbers given)
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: nvcc -O3 --use_fast_math -arch=sm_30 with host g++ -Ofast -march=native -flto (main.cpp header dated Oct 2016)
hardware: not stated (no GPU or CPU model, no OpenCV version)
tradeoffs: NVIDIA GPU only; two-file (CUDARGB2Y.h and .cu) drop-in; default weights match OpenCV, equal weighting optional; useful only when data already lives on the GPU.
caveats: Compares a GPU kernel with input already on the device (no host to device or device to host transfer timed) against OpenCV's CPU cvtColor, so it is not an end-to-end comparison; sm_30 build target is obsolete; no GPU, CPU or OpenCV version recorded; README range is the only number. Sibling komrad36 repos (CUDALERP, CUDAFLERP) make only qualitative claims and were not reported.
found_via: Blogs / talks: query 'RGB to HSV OR grayscale conversion AVX2 NEON "faster than OpenCV" cvtColor C++ library benchmark github' returned the CUDARGB2Y repo; README, main.cpp, Makefile and CUDARGB2Y.cu read

name: cvGPUSpeedup (OpenCV-style wrapper on the Fused Kernel Library)
baseline: OpenCV-CUDA (cv::cuda::resize, convertTo, crop and channel split, each launched as a separate kernel)
workload: GPU pre-processing before a neural network: crop 50 detections from an image, resize with cv::INTER_LINEAR, normalize and split colour channels, as separate OpenCV-CUDA calls versus one fused kernel built by cvGPUSpeedup.
claimed_speedup: '38x times faster' kernel execution for 50 crops of an image on an RTX A2000 12GB; '1/167th of the time' for variable-size crop, resize and normalize in the NSight Systems timelines; unit tests used as benchmarks 'show always positive speedups ranging from 2x to 10000x (in an RTX A2000)', larger the more small kernels are fused.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc -std=c++20 (README build line); tested with CUDA 11.8 to 12.8 and OpenCV 4.8 to 4.11; optimisation flags of the benchmark builds not stated
hardware: NVIDIA RTX A2000 12GB GPU; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: NVIDIA GPU and nvcc only; C++20; the OpenCV-facing wrapper needs OpenCV built with the CUDA modules and mandatory Fused Kernel Library submodule (github.com/morousg/FusedKernelLibrary, header-only C++20); code must be restructured into one fused operation list executed with cvGS::executeOperations on a CUDA stream.
caveats: First-party numbers. The 38x and 167x figures come from README examples and NSight screenshots, not a published table; the 2x to 10000x range comes from running unit tests that the author says can serve as benchmarks (benchmarks/ folder holds benchmark_CPU_OpenCV_vs_cvGS.cu, benchmark_CPUandGPU_cvGS_vs_fk.cu and benchmark_image_resolution_MAD_loop.cu; I did not read them). Gain comes from removing per-kernel launch and memory round trips of many small OpenCV-CUDA calls, so it is largest for chains of tiny kernels; the baseline is unfused OpenCV-CUDA, not a CPU resizer such as ImageMagick or stb_image_resize. Compiler flags and host CPU unstated, so tier C not A.
found_via: Blogs / talks (WebSearch snippet): query 'CV-CUDA image resize color conversion faster than OpenCV benchmark technical blog' returned github.com/morousg/cvGPUSpeedup; repo README and benchmarks folder opened on github.com

name: DeltaCV
baseline: OpenCV (cv::cvtColor RGB2GRAY and RGB2HSV on CPU, and OpenCV chains for fused colour-space plus threshold operations)
workload: CUDA RGB2GRAY and RGB2HSV on a 480x640 image (GTX 1070) versus OpenCV on an i5 7500 CPU; AVX2 fused colour-space plus segmentation functions (ycrcbWithSeg, inRange, weightedGrayWithSeg, grayBRWithSeg) on a 1024x1280 image versus the OpenCV equivalent.
claimed_speedup: GPU RGB2GRAY 0.008-0.010 ms vs 0.340-0.360 ms (README speed-up column says 3.4-45; ms columns imply about 34-45x, derived from page data); GPU RGB2HSV 0.150-0.200 ms vs 3.900-4.400 ms (19.5-29.3x); CPU AVX2 ycrcbWithSeg 0.88-0.90 ms vs 6.68-6.75 ms (7.4-7.6x), inRange 3.5-4.0x
compiler_and_flags: CPU part built with -mavx2 -march=haswell (compiler not stated)
hardware: GPU table: NVIDIA GTX 1070 8G versus OpenCV on Intel i5 7500; CPU SIMD table: CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Small collection of hand-written kernels rather than a full library; CPU kernels are fused operations (colour conversion plus segmentation) so they are not drop-in replacements for single OpenCV calls; GPU path needs CUDA and the transfer cost is not stated.
caveats: GPU kernels are compared with CPU OpenCV, not with OpenCV CUDA or NPP; unclear whether host-device transfers are included; OpenCV version and flags not stated; SIMD table has no CPU model; the RGB2GRAY speed-up cell (3.4 - 45) is internally inconsistent with its timings. Repository last updated April 2019.
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/image-processing?l=c%2B%2B&q=high+performance (listing 'A high performance library for image processing'), then README read

name: fast-srgb8
baseline: naive powf-based sRGB transfer function (reference implementation inside the crate's own benchmark)
workload: Convert linear f32 to 8-bit sRGB (scalar and four-wide SSE2) and 8-bit sRGB to f32, measured with Rust bench harness in ns per iteration.
claimed_speedup: README bench output: f32 to sRGB8 scalar 144 ns/iter vs 971 ns naive (about 6.7x, derived from page data); four-wide 440 ns vs 3,625 ns for four naive calls (about 8.2x, derived from page data); sRGB8 to f32 81 ns vs 4,026 ns (about 50x, derived from page data). README prose says '~5x for conversion to f32->srgb8, ~20x for srgb8->f32'.
tradeoffs: Table-driven conversion, no_std, no libm needed; 8-bit sRGB endpoints only (not a general color-management library). The repo lists three licenses (Apache-2.0, MIT, CC0-1.0); the CC0 option carries no patent grant.
caveats: Baseline is a naive per-call powf implementation written for the benchmark, not a named incumbent library; the numbers do not match the ratios in the README prose (derived ratios are larger). No CPU, compiler or flags stated; the last commit is from 2021. Not compared against ImageMagick, lcms or stb.
found_via: WebSearch: 'sRGB linear conversion OR Oklab conversion SIMD library benchmark' led to the linear-srgb crate; fast-srgb8 found while checking sibling crates for baseline comparisons (README read via raw.githubusercontent.com)

name: FastBoxBlur
baseline: OpenCV cv::blur (box filter)
workload: Box blur with reflection (mirror) padding on 45 RGB images from 1500x1000 to 11400x7600 pixels, box kernel size 2*width-1 (chart in data/bench.png).
claimed_speedup: README Performance section: 'designed to be a portable, easy, and faster replacement of cv::blur, using an i7-10750H, it's around 2x - 3x time faster'. The per-size chart is an image and could not be read as text.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile (not stated as the benchmark build): g++ fastboxblur.cpp -O3 -fopenmp -std=c++17
hardware: Intel Core i7-10750H
tradeoffs: Header-only (fast_box_blur.h), templated on pixel type and channel count, sliding-accumulator box blur plus cache-blocked transposition, N passes. Emulates mirrored border padding without extra memory, but the radius must stay below the image width. No SIMD (the README says SIMD could be faster); OpenMP in the demo build. Box blur only, and README says it is based on bfraboni/FastGaussianBlur.
caveats: Borderline for this category: a convolution/filter kernel, not a resampler or colour transform, included because the assignment asked for convolution kernels versus OpenCV. The only text figure is '2x - 3x' on one laptop CPU; benchmark flags, OpenCV version and OpenCV build (IPP, threads) are not stated and the benchmark driver is not clearly separated from the demo. A kernel as large as 2*width-1 favours an O(1)-per-pixel sliding sum, so typical small kernels were not measured. The README says MIT; the root file listing shows no LICENSE file. Last commit Nov 2022.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'fast Gaussian blur C++ faster than OpenCV GaussianBlur benchmark github box blur SIMD'; README opened

name: FastOpenCV (fastcv kernels)
baseline: OpenCV 4.14.0 cv::resize (INTER_CUBIC, INTER_AREA) and cv::transform, stock build
workload: cv::resize INTER_CUBIC and INTER_AREA x4 on a 1080p image (README table heading says 8UC1), plus cv::transform on 32FC3 (colour matrix), stock OpenCV versus the fastcv drop-in kernel with the same cv::Mat API.
claimed_speedup: resize INTER_CUBIC 3.4 ms -> 0.8 ms (4.1x, bit-exact); resize INTER_AREA x4 0.92 ms -> 0.02-0.25 ms (3.5-18.7x, +/-1 on 0.2% of pixels); transform 32FC3 7.9 ms -> 0.74 ms (10.7x, bit-exact); pow 32F (gamma) 19-22x
compiler_and_flags: g++ (version not stated), fastcv built with -O3 -march=native -fPIC (scripts/build-fastcv.sh); OpenCV built by scripts/build-linux-opt.sh with AVX2 baseline plus AVX512_SKX dispatch, LTO, CUDA 13.3, TBB
hardware: AMD Zen 5 (AVX-512 + VBMI, 32 threads, exact SKU not stated) with NVIDIA RTX 4090, Arch Linux
tradeoffs: Drop-in kernels that need OpenCV headers plus an OpenCV build with the repo's patches for best results; -march=native build so the library is machine specific; requires AVX-512 VBMI for some kernels; Rust FFI crate included.

name: Leptonica
baseline: ImageMagick convert -deskew
workload: Skew detection and deskew of a 'mixed bag' of scanned page files inside OCRmyPDF's pre-processing, Leptonica versus ImageMagick convert -deskew; also the whole deskew plus Tesseract OCR job.
claimed_speedup: Standalone deskew: "around 30-40x faster" than ImageMagick's convert -deskew (PR author's claim, no per-file times). Whole deskew+OCR job: 371 seconds with ImageMagick baseline versus 216 seconds with Leptonica doing the deskew, about 40% less total time.
stars_or_usage: 2.1k stars; used by Tesseract, OpenCV (optional) and jbig2enc per its README
tradeoffs: ANSI C library with packed 32-bit-word image data and 1 bpp document-image focus. The deskew speed comes from a cheaper algorithm (Postl's variance of differential line sums) than ImageMagick's Hough transform, so it targets text pages and is not a general-purpose equivalent. The PR author also reports Leptonica gave better output (ImageMagick sometimes added a halftone pattern to the background after rotation).
caveats: Third-party contributor's pull-request comment from January 2014, closed unmerged in July 2015. No hardware, no Leptonica/ImageMagick/Tesseract versions, no commands, no file set beyond 'a mixed bag of files', no repeat counts. Algorithms differ, so the gap is algorithmic rather than implementation speed, and the process-launch overhead of calling the convert binary is probably part of the ImageMagick side (not stated). The 30-40x claim is quoted from the PR text; the 371 s and 216 s figures include OCR time, so the end-to-end gain is only about 40%. Leptonica's own docs claim DWA morphology is 3-4x faster than its own rasterop morphology (an internal comparison, not recorded as a baseline). No comparison against OpenCV or other image libraries was found. Category set to color-and-resampling because the measured operation is rotation/deskew, though Leptonica is a general image-analysis library (guessed category was image-codecs).

name: LibGaussianBlur (FFT Gaussian blur, from Blur_algorithms)
baseline: OpenCV cv::GaussianBlur
workload: True Gaussian blur of RGB 24-bit images with sigma = sqrt(width) (very large kernels), FFT convolution with pffft (1D, separable) versus cv::GaussianBlur, 46 image sizes from 1500x1000 to 24000x14500 (README text says 45 images up to 11400x7600), Apple M3 Pro 12 cores.
claimed_speedup: README of the archived predecessor Blur_algorithms: 'surprisingly fast is the 1D implementation in pffft compared to OpenCV that is the standard market reference', linear versus exponential growth with size. Timings in py/performance.ipynb (ms, pffft vs cv::GaussianBlur): 2000x1300 11.52 vs 107.43; 6500x4000 114.97 vs 1604.24; 12000x7300 433.94 vs 6317.43; 24000x14500 1728.56 vs 33509.56. Derived from page data: 9x to 20x lower time for every size except the smallest; at 1500x1000 OpenCV was faster (24.97 ms vs 32.05 ms).
hardware: Apple M3 Pro, 12 cores, 16 MB cache setting for PocketFFT
tradeoffs: C++20 library using FFT tiles and pffft (a bundled FFT library); pads images to FFT-friendly sizes, so more memory than direct convolution; Python wheels, WebAssembly and mobile builds provided. The FFT approach pays off only for large sigma; small kernels are the OpenCV regime.
caveats: The numbers live in the archived predecessor repo Blur_algorithms (hard-coded timing arrays in a notebook; that repo shows no license), not in LibGaussianBlur's own README. Compiler, flags, OpenCV version and OpenCV build (IPP, threads, ARM NEON) are not stated. sigma = sqrt(width) means kernels of hundreds of taps, which is the case where direct separable convolution is slowest; the result does not transfer to small sigma, and OpenCV won at the smallest size. Gaussian blur is a filtering kernel, not resampling or colour conversion, so the fit to this category is borderline. The README and the notebook disagree on the size range. Last commit is an automated coverage-badge commit.

name: odiff
baseline: ImageMagick compare (and pixelmatch)
workload: Pixel-by-pixel visual diff of two full-size cypress.io page screenshots and of two 8k water images, writing a diff image, timed end to end with hyperfine.
claimed_speedup: cypress.io screenshots: odiff 1.168 s vs ImageMagick compare 8.881 s (README relative 7.65) vs pixelmatch 7.712 s (relative 6.67). 8k water image: odiff 1.951 s vs ImageMagick compare 9.326 s (relative 5.24) vs pixelmatch 10.614 s (relative 5.50). README text: 'Odiff is 6 times faster than imagemagick and pixelmatch'.
hardware: MacBook Pro 16, macOS 11 Big Sur beta (stated in images/README.md); CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 3.2k stars; used by the Argos visual testing platform (README)
tradeoffs: Command-line tool plus Node bindings (odiff-bin); YIQ NTSC perceptual metric with anti-aliasing detection, region ignoring, cross-format compare (png, jpeg, webp, tiff); single-thread; Zig toolchain with SSE2, AVX2, AVX512 and NEON paths.
caveats: The README table carries no software version and likely predates the Zig and SIMD rewrite (README says originally OCaml, currently Zig), so current numbers may differ. The README relative column does not match the listed means for the water image (9.326/1.951 = 4.78 and 10.614/1.951 = 5.44 vs stated 5.24 and 5.50; cypress 8.881/1.168 = 7.60 and 7.712/1.168 = 6.60, derived from page data). Hyperfine wall time includes image decode, encode and process start-up. No compiler flags or CPU model. Image comparison is only loosely in color-and-resampling (a color-distance task); consider moving it to the image category.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch on news.ycombinator.com for '"times faster than ImageMagick" image processing tool' surfaced the thread 'Imgdiff: Faster than the fastest pixel-by-pixel image difference tool'; imgdiff's README names odiff as the previous fastest tool, so odiff's repo, README and images/README.md were opened on github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com.

name: Photon (photon-rs)
baseline: libvips (vips CLI, Windows vips.exe)
workload: Invert all pixels of one image and save it again, once for a PNG and once for a JPG; Photon timed with criterion (cargo bench), libvips timed with hyperfine on the vips.exe command line.
claimed_speedup: PNG invert and save: Photon 244.87 ms (criterion interval 238.46-254.62 ms) vs libvips 915.1 ms +/- 36.0 ms, about 3.7x faster (derived from page data). JPG invert and save: Photon 117.26 ms vs libvips 84.2 ms +/- 12.0 ms, so libvips is faster there.
tradeoffs: Rust crate that also compiles to WebAssembly for browser and Node.js; about 96 image functions (channel ops, filters, color effects, resize). Native Rust, not a C or C++ API.
caveats: First-party wiki numbers, no hardware, compiler or OS details. The two sides are measured differently: Photon through an in-process criterion loop of open, invert and save, libvips through hyperfine on the vips.exe command line including process start-up. The wiki page says it compares against libvips, ImageMagick and PIL but only libvips numbers appear. Only one of the two workloads is a win (PNG); libvips wins on JPG. The PNG test image is an imgur link, not in the repo, and the current benches/photon_benchmark.rs invert_image opens examples/input_images/underground.jpg, so the wiki PNG numbers may come from an older bench revision. Invert is a trivial per-pixel color op and says little about resampling. Baseline is not ImageMagick or stb_image_resize.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch on news.ycombinator.com for 'Show HN Photon Rust WebAssembly image processing library' surfaced the threads 'Rust/WebAssembly image processing library' and 'I've been developing a WebAssembly image processing library, and its performance...'; repo, wiki Benchmarks page, Cargo.toml and bench source opened on github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com.

name: Pillow-SIMD
baseline: ImageMagick 6.9 (via Wand) in the pillow-perf results; ImageMagick 7.1.1 in the libvips wiki table. pillow-perf also compares Pillow, OpenCV, Skia, libvips and Intel IPP.
workload: Resize of a 2560x1600 RGB image to 26x16, 320x200, 2048x1280 and 5478x3424 with bilinear, bicubic and Lanczos convolution filters, single core, mean of 11 runs (pillow-perf suite).
claimed_speedup: README: 'Pillow-SIMD with AVX2 is always 16 to 40 times faster than ImageMagick and outperforms Skia'; resize 4-6x faster than Pillow. Result file (c5.large.txt), 2560x1600 RGB to 320x200 Lanczos: Pillow 7.0.0.post3 -mavx2 0.00523 s vs Wand (ImageMagick 6.9) 0.10633 s, about 20x (derived from page data); bilinear 0.00192 s vs 0.03792 s; bicubic 0.00313 s vs 0.07111 s; Lanczos to 5478x3424 0.10035 s vs 1.22571 s (about 12x, derived). Independent row in the libvips wiki table (crop, bilinear shrink, sharpen on a 10000x10000 TIFF, 16-core Threadripper PRO 3955WX): pillow-simd 9.5.0 1.51 s vs ImageMagick 7.1.1 convert 4.44 s (about 2.9x, derived).
tradeoffs: Drop-in replacement for Pillow in Python only (must replace the Pillow install; x86 only, SSE4 and AVX2). C core is not a standalone library, so it is not callable from C++ without embedding Python. Pillow license is HPND (listed in the repo as PIL/PILLOW license).
caveats: Benchmark code is public (python-pillow/pillow-perf: run.py suites with Wand and cv2) and result data is checked in, but the C compiler and exact CPU model are not stated (only 'c5.large' and -msse4/-mavx2 labels) and the suite is run by people close to Pillow-SIMD, so C (one step short of A; the libvips table is an independent third-party measurement and could justify B). Wand is the ImageMagick binding, so Python call overhead is included, and the ImageMagick version in the result file is 6.9 (old). The README '16 to 40 times' figure lives on the pillow-perf github.io page, which was not reachable; numbers quoted here come from the checked-in result file. Result file covers Pillow-SIMD 7.0.0; current Pillow-SIMD tracks newer Pillow.

name: quantette
baseline: libimagequant (imagequant crate 4.4.1, the engine behind pngquant); also color_quant 1.1.0 (NeuQuant) and exoquant 0.2.0
workload: 256-colour image quantization plus remapping of 11 Unsplash photos at about 5500 to 6700 px wide and at 1920 px wide, with and without dithering, total ms per image averaged over 30 trials; Wu, k-means and imagequant columns on 4 threads, color_quant and exoquant single-threaded.
claimed_speedup: No dithering, 5663x3769 (Akihabara): Wu sRGB 25 ms, Wu Oklab 80 ms, k-means 97 ms versus imagequant 1044 ms, color_quant 2155 ms, exoquant 4815 ms (imagequant about 10.8x slower than k-means and about 41.8x slower than Wu sRGB, derived from page data). 1920x1278: Wu sRGB 3 ms, Wu Oklab 10 ms, k-means 31 ms versus imagequant 266 ms. With dithering, 5663x3769: Wu Oklab 137 ms, k-means 282 ms versus imagequant 1303 ms.
compiler_and_flags: rustc with -C target-feature=+avx2
hardware: not stated
tradeoffs: Rust crate (no C API verified); no alpha channel support while imagequant has it; Wu sRGB mode is the fastest but has visibly worse DSSIM (for example 0.007178 versus imagequant 0.004436 on Akihabara full size); k-means mode in Oklab matches imagequant DSSIM on most images. Category fit is colour quantization and palette generation rather than resampling.
caveats: Numbers are in the benchmarks doc quantette/docs/Benchmarks and Accuracy.md (read via raw.githubusercontent.com); CPU model and rustc version are not stated, so not tier A. Gap narrows in other harnesses: the imazen/zenquant README (50 images, 2026-03-04, default dithering) lists quantette k-means about 265 ms versus imagequant 546 ms (speed 1) and 315 ms (speed 4), and color_quant at 180 ms, i.e. roughly 1.2x to 2x rather than 10x. The author notes each library behaves differently by options; imagequant ran with defaults at quality 100. With dithering on Futuristic 6000x4000 k-means is 318 ms versus imagequant 360 ms (derived from the dithering time table).

workload: JPEG task: decompress a 2725x2225 JPEG, resize to 720x588 with Lanczos3, recompress at quality 80. PNG task: decompress a 2048x1536 RGBA PNG, premultiply alpha, resize to 720x540 Lanczos3, unpremultiply, compress with zlib level 6.
claimed_speedup: AMD64 JPEG: sharp 88.21 ops/s (file) and 89.63 (buffer) vs imagemagick 16.23 ops/s (file) and gm 21.04 ops/s (file); about 5.4x vs ImageMagick (derived from page data). ARM64 JPEG: sharp 52.42 vs imagemagick 5.85 ops/s (about 9x, derived). AMD64 PNG: sharp 47.17 (file) vs imagemagick 10.37 (file), page speed-up 4.5 vs 1.0. The 'imagemagick' npm baseline spawns the ImageMagick CLI per image, adding process start-up and file I/O overhead, and it is described on the page as unmaintained. Multi-core libvips vs a single-process CLI. Compare libvips entry for the same engine.

name: Smolscale
baseline: libswscale (FFmpeg), Pixman, stb_image_resize, GDK-Pixbuf, SDL_gfx and Skia (as wired into the project's own benchmark harness)
workload: Smooth downscaling of 32-bit RGBA images with the repo's test.c / bench.sh harness (default cases 1920x1080, 3840x2160 and 7680x4320 sources; larger 16383x16383 cases listed as available).
claimed_speedup: No ratio verified. The README and bench.sh contain no results. Snippet only (author's blog post 'Battle of the Bilerps: Image Scaling on the CPU', page blocked here): Smolscale scaled a 16383x16383 image to a much smaller image in roughly 50 ms on 8 threads, about 5.3 gigapixels per second. The relative figures against the other scalers are in the blocked post and were not seen.
compiler_and_flags: README: build with -DSMOL_WITH_AVX2 and -mavx2 for the AVX2 path (runtime pick); other flags not stated
tradeoffs: Three files (smolscale.c, .h, -private.h) plus an optional AVX2 file; copyable into a project. Handles 4-channel 32 bpp packed data (RGBA, ARGB, BGRA) and 3-channel data, premultiplied or unassociated alpha, host-byte-order agnostic, maximum 65535x65535. Quality goal is 'reasonable' (no aliasing), not Lanczos-class. Row-batch and one-shot APIs, easily parallelised. Dual licence: BSD 4-clause (advertising clause) or LGPLv3; closed-source use needs credit or an LGPL library split.
caveats: Snippet-only evidence: the comparison numbers are in a blog post that could not be opened (egress blocked), so the speedup against each baseline is unconfirmed and the tier is capped at C. The benchmark harness is public but no results ship in the repo. README says the AVX2 file was 'mostly just a straight copy of the generic code' at the time. Benchmark is from 2019 era libraries. Last commit April 2023. The harness lists stb_resize as the stb baseline (old stb_image_resize.h is vendored in the repo).

name: zenquant (imazen)
baseline: libimagequant (imagequant crate 4, presets s1 d50, s1 d100, s4 d100); also quantette 0.5 k-means, quantizr, color_quant
workload: 256-colour quantization of 50 images from three corpora (CID22, CLIC 2025, screenshots) with default dithering; scored by butteraugli, SSIMULACRA2, DSSIM, PNG size (zenpng aggressive deflate), GIF size and approximate per-image milliseconds from the multi-threaded default run.
claimed_speedup: Not a speed claim; zenquant's pitch is smaller files and better butteraugli at similar time. README table: zenquant Best butteraugli 3.17, SSIMULACRA2 82.9, DSSIM 0.00058, PNG 586 KB, GIF 764 KB, ~542 ms; imagequant s1 d100 4.10, 82.2, 0.00056, 637 KB, 848 KB, ~546 ms; imagequant s4 d100 4.39, 81.9, 0.00057, 640 KB, 854 KB, ~315 ms; quantette k-means 3.86, 83.9, 0.00050, 616 KB, 799 KB, ~265 ms; zenquant Fast 3.29, 82.6, 0.00069, 582 KB, 749 KB, ~321 ms. Derived from page data: Best PNG is 8% smaller than imagequant s1 d100 at the same ~ms; Fast is 1.7x faster than imagequant s1 d100 (321 vs 546) but no faster than imagequant s4 (315) or quantette (265).
compiler_and_flags: cargo run --example quantizer_comparison --release; runtime SIMD dispatch (AVX2+FMA, NEON, WASM128), no -C target-cpu=native; rustc version not stated
stars_or_usage: crates.io zenquant 0.1.3 (8,680 downloads); default quantizer in zenpng, zengif, zenwebp
tradeoffs: OKLab pipeline with butteraugli-inspired adaptive-quantization masking, median cut, k-means, format-aware palette sort, Floyd-Steinberg and optional Viterbi run optimization; no_std plus alloc, forbid(unsafe_code), SIMD dispatch. AGPL-3.0 network copyleft unless a commercial licence is bought ($1 startup tier); the README says quantette leads on per-pixel metrics and imagequant looks best to the eye.
caveats: Not faster than the incumbents in the README table: zenquant Best takes the same ~542 ms as imagequant s1 and the Fast preset only ties imagequant s4 and loses to quantette. The ~ms column comes from the default multi-threaded run, which the repo's own benchmarks/README.md says is 'fine for the quality columns, not for timing claims'; the single-thread --benchmark mode has no committed result and the cross-library run records no CPU, RAM or compiler. Evidence is first-party and the README notes AI-generated code ('Not all code manually reviewed'). Licence is dual, so the AGPL branch is copyable but with network copyleft.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/imazen/zenquant (README Benchmarks section, benchmarks/README.md, Cargo.toml) plus crates.io API for zenquant

name: zimg
baseline: FFmpeg libswscale 4.0.2
workload: Time in ms to resize a FHD frame to UHD with the Lanczos filter (swscale flags scale=3840:2160:sws_flags=lanczos+accurate_rnd:sws_dither=none), and to convert a FHD frame from BT.709 YUV to BT.2020 (swscale colorspace filter, format yuv420p10).
claimed_speedup: Lanczos FHD->UHD resize: 7.7 ms vs 15.2 ms (Core i7-8565U), 10.8 ms vs 22.2 ms (Xeon Platinum 8176). BT.709 -> BT.2020 conversion: 8.3 ms vs 17.5 ms (i7-8565U), 11.5 ms vs 25.6 ms (Xeon 8176). About 2x on each row (derived from page data).
hardware: Intel Core i7-8565U and Intel Xeon Platinum 8176
tradeoffs: C++17 library covering scaling, colorspace conversion (Rec.709, Rec.2020, SMPTE-C, BT.2020 constant luminance) and depth conversion with dithering; designed to be thread-safe with allocation and I/O separated from processing. The README says it is optimized for Intel architecture. Not a colour management system (no drastic gamut reduction). Autotools is the supported build system.
caveats: README numbers only: no benchmark harness in the repo, no compiler or flags, no frame content or thread count. Compares against an old swscale (4.0.2) and zimg 2.8, so numbers are likely several years old; swscale has had x86 improvements since. WTFPL is a permissive public-domain-style licence not on the OSI list, so verify before copying code.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'swscale vs libyuv vs zimg benchmark RGB to YUV conversion speed comparison repository' (github.com only) surfaced the zimg README Performance section
WebFetch of github.com/sekrit-twc/zimg (candidate from image-scaling library knowledge)
WebSearch: 'libyuv OR zimg faster than swscale benchmark scaling colorspace conversion speed comparison ffmpeg'

name: AVIR / LANCIR (Aleksey Vaneev)
baseline: No third-party incumbent timed; LANCIR is compared only with the project's own AVIR algorithm
workload: Downscale an 8-bit RGB 5184x3456 (17.9 Mpixel) image to 1920x1280 (2.5 Mpixel) with AVIR, single thread and 8 threads; LANCIR (Lanczos resizer in the same header library) is described as faster than AVIR.
claimed_speedup: README: 'LANCIR offers up to three times faster image resizing in comparison to AVIR'; LANCIR 'is likely one of the fastest available for CPUs' (no numbers or named competitor). AVIR timing: 245 ms single thread, 74 ms with 8 threads for the 17.9 to 2.5 Mpixel downscale.
compiler_and_flags: Intel C++ Compiler 18.2 with AVX2 enabled, no explicit SIMD resizing code (AVIR timing only)
hardware: Intel Core i7-7700K, no overclocking (AVIR timing only)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++ (lancir.h has scalar, SSE2, AVX, NEON and WASM SIMD128 paths); AVIR targets high quality (sinc with Peaked Cosine window), orthogonal resizing may show diagonal aliasing; LANCIR precision limited to 8-bit; LANCIR object is not thread-safe.
caveats: Tier D: the only speed comparison is LANCIR vs the author's own AVIR, with no ImageMagick, stb_image_resize or other incumbent timed, so it does not meet the named-baseline rule and is reported only as a directional, attributable claim. Notability is borderline (502 stars, one Hacker News thread 'High-quality pro image resizing / scaling C++ library', which could not be opened). AVIR's own focus is quality, not speed.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch on news.ycombinator.com for 'Show HN image downscaling Lanczos fast C library faster than stb_image_resize' surfaced the thread 'High-quality pro image resizing / scaling C++ library'; repo page, README, LICENSE and lancir.h opened on github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com.

claimed_speedup: No numeric speedup against a named library. README: 'blurs 2000k pixels in ~7ms on all cores of a Ryzen 7 2700X CPU with OpenMP'; the time graph is an image without numbers and shows a 'huge speedup' over true Gaussian blur.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile default target: g++ -O3 -fopenmp -std=c++17 (README does not say which compiler produced the timings)

Lead for the orchestrator: the derivative michelerenzullo/FastBoxBlur (box blur only, based on this code) states in its own README about 2x-3x faster than cv::blur on an i7-10750H; that is a different project and not evidence for this one. name: pic-scale
baseline: fast_image_resize (the baseline series of the repo's speedtest harness; no published result)
workload: No published result found. speedtest/src/runner.rs times RGBA8, u16 and f32 resizes of a 4928x3279 PNG, winter_huge.jpg and sample_fhd.jpg against fast_image_resize 6.0.0, pic-scale-safe 0.1.10 and Apple Accelerate and plots SVG charts.
claimed_speedup: none: no numbers on the README or any page opened
compiler_and_flags: speedtest crate: pic-scale features nightly_f16, rdm, nightly_i8mm, avx, sse; edition 2024; geometric mean of per-iteration times after 10 warm-up runs
tradeoffs: Rust crate with C bindings (picscale/), JS, Python and WASM bindings; runtime-dispatched NEON, SSE4.1, AVX2, AVX-512 and AVX-VNNI; nightly compiler needed for f16, i8mm and AVX-512 paths; 30+ resampling filters and colour-space-aware scaling (Lab, Luv, Oklab, linear, sigmoidal). README table says several paths (planes, SVE, some AVX-512) are only partly SIMD.
caveats: No speed number in the README, repo page, or search results; the speedtest harness writes charts and no checked-in results were found (speedtest folder shows src and Cargo.toml only). Harness bug found: in runner_rgba_fir the baseline destination is allocated with Image::new(target_size.width, target_size.width, ...), i.e. width x width instead of width x height, so for non-square targets fast_image_resize resizes to a different output size than pic-scale, which would skew any chart. pic-scale reuses scratch and destination buffers; fast_image_resize runs with default (single-thread) options. Same author as libblur, sparkyuv and yuvutils-rs.
