name: Fontations (skrifa / read-fonts)
baseline: HarfBuzz OT font backend (hb-ot font functions: cmap lookup, advances, extents, outline drawing)
workload: HarfBuzz perf/benchmark-font (Google Benchmark) run with the Fontations backend versus the native OT backend on Roboto, Roboto Flex, Source Sans Pro, Adobe VF Prototype, Source Serif Variable, Comfortaa, Noto Nastaliq Urdu and Noto Serif Myanmar, default and wght=500 instances: nominal glyph lookup, horizontal and vertical advances, vertical origins, glyph extents, drawing, painting, load face and shape.
claimed_speedup: Mixed, not faster overall. Fontations/OT time ratio (above 1 means Fontations is slower), geometric mean over 12 fixture cases: nominal glyphs 1.53x, horizontal advances 1.39x, vertical origins 1.58x, glyph extents 1.29x, drawing 1.51x, load face and shape 1.05x. Faster rows on the page: varied Roboto Flex (wght=500) vertical origins 1,590 us (OT) vs 1,020 us (Fontations), ratio 0.64x; varied Roboto Flex glyph extents 1,540 us vs 966 us, ratio 0.63x; Adobe VF Prototype CFF2 glyph extents 0.87x (default) and 0.89x (wght=500); nominal glyphs 0.99x on Roboto-Regular and Source Sans Pro; Noto Nastaliq Urdu load face and shape 2,089 us vs 2,055 us. The skrifa crate is stated to be intended to replace FreeType in Google applications, but no FreeType timing is on the page.
compiler_and_flags: Clang 21.1.7 for HarfBuzz, meson --buildtype=release -Db_lto=true -Dfontations=enabled -Dbenchmark=enabled; Rust 1.94.0-nightly (2025-12-20), release profile, fat LTO, one codegen unit; HarfBuzz commit eff2d6b995e0b45e3224079640457fa524c411b9, Fontations commit ec902bd22b5b045e0178bcc3010604e36a7b8342; run as taskset -c 6 b/perf/benchmark-font --benchmark_filter="/(fontations|ot)$" --benchmark_min_time=0.05s --benchmark_repetitions=7
hardware: Linux x86_64, AMD Ryzen 9 5900X (12 cores / 24 threads), pinned to CPU 6, seven repetitions, CPU medians
stars_or_usage: 835 stars; skrifa is the Rust font stack Google builds to replace FreeType in its applications (README)
tradeoffs: Memory-safe Rust, no allocation or copying in read-fonts, usable from C++ only through the HarfBuzz hb-fontations backend or a C wrapper (not a native C API). Hinting, autohinting and variable-font caches are separate costs that the issue does not isolate.
caveats: Weak 'faster' evidence: the page is a performance gap report written by the HarfBuzz maintainer (Behdad Esfahbod, issue dated 4 October 2026, updated 3 October 2026). Fontations is slower than HarfBuzz OT in most rows (unvaried glyf extents and origins about 1.7-1.8x slower, unhinted drawing about 1.5x slower, varied Adobe CFF2 advances 2.74x slower) and faster in a handful of varied-instance cases. Both sides were tuned during the same work (Fontations PR #2197, HarfBuzz PR #6318), so the table is a snapshot of an in-flight optimisation effort. The numbers were read from a fetched copy of the issue page (tables and complete CPU-median list); they cover the font model, not shaping or rasterization, and there is no direct skrifa versus FreeType timing here (the fauntlet README in the repo compares output, not speed; the Chrome blog post that may carry FreeType claims was blocked). Include as a flagged entry only if the orchestrator keeps not-faster results.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Fontations skrifa faster than FreeType glyph outline loading benchmark' surfaced fontations issue #2196 'Font model performance vs HarfBuzz OT: default and varied glyf/CFF/CFF2'; repo README then points to HarfBuzz perf/README.md

name: libutf
baseline: ICU 78.3 (ICU4C: ubrk grapheme break iterator, unorm2 NFC, ucol DUCET collation)
workload: Extended grapheme cluster segmentation (UAX #29), NFC normalization, NFC quick-check and DUCET collation over a small set of short UTF-8 test strings (about 8 to 10 strings, repeated for many iterations; bench/bench_grapheme.c and bench/bench_nfc.c), with ICU run on UTF-16 either including or excluding the UTF-8 to UTF-16 conversion.
claimed_speedup: UTF-8 input: NFC 28 ms vs 59 ms (2.1x faster), NFC quick-check 62 ms vs 237 ms (3.8x), DUCET collation 31 ms vs 40 ms (1.3x), grapheme segmentation 237 ms vs 337 ms (1.4x). Core-to-core with ICU on native UTF-16: NFC 28 ms vs 39 ms (1.4x faster), grapheme segmentation 237 ms vs 277 ms (1.2x faster), but DUCET collation 31 ms vs 22 ms (ICU 1.4x faster).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O2 (bench build lines in bench/bench_grapheme.c and bench/bench_nfc.c; Makefile CFLAGS = -O2 -Wall -Wextra -std=c11 -g). Compiler version and ICU 78.3 build flags are not stated.
hardware: MacBook Pro, Apple M5 Max (stated in README)
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (new repo, first visible commit 2026-03-24); code extracted from TinyMUX, in production there since 2008
tradeoffs: Pure C11, no malloc, no dependencies, 702 KB static library versus about 42 MB for ICU static libraries (README). Works directly on UTF-8 with compressed DFAs, so its advantage is largest when the application holds UTF-8 and ICU has to convert to UTF-16. Covers only grapheme segmentation, NFC, collation (DUCET), classification and case/width tables; no word, sentence or line-break segmentation, no bidi, no locale-tailored collation, no shaping. Unicode 16.0.
caveats: First-party benchmark on a tiny corpus of short hand-written strings repeated many times, so it measures per-call overhead more than bulk throughput. Times are totals for a fixed iteration count, not per-operation rates. The headline 1.3x to 3.8x numbers include ICU's UTF-8 to UTF-16 conversion; core-to-core the gaps shrink (1.2x and 1.4x) and ICU wins collation by 1.4x. ICU build configuration and compiler version are not stated. Category fit is marginal: this is Unicode text segmentation, normalization and collation, not font shaping or rasterization, so the named category baselines (HarfBuzz, FreeType) do not apply; the baseline is ICU, as for uni-algo. NFC and collation are differentially tested against ICU (README), the README lists a 499-test suite, but grapheme segmentation conformance was not checked here.
found_via: WebSearch 'grapheme cluster segmentation line break library "faster than ICU" benchmark site:github.com' surfaced github.com/brazilofmux/utf; README and bench/bench_grapheme.c, bench/bench_nfc.c, Makefile opened via raw.githubusercontent.com; commits page opened.

name: unicode-segmenter
baseline: Intl.Segmenter (the built-in JavaScript grapheme segmenter, ICU in V8/JavaScriptCore/SpiderMonkey); also graphemer, grapheme-splitter, @formatjs/intl-segmenter and a WebAssembly build of Rust unicode-segmentation
workload: Grapheme cluster segmentation (UAX #29) of six corpora (Lorem ipsum ASCII, emojis, Hindi, 'demonic' combining characters, tweet text, code snippet), per-iteration time in Node.js, Bun, Deno and browsers.
claimed_speedup: README: '1.3~2.5x faster than built-in Intl.Segmenter' and '3.5~8x faster than WASM binding of the Rust unicode-segmentation' and '5~48x faster than other JavaScript libraries' in Node.js/Bun/Deno. Archived record 20260727, Apple M4 Pro, node 26.5.0: ASCII 2.65 us vs Intl.Segmenter 5.30 us (2x), emojis 829.70 ns vs 2.24 us (2.7x), Hindi 2.75 vs 5.44 us (1.98x), demonic characters 457.21 ns vs 1.05 us (2.3x), tweet text 4.12 vs 8.53 us (2.07x), code snippet 9.99 vs 18.97 us (1.9x). Record 20251213, Intel Core Ultra 7 258V, node 25.2.1 x64-linux: ASCII 3.71 vs 8.07 us (2.17x).
compiler_and_flags: Not applicable (JavaScript). Each record states the runtime and version in its header (for example 'node 26.5.0 (arm64-darwin)'); `yarn perf:grapheme` reproduces.
hardware: Apple M4 Pro (~4.43 GHz) macOS 26.5; Intel Core Ultra 7 258V (~4.65 GHz) Linux; 48 archived runs from 2024 to 2026 across Node, Bun, Chrome, Firefox and Safari
tradeoffs: Grapheme segmentation only (a few KB; 2,321 bytes min+gzip for the count/split API); keeps lookup tables in typed arrays (about 217 kB JS heap plus 19 kB ArrayBuffers retained, versus 86 kB for Intl.Segmenter). Unicode 17.0.0 data bundled, whereas Intl.Segmenter's Unicode version depends on the host. Works where Intl.Segmenter is missing (Hermes, QuickJS, old browsers). JavaScript only, not usable from C++.
caveats: Benchmark is the project's own, but code, per-run records with CPU model and runtime versions are public, so tier A under the 'whoever ran it' rule. README says browser results vary and that it is 'generally' faster than the built-in segmenter in most browsers 'except the Firefox'. Baseline is the host JavaScript engine's ICU-backed Intl.Segmenter, not HarfBuzz or FreeType and not a C++ library; the other JavaScript libraries are weak baselines. The Rust port fast-grapheme-segmenter is recorded separately. Only a part of the numbers (two record files) was read by the researcher; the 1.3x lower bound of the README range was not located in the two files read.
found_via: Found from the fast-grapheme-segmenter commit message ('directly ported from unicode-segmenter'); README, benchmark/grapheme/_records listing and two record files read via github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com

name: harfbuzz
baseline: rustybuzz (Rust port of HarfBuzz); the guessed 'built-in text shaping' baseline has no published numbers
workload: Time per shaping call (face and buffer creation included in each iteration) of HarfBuzz via harfbuzz_rs versus rustybuzz on 70 text/font pairs (English, Arabic, Hebrew, Hindi, Khmer, Myanmar, Thai; words, sentences, paragraphs, AAT fonts, zalgo, variable fonts), Rust nightly cargo bench on an Apple M1 Pro.
claimed_speedup: rustybuzz README: "At the moment, performance isn't that great. We're 1.5-2x slower than harfbuzz." benches/README.md rows (ns/iter, hb vs rb): english paragraph_long 134,123.63 vs 350,304.15 (2.61x, derived from page data); arabic paragraph_long 164,095.44 vs 336,837.60 (2.05x, derived); hindi paragraph_long 518,143.75 vs 835,427.60 (1.61x, derived); myanmar paragraph_long 1,037,674.90 vs 2,947,060.40 (2.84x, derived); english paragraph_medium 95,546.23 vs 251,779.15 (2.64x, derived); english aat_paragraph_long 427,435.42 vs 536,666.60 (1.26x, derived). Over all 70 rows the rb/hb time ratio has geometric mean 1.76x, median 1.89x, range 0.42x to 4.38x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: cargo +nightly bench (#![feature(test)]); rustc nightly version not stated; HarfBuzz comes from harfbuzz_rs git rev 43f0fb5 (bundled C++ HarfBuzz built by its build script); optimization flags and HarfBuzz version not stated. Harness: harfbuzz/rustybuzz benches/src/lib.rs.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (heading 'Results (on M1 Pro)')
stars_or_usage: 6.1k stars; used in Android, Chrome, Firefox, Flutter, GNOME, GTK, KDE, Qt, LibreOffice, OpenJDK, Godot and Unreal Engine per its README
tradeoffs: The Old MIT licence in COPYING (no SPDX id of its own; effectively MIT). Written in C++ without the C++ standard library (README of the Rust ports notes 'harfbuzz doesn't use C++ std') and amalgamated single-file builds exist. HarfBuzz is optimized for 'robustness, correctness, and performance - in that order'. Malformed fonts fall back to a dummy shaper instead of failing; it has no hinting.
caveats: The only numbers against an outside baseline come from the rival Rust port's own benches (rustybuzz, archived 2026-07-26, tracked HarfBuzz v10.1.0), not from the HarfBuzz project, and rustybuzz admits it is not a faithful port and that HarfBuzz's 'accelerators and caches' were deliberately left out of it, which explains much of the gap. HarfBuzz is faster on 65 of 70 rows; rustybuzz wins five short-text rows (arabic word_1/2/3 at 0.82x/0.87x/0.82x rb/hb time ratio, english aat_word_1 at 0.42x, hindi aat_word at 0.62x, all derived from page data). Each iteration also builds the face and buffer, so setup cost is included for both sides. The HarfBuzz revision bundled by harfbuzz_rs rev 43f0fb5 is not stated and is older than current 14.x, so today's gap may differ. Successor HarfRust's README says it is 'less than 25% slower than HarfBuzz on most common fonts' but backs it only with a Google spreadsheet that was not reachable (docs.google.com blocked). HarfBuzz's own NEWS and perf/README.md contain only before/after self-comparisons (for example 10.3.0: AAT shaping of LucidaGrande 14.6 ms to 5.9 ms) and no comparison with CoreText, DirectWrite, Uniscribe, ICU or FreeType; no hb-subset versus fonttools figure was found. The listed 'built-in text shaping' baseline therefore has no numbers here.
found_via: seed-record pass: awesome-cpp lead https://github.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp#Font, then github.com/harfbuzz/harfbuzz README, NEWS and perf/README.md, then WebSearch 'text shaping benchmark HarfBuzz vs DirectWrite vs CoreText vs rustybuzz' which surfaced the rustybuzz and harfrust READMEs

name: Typst
baseline: pdfLaTeX (pdfTeX 1.40.24, TeX Live 2022) and LuaLaTeX (LuaHBTeX 1.15.0); the same shootout also ran WeasyPrint 68.1, Apache FOP 2.11 and speedata Publisher 5.3.18 Pro
workload: Mail-merge letters (logo, sender and recipient blocks, hyphenated 105 mm body text) built to PDF from XML data, 1 page and 500 pages, timed with hyperfine.
claimed_speedup: Repo README results, macBook Air M4 16 GB, Typst 0.14.2: 500 pages Typst 156.6 ms vs pdflatex 712.3 ms (4.55x), LuaLaTeX 2.356 s (15.04x), FOP 1.607 s (10.27x), speedata sp 4.354 s (27.80x), WeasyPrint 8.672 s (55.38x). 1 page: Typst 105.7 ms vs pdflatex 329.1 ms (3.1x, derived from page data), LuaLaTeX 518.6 ms (4.9x, derived from page data); speedata sp is fastest at 94.5 ms (1.12x faster than Typst).
compiler_and_flags: Not applicable (prebuilt tools); versions are listed in the README (Typst 0.14.2, pdfTeX 3.141592653-2.6-1.40.24, LuaHBTeX 1.15.0, hyperfine 1.17.0, Python 3.14.3).
hardware: macBook Air M4, 16 GB RAM
tradeoffs: A different markup language and ecosystem from LaTeX (fewer packages, no TeX compatibility); incremental compilation and an instant-preview mode are the design goal. Rust, not usable as a C++ library (CLI or Rust crate).
caveats: The benchmark comes from speedata, the maker of a competing engine (speedata/typesetting-benchmark, 1 star), not from the Typst project; the repo has public templates and runner scripts, a named machine and versions, but a single trivial mail-merge workload and a TeX Live 2022 toolchain (pdfTeX 1.40.24), so it is a narrow shootout (tier B, not A, since TeX build flags are not known). Typst's 500-page time (156.6 ms) is barely above its 1-page time (105.7 ms), which suggests startup dominates and something about the template is cheap. The Typst README itself says 'fast compile times thanks to incremental compilation' and gives no LaTeX comparison. Independent caution: texlode/luatex-benchmark (MIT, TUGboat 2026 paper) reports that Typst 0.14 and later is 1.6x to 2.2x slower per incremental edit than 0.12/0.13 at 300 pages on x86 (no change on Apple M4), and its own paper claim of about 1 ms per paragraph in a live LuaTeX session is a different workload; the paper's Typst figures do not reproduce with the repo's script. Baselines are not HarfBuzz or FreeType, although Typst shapes text with a HarfBuzz port internally. Not on the known list.
found_via: WebSearch 'typst compile time benchmark vs LaTeX faster layout performance numbers github' surfaced speedata/typesetting-benchmark and texlode/luatex-benchmark; raw README of both repos read; typst/typst page and commits page read

name: ab_glyph
baseline: rusttype 0.9 (Rust OpenType/TrueType glyph layout and rasterization crate, which describes itself as a pure Rust alternative to FreeType)
workload: Criterion benchmark layout_a_sentence: laying out the glyphs of one sentence into a paragraph with the exo2 font, as .ttf and as .otf.
claimed_speedup: layout_a_sentence exo2-ttf: ab-glyph 11.1us vs rusttype 17.3us (1.56x faster per the table); exo2-otf: ab-glyph 11.1us vs rusttype 98.1us (8.85x faster per the table). README text: 'faster than rusttype using .ttf fonts & much faster for .otf fonts'.
tradeoffs: Rust crate (callable from C++ only through FFI). Loads, scales, positions and rasterizes glyphs; it does no complex-script shaping, so it is not a HarfBuzz replacement. no_std supported with libm. Rasterization comes from the companion ab_glyph_rasterizer crate, which is inspired by font-rs and stb_truetype.
caveats: Baseline is rusttype 0.9, the crate ab_glyph replaced, not HarfBuzz or FreeType; the README does not compare with FreeType. Numbers are first-party and dated May 2020 (the README says performance has likely improved since); CPU, compiler version and flags are not stated. Layout only, glyph rasterization speed is not compared. rusttype is no longer the main Rust incumbent for this work, so the win may be of limited interest.
found_via: github.com/topics/truetype page (opened via WebFetch) after Hacker News queries 'Show HN single-header TrueType font rasterizer C library faster' and 'Show HN FreeType alternative font engine hinting rasterizer benchmark faster' surfaced libschrift and font-rs threads but no ab_glyph thread; no Hacker News thread for this project was found.

name: canvas-hypertxt
baseline: canvas-txt (JavaScript canvas multi-line text library)
workload: Laying out and drawing wrapped text on an HTML5 canvas for strings of 20 to 1800 characters, 5000 iterations each, with font rendering time included.
claimed_speedup: Seconds for 5000 iterations, canvas-txt vs canvas-hypertxt vs canvas-hypertxt with HyperWrapping: 100 char 0.59 vs 0.11 vs 0.11; 300 char 2.63 vs 0.40 vs 0.26; 1000 char 11.19 vs 1.43 vs 0.77 (about 7.8x and 14.5x, derived from page data); 1800 char 22.47 vs 2.29 vs 1.19 (about 9.8x and 18.9x, derived from page data). README also claims HyperWrapping measure-pass gains of over 100x.
tradeoffs: HyperWrapping trains a weighting model to estimate string widths without calling measureText, trading accuracy for speed: wraps slightly early by a word in a small number of cases (README says estimates are within 1% of measured size). Justified text is not supported.
caveats: Baseline is canvas-txt, a niche library whose README is described by the project as not written with performance in mind; not HarfBuzz or FreeType, and text wrapping is at the edge of the shaping and layout category. Browser, machine and Node versions are not stated. The README says it is not a drop-in replacement. It is also the baseline that uWrap claims to beat by about 10x. Repository last committed in November 2023. Found while reading uWrap, not on its own Hacker News thread.
found_via: Hacker News: reached from the uWrap.js thread (item 43583478, surfaced by WebSearch 'Show HN text layout engine paragraph line breaking bidi shaping fast written from scratch') because uWrap names canvas-hypertxt as its baseline; repo README then opened.

name: Canvas-Txt v5
baseline: canvas-hypertxt (standard measuring mode)
workload: Word-wrap of 600-character lorem-ipsum strings at width 400 px, 16px Arial, 5000 iterations per scenario, node-canvas measureText, three scenarios: same text repeated, 500 strings cycled, never-repeating strings (bench/compare.mjs, calls splitText against canvas-hypertxt split).
claimed_speedup: README table, 600-char strings, µs/op: same text repeated 1.1 (canvas-txt v5) vs 0.9 (canvas-hypertxt, hypertxt faster); 500 strings cycled 5.6 vs 48.3 (about 8.6x, derived from page data); never-repeating strings 51.3 vs 566.2 (about 11.0x, derived from page data). canvas-txt v4: 1,566 / 1,423 / 1,382 µs/op.
compiler_and_flags: Node.js (version not stated; engines >=18), node-canvas ^3.2.3, canvas-hypertxt ^1.0.3 and canvas-txt@4.1.1 per packages/canvas-txt/package.json devDependencies; not a compiled benchmark
hardware: Apple Silicon (chip model not stated)
tradeoffs: Per-font width cache and bounded memoised layouts (about 500 entries); memoised layouts come back frozen; the cache must be cleared with clearMeasurementCache() after web fonts load. Uses Intl.Segmenter for Unicode-correct breaks (CJK, Thai, emoji). About 4 kB gzipped, zero dependencies.
caveats: Benchmark code is public (packages/canvas-txt/bench/compare.mjs, read in full) but the CPU model, Node version and run-to-run variance are not stated, so tier C rather than A. It times line-wrapping and measurement only (splitText), not drawing, and not node-canvas fillText, so the lead's second baseline is not measured. The README row shows canvas-hypertxt faster on repeated identical text (0.9 vs 1.1 µs/op) and the README admits hypertxt's estimation mode is faster on long never-seen strings. The script clears only canvas-hypertxt's cache between contenders (hyperClearCache), not canvas-txt's own width cache, though each contender gets 100 warm-up iterations. Never-repeating scenario keeps the vocabulary warm. README numbers are for 600 characters; the script also runs 100 and 1000. Lead said issue #13 holds these numbers: it does not, issue #13 is an unrelated request to return the computed text height. The repo's recent commits are co-authored with an AI assistant. Not C++ (TypeScript); baseline is another JavaScript library, so no std comparison applies.

name: displaywidth
baseline: mattn/go-runewidth (the common Go terminal display-width library) and rivo/uniseg; ICU, HarfBuzz and FreeType are not involved
workload: Measuring monospace display width of Go strings, bytes and runes on mixed, East Asian, ASCII and emoji text, plus truncate-to-width with and without a tail.
claimed_speedup: Go benchmark output in README (Apple M2): String_Mixed 6085 ns/op vs 9970 ns/op (go-runewidth) and 19060 ns/op (uniseg); String_ASCII 54.54 ns/op (2347 MB/s) vs 125.5 ns/op (1020 MB/s) and 1478 ns/op; String_EastAsian 6118 vs 13917 vs 19263 ns/op; TruncateWithoutTail 2456 vs 5182 ns/op, all with 0 allocations.
compiler_and_flags: go test -bench=. -benchmem in comparison/ (go.mod says go 1.18 minimum; the toolchain version actually used is not stated)
hardware: Apple M2 (darwin/arm64)
tradeoffs: Uses Unicode trie lookups from clipperhouse/uax29; README says outputs match go-runewidth and uniseg for most real-world text but differ on some edge cases (East Asian ambiguous width, emoji sequences).
caveats: Own benchmark; benchmark code is public in comparison/ and the CPU is named, but the Go toolchain version is not, so it falls just short of tier A. The baselines are Go libraries, not C++ HarfBuzz or FreeType, and display width is a text-layout primitive rather than shaping.

name: fast-grapheme-segmenter
baseline: icu_segmenter 2.3.0 (ICU4X grapheme cluster segmenter) and unicode-segmentation 1.13.3 (the common Rust crate)
workload: UAX #29 extended grapheme cluster segmentation of about 300-byte samples in nine corpora (English, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Japanese, Korean, Mandarin, emoji, source code), three modes: counting clusters, collecting every cluster, collecting offsets; criterion.
claimed_speedup: README tables, this crate vs icu4x vs unicode-segmentation: counting clusters English 0.05 us vs 1.82 us vs 3.40 us (35.7x and 66.6x), Russian 0.42 vs 2.31 vs 3.77 us (5.4x, 8.9x), Hindi 0.47 vs 1.27 vs 5.01 us (2.7x, 10.6x), emoji 0.35 vs 1.06 vs 2.52 us (3.0x, 7.2x), source code 0.21 vs 2.74 vs 6.05 us (13.1x, 28.9x); collecting every cluster English 1.24 vs 2.28 vs 4.76 us (1.8x, 3.8x), Hindi 1.04 vs 1.33 vs 5.29 us (1.3x, 5.1x), source code 2.20 vs 2.99 vs 7.33 us (1.4x, 3.3x).
hardware: 'x86_64 Linux' only (no CPU model)
tradeoffs: Forward-only grapheme segmentation (UAX #29) only: no word, sentence or line breaking, no bidi. Rust crate, not callable from C++ without an FFI layer. Direct port of the author's JavaScript unicode-segmenter, which compresses the Unicode tables.
caveats: First-party numbers: the repo's own cargo bench (benches/ directory) with criterion on 'x86_64 Linux'; no CPU model, rustc version or flags. The repo has one day of history (initial commit 2026-09-17 'directly ported from unicode-segmenter'). The headline 35.7x/66.6x is a count-only English (mostly ASCII) fast path; for the realistic collect-every-cluster mode the lead over icu_segmenter is 1.3x to 2.0x. Claims agreement with icu_segmenter on Unicode 17 GraphemeBreakTest.txt and 20,000 random strings (tests/conformance.rs, not run by the researcher). Baseline is ICU4X's Rust segmenter, not ICU4C. Not HarfBuzz or FreeType, so the baseline is out of the assignment's list; kept for the text-segmentation part of text layout, next to the already recorded uni-algo, libutf and ICU4X.
found_via: WebSearch 'Unicode line break OR bidi OR grapheme segmentation library benchmark faster than ICU fribidi github C++'; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com, commits page via github.com

name: font-rs
baseline: FreeType (glyph rasterization); freetype-go also mentioned
workload: Rasterizing TrueType glyphs to an anti-aliased coverage bitmap at several pixel sizes, using an accumulation-buffer rasterizer (libart-style exact area coverage) with a SIMD cumulative sum.
claimed_speedup: Repo README: 'extremely promising performance compared with Freetype and freetype-go', no numbers. Snippet only (the author's Medium post was blocked): about 7.6x faster than FreeType at larger sizes with the SIMD speedup, and over 4x faster at 12 pixels/em.
hardware: 2.9 GHz Xeon E5-2690 (search snippet only)
stars_or_usage: 774 stars; algorithm lineage of fontdue and ab_glyph_rasterizer
tradeoffs: TrueType (quadratic) outlines only, no CFF; no hinting; README says 'basically not ready for prime time' and the code is rough. Rust, so C++ use needs FFI; the SIMD cumulative-sum module is C.
caveats: Numbers are snippet only: the blog post (Medium, 2016) could not be opened. The repo's benches (benches/glyph.rs, benches/raster.rs) only time font-rs itself and do not run FreeType, so the FreeType comparison cannot be reproduced from the repo. A secondary summary in the search results says FreeType's rasterizer has been optimized since 2016, so the gap today is likely smaller. Last commit 2020-09-05 per the commits page.
found_via: WebSearch (paper sites blocked): 'font rendering glyph rasterization text layout paper faster than FreeType' and 'Raph Levien Inside the fastest font renderer in the world'; repo page, README and benches read on github.com

name: fontdue
baseline: FreeType 2 (glyph rasterization, via freetype-rs); also rusttype 0.9.2 and ab_glyph 0.2.3 for rasterization, glyph_brush_layout 0.2.0 for layout
workload: Time to produce glyph metrics and bitmaps for the 37-character string 'Sphinx of black quartz, judge my vow.' at 10, 20, 40, 80, 160 and 200 px/em, for an Exo2 TrueType (glyf) font and the OpenType (CFF) version of it; separate layout benchmark of 100-1000 Roboto-Regular characters with word wrapping.
claimed_speedup: README says it 'currently has the lowest end to end latency for a font rasterizer' and gives plots only, no numbers. Reading the plotted lines (approximate, derived from page data): TrueType, fontdue about 15 us vs FreeType 2 about 45 us at 10 px/em (about 3x) and about 235 us vs about 545 us at 200 px/em (about 2.3x); OpenType/CFF, fontdue about 12 us vs FreeType about 135 us at 10 px/em (about 11x) and about 220 us vs about 625 us at 200 px/em (about 2.8x). Layout plot: fontdue about 24 us vs glyph_brush_layout about 139 us at 1000 characters (about 5.8x, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Rust, no_std, pure-Rust rasterizer and naive layout only; no text shaping (author points to Cosmic Text for that), no hinting. Fonts are fully parsed into custom structures on load (slow, allocating load is an explicit non-goal to fix), so it wins on per-glyph latency, not load time. Not directly usable from C++ without writing an FFI layer.
caveats: Evidence is plots in /images (rasterize_glyf.png, rasterize_cff.png, layout.png) with no table, CPU model, compiler or flags. Benchmark code is public (dev/benches/rasterize.rs and layout.rs, criterion, FreeType benchmark behind the freetype_benchmark feature, freetype-rs 0.26). The FreeType side calls load_char with LoadFlag::RENDER only, so FreeType runs with its default hinting on while fontdue does not hint, and set_char_size is called inside the timed loop; this is not an apples-to-apples comparison. Numbers above are eyeballed from the chart images. fontdue began as a fork of font-rs and was rewritten; font-rs itself is a separate entry.
found_via: WebSearch (paper sites blocked): 'fontdue fastest font rasterizer benchmark vs FreeType ab_glyph'; README and dev/benches read on github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com

name: ICU4X
baseline: ICU4C (line break and word break iterators)
workload: Line and word segmentation (UAX #14 and UAX #29) of non-complex-script text and of Chinese text, ICU4X segmenter versus ICU4C equivalents.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: 'line and word segmenters are 19.1% and 52.2% faster in non-complex scripts and 46.9% and 32.1% faster in Chinese than the equivalents in ICU4C, respectively' (ICU4X 1.2 announcement on the Unicode blog).
stars_or_usage: 1.9k stars; maintained by the Unicode Consortium
tradeoffs: Implemented in Rust with Diplomat-generated C and C++ headers (ffi/capi), so callable from C++ but needs a Rust-built library. Design goals are small, modular code and pluggable locale data. The segmenter covers grapheme, word, sentence and line breaking; normalizer, collator and other components also exist. The speed claim found concerns only the segmenter.
caveats: The percentages appear only in a web-search result snippet of blog.unicode.org (ICU4X 1.2 announcement); that site and the numbers could not be opened from this environment (egress blocked), and the GitHub repo, the 1.2.0 release page and issue #66 carry no ICU4C comparison numbers (components/segmenter/benches/bench.rs exists but is Rust-only). Test data, hardware, compiler and ICU4C version are unknown, and the 2023 numbers may be stale. A verifier with blog access should confirm the quote. Category fit is marginal: Unicode segmentation, not shaping or rasterization. Rust implementation, with C++ bindings, not a native C++ library.
found_via: WebSearch 'ICU4X benchmark faster than ICU4C normalizer OR segmenter OR collator OR "case mapping" performance numbers' (snippet from blog.unicode.org 2023/04 ICU4X 1.2 post); repo page, segmenter and ffi/capi directories and commits page opened on github.com.

name: kb_text_shape
baseline: HarfBuzz
workload: OpenType text segmentation and shaping; the author's claimed run used HarfBuzz's own test suite extended with the author's tests, while the HarfBuzz maintainer's run used Roboto-Regular (paragraphs and single words), Amiri-Regular (Arabic), Gulzar-Regular (Urdu and English) and NotoSansDevanagari-Regular (Hindi words).
claimed_speedup: No speedup verified. The kb repo README and header carry no benchmark numbers. The page at benchmark_url, a HarfBuzz maintainer's comparison, shows kb slower than HarfBuzz: HarfBuzz 2.9x faster on Roboto-Regular paragraph text, 3.3x faster word by word, kb about 20% slower on Amiri-Regular, kb 6.6x slower on Gulzar-Regular Urdu, kb 160x slower on Gulzar-Regular English text, kb 2x slower on NotoSansDevanagari-Regular, and kb needs 40x to 760x more time to load a font. See caveats for the author's own opposite claim, which this session could not open.
compiler_and_flags: Author's claim only (not opened): clang 20 on Linux, flags not stated. HarfBuzz maintainer run: compiler and flags not stated.
hardware: Author's claim only (not opened): Ryzen 9 5900HX. HarfBuzz maintainer run: CPU not stated.
tradeoffs: Single-header C/C++ library (about 22k lines at announcement; header is v2.28e) that bundles Unicode segmentation and OpenType shaping with no dependencies. README says it does not handle rasterization, paragraph layout or system font loading. The header states it gives NO SECURITY GUARANTEE and must not be used on untrusted font files. HarfBuzz maintainer notes it copies whole font files into memory and lacks cluster information needed for cursor positioning, selection and editing.
caveats: Disputed speed claim, kept so the orchestrator can decide. A WebSearch result snippet attributed to the author (X post and developer blog, both unreachable here: x.com and handmade.network are blocked) says kb is on average 4.5x faster than HarfBuzz at shaping, measured on HarfBuzz's test suite extended with the author's own tests, Ryzen 9 5900HX, clang 20, Linux. The number 4.5x was not seen on any page opened this session. The only opened comparison, written by the HarfBuzz maintainer (a party with an interest in the result) in July 2025 against the release current at that time (version not stated), found kb slower on every listed font and workload, with crashes in some test suites. Later kb releases (the header is v2.28e now) may have changed this. A search snippet (page not opened) says HarfBuzz added a kb backend to its own perf benchmark suite (perf/README.md in the HarfBuzz repo describes that suite); running it would settle the question. Best treated as reference or a flagged entry, not a verified win.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch (allowed_domains news.ycombinator.com) 'Show HN text shaping library faster than HarfBuzz' surfaced the thread 'Kb_text_shape: Harfbuzz like single file C/C++ text shaping library' (item 46750420); a second WebSearch 'kb_text_shape benchmark vs HarfBuzz shaping speed single-header' surfaced the claim snippet and the HarfBuzz discussion 5375.

name: msdfgl
baseline: msdfgen (Chlumsky's CPU multi-channel signed distance field generator, single-threaded and OpenMP builds); incumbent for MSDF font atlas generation, not one of HarfBuzz or FreeType
workload: Generating an MSDF texture for ASCII characters 0-127 of the font DejaVu Sans at four scale factors (1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0), mean of 100 runs, OpenGL context creation and destruction time and shader compilation excluded.
claimed_speedup: Chart numbers in README image (msdfgl vs msdfgen vs msdfgen with OpenMP): scale 1.0 0.0081 s vs 0.4890 s vs 0.1334 s; scale 2.0 0.0164 s vs 1.9390 s vs 0.5182 s; scale 4.0 0.0645 s vs 7.7407 s vs 1.9939 s; scale 8.0 0.2345 s vs 31.0000 s vs 8.0000 s (the two msdfgen values at 8.0 were extrapolated by the author). Ratios (derived from page data): about 60x, 118x, 120x and 132x faster than single-threaded msdfgen, and about 16x, 32x, 31x and 34x faster than OpenMP msdfgen.
hardware: Core i7 8550m (as written in README) with Intel UHD Graphics 620, Debian Linux
tradeoffs: GPU implementation written from scratch in C; needs an OpenGL 3.3 core or OpenGL ES 3.2 context. The algorithm was reworked to run in shaders: no cubic Bezier segments (so CFF/PostScript-flavoured OpenType outlines are not handled), constant memory, no pointers. Shader compilation takes about one second once. Output is a ready-to-use GPU atlas and index texture, so no upload step.
caveats: First-party benchmark on one weak integrated GPU and one laptop CPU; the benchmark code, compiler and flags for msdfgen and msdfgl are not given. The README says the msdfgen timing excludes transferring bitmaps to a texture whereas msdfgl's includes being render-ready. Largest-scale msdfgen points are extrapolated, not measured. Image quality parity with msdfgen (error correction, cubic segments) is not evaluated. Baseline is msdfgen, not FreeType or HarfBuzz, and the speedup is GPU versus CPU rather than a like-for-like algorithm win. Numbers were read from the chart image /img/benchmarks.png in the README (labels printed on the bars).

name: Parley
baseline: cosmic-text 0.19.0 (pop-os/cosmic-text), the other Rust rich-text shaping and layout library; both sit on HarfRust shaping
workload: Shaping and laying out text in six corpora (Latin, pure-RTL Arabic, bidirectional Arabic plus Latin, CJK, ZWJ emoji, Devanagari) at paragraph and 10,000-line document scale with warm and cold caches (parley 0.11.1 vs cosmic-text 0.19.0); a second, terminal workload measured with criterion.
claimed_speedup: flui PR 1276 (merged 2026-09-23): 'parley wins on timing across all six corpora (2.4x-8.4x faster)', final figures 2.4x-9.0x faster after methodology corrections, and 1.2x-4.2x less memory. massive PR 154 (merged 2026-09-15, criterion, M-series Mac, bundled JetBrains Mono 13 px): parley wins full mixed line (~4.8x), full-screen throughput (~2x) and fallback stress (~2.7x); cosmic-text wins the single-cluster hot path (~16%) and cold FontSystem construction (~600x).
hardware: PR 1276: 'an otherwise-idle machine' (no CPU model); PR 154: 'M-series Mac'
tradeoffs: Rust-only (not callable from C++ without bindings). Depends on Fontique, HarfRust, Skrifa and ICU4X. Larger binary than fontdue-style rasterizers (a separate PR measured +40% binary size when replacing fontdue with parley and swash). cosmic-text starts faster cold (FontSystem construction) and wins the single-cluster hot path.
caveats: Third-party measurements, both from downstream projects' own research PRs, not from the Parley project and not peer reviewed. PR 1276 is co-authored with an AI assistant, uses a custom harness (not criterion), states no CPU or rustc flags, and went through two rounds of self-correction (an O(n squared) cost in parley's single-Layout approach and a memory-retention asymmetry); its raw data sits in tools/text-spike/ of the flui repo and was not opened. flui issue 931 relays an unverified downstream report that floem found parley '93% slower on Arabic wrap' and says not to cite it as settled. A bevy issue (21765) has only qualitative 'significantly better' remarks. Baseline is cosmic-text, not HarfBuzz or FreeType. Not on the known list.
found_via: WebSearch 'text layout benchmark cosmic-text parley swash skrifa Pango comparison results performance'; flui PR 1276, flui issue 931, massive PR 154, bevy issue 21765, linebender/parley README and commits page read

name: rustybuzz-wasm
language: Rust (compiled to WebAssembly, driven from NodeJS)
baseline: harfbuzzjs (HarfBuzz compiled to WebAssembly, driven from NodeJS); also the HarfBuzz command-line tools spawned per line, opentype.js and fontkit
workload: Shaping 100 lines of text with 100 words per line (65,732 Unicode code units), measured as items per second from NodeJS; several runs in randomized order.
claimed_speedup: README prose: 'rustybuzz-wasm would appear to be 1.5 times faster than harfbuzzjs'. Table in the introduction: rustybuzz_wasm_rusty_shaping 218,840 Hz vs harfbuzzjs_shaping 176,392 Hz (about 1.24x, derived from page data); bar-chart rows 220,399 Hz vs 143,434 Hz (about 1.54x, derived from page data). The same tables show 'over 12 times' against the HarfBuzz command line (harfbuzz_shaping 17,553 Hz), which the author says is dominated by spawning one process per line and re-reading fonts and 'does not tell you how fast HarfBuzz itself is'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark; README says to build with 'wasm-pack build --target nodejs' (release) because debug builds are orders of magnitude slower. Node.js version not stated.
hardware: '2015 customer grade, not fast, not new, not fancy laptop' (no CPU model)
tradeoffs: Not feature-complete with rustybuzz: values cross the WASM boundary as JSON and hex-encoded strings; the README says harfbuzzjs does not allow arbitrarily long lines and does not support font features, and that rustybuzz-wasm is not feature-complete with rustybuzz yet. The repo also does SVG glyph rendering via ttf-parser and line wrapping via textwrap. Needs a Rust toolchain and wasm-pack to build; WASM artifacts are committed and may be unoptimized. Not callable from C++.
caveats: Weak evidence: the benchmark code is not in this repo (README links loveencounterflow/hengist, dev/glyphshapes-and-typesetting-with-harfbuzz/src/textshaping.benchmarks.coffee; that file was not opened). No CPU, Node version or font file is given. The win over the nearest comparable baseline (harfbuzzjs) is only about 1.2x to 1.5x; the 12x to 17x figures are against a per-line process-spawning command-line setup and say nothing about HarfBuzz itself. The LICENSE file contains the placeholder text 'the liecense goes here', so no license is granted (rustybuzz itself is MIT). Last commit February 2022, and the README says it is a fragmentary work in progress. Separately, HarfBuzz's maintainer reports (harfbuzz/harfrust discussion 257, 2025-09-10) that the Rust port HarfRust is within about 25% of, i.e. slower than, native HarfBuzz, so this is a WASM-versus-WASM result only.
found_via: WebSearch 'harfrust OR rustybuzz benchmark vs HarfBuzz shaping speed results table' surfaced the repo; README and LICENSE read via raw.githubusercontent.com and github.com

name: sigilbuzz
baseline: rustybuzz (Rust port of HarfBuzz); HarfBuzz itself is not measured
workload: Shaping the same 200-codepoint string per script through sigilbuzz and rustybuzz back to back (Latin Open Sans with liga and kern, Arabic Amiri, Devanagari Noto, Khmer Noto, Hebrew Noto), Criterion medians from the 0.6.0 release.
claimed_speedup: Faster than rustybuzz on two of five scripts: Latin 11.39 us vs 15.03 us (page ratio 0.76x, about 1.32x faster, derived from page data) and Hebrew 10.99 us vs 17.28 us (page ratio 0.64x, about 1.57x faster, derived from page data). Slower on the other three: Arabic 290 us vs 108 us (2.70x slower), Devanagari 419 us vs 85.8 us (4.89x slower), Khmer 91.6 us vs 49.0 us (1.87x slower).
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench with Criterion; rustc version and profile flags not stated
hardware: maintainer's macOS arm64 workstation; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Pure Rust core (no_std, no runtime dependencies, deterministic output). C and C++ callers go through the sigilbuzz-capi crate, which exports HarfBuzz hb_* symbols so it can be linked in place of libharfbuzz. Pre-1.0 API, no bug-for-bug compatibility with older HarfBuzz. Also ships a subsetter, WOFF/WOFF2 wrap and unwrap, UAX 14 line breaking, hyphenation, a CPU rasterizer and a Slug-style GPU outline encoder.
caveats: Baseline is rustybuzz, not HarfBuzz or FreeType; the benchmark never runs the sigilbuzz C API against libharfbuzz. rustybuzz's own README (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/harfbuzz/rustybuzz/main/README.md) says it is 1.5-2x slower than HarfBuzz and recommends HarfRust instead, so nothing here shows sigilbuzz beating HarfBuzz. The win is mixed: it loses to rustybuzz on Arabic, Devanagari and Khmer by 1.9x to 4.9x. Numbers are first-party, from one unnamed Apple arm64 machine, one 200-codepoint input per script; the repo is about one day old with 0 stars. Kept only as a registry-found C-callable HarfBuzz alternative with a published, honest comparison; expect a keep-and-document decision at best.
found_via: crates.io API query q=harfbuzz (sigilbuzz-capi, 'HarfBuzz-symbol-compatible C API ... Drop-in -lharfbuzz replacement'), then github.com/Oneiriq/sigilbuzz README and docs/PERFORMANCE.md

name: SixLabors.Fonts
baseline: HarfBuzz via HarfBuzzSharp 14.2.1.1 (native HarfBuzz called from .NET, single-run text shaping)
workload: End-to-end shaping of one short text run per script (Latin, Arabic, Hebrew, Thai, Hangul, Devanagari, Khmer, Myanmar, Myanmar Zawgyi, Balinese), same font file bytes on both sides, BenchmarkDotNet on .NET 10.
claimed_speedup: Release post for Fonts 3.1.0, as quoted by a search-result snippet: on .NET 10 it wins three of the ten scripts outright and runs within 12% in another four; time ratios (Fonts over HarfBuzzSharp) Devanagari 0.83x, Balinese 0.88x, Hebrew 0.98x, Myanmar Zawgyi 0.95x, Thai 1.09x, Myanmar 1.10x, Khmer 1.12x (three scripts not quoted).
compiler_and_flags: BenchmarkDotNet 'Gate' job: 3 launches, 5 warmup and 15 iterations on the host .NET 10 runtime (read from tests/SixLabors.Fonts.Benchmarks/SixLabors.Fonts.Benchmarks/Config.cs); no extra compiler flags
stars_or_usage: 350 stars; managed text layout engine for the SixLabors.ImageSharp.Drawing stack
tradeoffs: Pure managed .NET shaper with no native dependency, so it ships to any .NET 8+ target; it covers GSUB/GPOS and complex scripts, but the glyph output is not guaranteed identical to HarfBuzz; the Six Labors Split License gives Apache-2.0 terms only to qualifying open-source use and requires a paid licence for other commercial use, so it is not an OSI licence (no SPDX id; license field left null).
caveats: Snippet only: sixlabors.com is blocked here, so the ratios come from a web-search result summary of the release post and were not seen on the page; the three remaining scripts (Latin, Arabic, Hangul) were not quoted and by the post's own wording trail HarfBuzz by more than 12%, so the honest claim is competitive, not faster overall; the quoted ratios list four values below 1.0 (Devanagari, Balinese, Zawgyi, Hebrew) while the summary says three outright wins, so the snippet is internally inconsistent. The benchmark code is public (ShapeTextBenchmark.cs sets HarfBuzz via HarfBuzzSharp as the BenchmarkDotNet baseline, shaping one short run per script) but the repo does not carry result files, CPU model or OS, so tier A is not met.

name: text-shaper
baseline: harfbuzzjs (HarfBuzz compiled to WebAssembly, driven from JavaScript); opentype.js also compared
workload: OpenType shaping of word, sentence and paragraph texts in Latin, Arabic, Hebrew, Hindi, Thai, Khmer, Myanmar and CJK with Noto fonts, plus glyph path extraction and text to SVG, run under Bun with a batch timer (bench/shaping.test.ts).
claimed_speedup: README table, text-shaper vs harfbuzzjs: path extraction 16x faster, text to SVG 1.2-1.5x, Latin shaping 1.5x, Arabic 1.2x, Hebrew 1.6x, Hindi 3.6x, Myanmar 10.5x, CJK 1.3-1.5x. Versus opentype.js: 4x to 86x faster.
tradeoffs: Pure TypeScript (zero dependencies, runs in browsers and Bun/Node), so not usable from C++. Also does TrueType hinting and FreeType-style or libass-style rasterization. Young project (npm 0.1.x).
caveats: The baseline is the WebAssembly build of HarfBuzz called through the harfbuzzjs API, and each timed call creates a buffer, adds text, shapes and reads the result, so JavaScript-to-WASM boundary overhead is part of what is measured; this is not a comparison with native HarfBuzz, which is faster than both in practice. No hardware, Bun version or runtime flags are stated. Only 3 timed iterations per benchmark in the harness. Test fonts and texts come from a reference/rustybuzz/benches path that is not in the repo tree I opened.
found_via: Linked as 'text-shaper (a HarfBuzz alternative)' from the diffusionstudio/slug-webgpu README, found by WebSearch 'Slug library GPU glyph rendering directly from outlines'; README and bench/shaping.test.ts read via npm registry metadata, github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com

name: TiTanF
baseline: RustType and ab_glyph (widely used pure-Rust glyph rasterizers); Fontdue also measured; FreeType is not included
workload: Rasterizing an 84-character string of mixed CJK and Latin characters with NotoSansSC-Medium at 10px, 200px and 320px.
claimed_speedup: README table: 10px 71.0 us (TiTanF) vs 245.6 us (RustType) and 222.6 us (ab_glyph); 200px 1.45 ms vs 3.21 ms and 3.07 ms; 320px 3.13 ms vs 7.27 ms and 6.77 ms; Fontdue is faster at 10px (54.3 us) but slower at 200px (1.60 ms) and 320px (4.02 ms).

caveats: Own-repo benchmark with no compiler flags, CPU or run count in the README, and only one font and string; baselines are other Rust rasterizers, not FreeType, so the claim does not transfer to the stated FreeType baseline. Tiny, new project (3 stars).

name: ttf-parser
baseline: FreeType (FT_Load_Glyph with FT_LOAD_NO_SCALE, glyph outlining); stb_truetype also compared
workload: Time to outline every glyph of a font (callbacks that only count move/line/quad/cubic segments) for glyf, glyf with gvar variations, CFF and CFF2 fonts; benchmark is C++ (benches/outline/outline.cc, Google Benchmark) calling FreeType, stb_truetype and the ttf-parser C API.
claimed_speedup: x86 (AMD 3700X), ms to outline all glyphs, ttf-parser vs FreeType: glyf 0.901 vs 1.171, gvar 2.972 vs 4.132, CFF 1.197 vs 5.647, CFF2 1.968 vs 6.392. ARM (Apple M1): glyf 0.550 vs 0.854, gvar 2.270 vs 4.594, CFF 1.054 vs 5.223, CFF2 1.765 vs 5.995. Derived from page data: x86 1.30x, 1.39x, 4.72x, 3.25x; M1 1.55x, 2.02x, 4.96x, 3.40x. On plain glyf, stb_truetype is faster than ttf-parser on x86 (0.675 ms) but slower on M1 (0.703 ms).
compiler_and_flags: Release builds per benches/outline/README.md (cargo build --release for the C API, meson --buildtype release); compiler names and versions not stated; FreeType is the system freetype2 library (>=2.8) and its version is not stated
hardware: AMD 3700X (x86) and Apple M1 (ARM)
tradeoffs: Parser and outliner only: no rasterization, no shaping, no hinting. Safe Rust, zero allocation, zero dependencies; C API is basic. The repo is in maintenance mode (bug fixes only, no new features or performance work) and recommends fontations (read-fonts and skrifa) for new projects.
caveats: The performance table is no longer in the current README; it is in tagged releases (read from v0.25.1, same table in v0.20.0). The author's own note under the table: 'FreeType is surprisingly slow, so I'm worried that I've messed something up.' FreeType is only asked for unscaled outlines, which is a narrow task (not rasterization). Benchmark code is public and CPUs are named, but compiler and flags are only 'release', so this sits just under tier A. Wins on plain glyf are modest (1.3x to 1.55x).

name: Typr.js
baseline: opentype.js (the widely used JavaScript OpenType font parser; HarfBuzz and FreeType are not measured)
workload: Parsing TTF/OTF/TTC/WOFF font files into a JavaScript font object, compared with opentype.js; the README gives no corpus, machine or timing table.
claimed_speedup: README: 'ultra fast (2x to 5x faster parsing than opentype.js)'

name: ucstrcase
baseline: icu::UnicodeString::caseCompare (ICU4C); strcasecmp also timed
workload: Case-insensitive comparison of generated UTF-8 strings, generated ASCII strings and worst-case matching UTF-8 strings (README timing loop; sizes and iteration counts not stated).
claimed_speedup: README: '5x-10x faster than icu::UnicodeString::caseCompare'. Timings: generated UTF-8 225 ms vs 3604 ms for ICU (strcasecmp 368 ms); generated ASCII 194 ms vs 4486 ms (strcasecmp 360 ms); worst-case matching UTF-8 3069 ms vs 12730 ms (strcasecmp 1988 ms). Ratios (derived from page data): about 16x, 23x and 4.1x faster than ICU.
tradeoffs: C library (usable from C++; vcpkg port files are in the ports directory) for caseless UTF-8 comparison using perfect hashing, adapted from Charlie Vieth's strcase (Go). Handles Unicode simple case folding only as implemented by its tables; not a full-collation or normalization-aware comparison. Worst case is about 50% slower than strcasecmp, which ignores non-ASCII.
caveats: README gives timings with no hardware, compiler, flags, workload sizes, ICU version or benchmark source link, so numbers are unverifiable first-party figures. The text's '5x-10x' headline is inconsistent with its own table (ratios from 4.1x to 23x). Only 8 commits, all on one day in July 2024. Category fit is poor: case-insensitive string comparison, not shaping, rasterization or layout; probably belongs with string or Unicode utilities.
found_via: WebSearch 'C++ Unicode library case folding normalization "faster than ICU" "utf8proc" benchmark github'; README fetched via raw.githubusercontent.com and repo and commits pages opened.

name: ugrapheme
baseline: PyICU (ICU character BreakIterator); also pyuegc, uniseg and grapheme, the other Python grapheme splitters
workload: Splitting the string 'Hello 👩🏽‍🔬! 👩🏼‍❤️‍💋‍👨🏾 अनुच्छेद' into extended grapheme clusters (UAX #29) in IPython %%timeit.
claimed_speedup: README: ugrapheme grapheme_split 337 ns vs PyICU 2.84 us (about 8x); pyuegc 8.19 us (24x); uniseg 14.6 us (45x, also splits Devanagari conjuncts incorrectly); grapheme 17.4 us (52x, also incorrect).
tradeoffs: Cython extension with sparse bitmap property tables (under 11 KB) and a small DFA; passes the Unicode 16.0 UAX #29 grapheme break tests; behaves like a Python str with grapheme indexing; needs a compiled wheel.
caveats: Single short string, interactive %%timeit, no hardware, CPU or Python version stated; the PyICU run pays UnicodeString conversion cost per call (the README notes this itself), so the 8x ICU gap is partly binding overhead. Last commit 2024-10-28.
found_via: Fetched raw README after browsing github.com/topics/grapheme-clusters

name: uni-algo
baseline: ICU (word break and extended grapheme cluster break iteration over UTF-16 text)
workload: Unicode text segmentation (UAX #29 word breaks and extended grapheme cluster breaks) over a 'real text' sample in UTF-16, five consecutive runs per configuration.
claimed_speedup: MSVC 19.12 x64, first run: word breaks 2355.47 (uni-algo) vs 11379.4 (ICU), ~4.8x; grapheme breaks 2067.16 vs 5600.95, ~2.7x. MSVC 19.12 x86: word breaks 2544.55 vs 13137.1, ~5.2x; grapheme breaks 2239.48 vs 6766.44, ~3.0x (ratios derived from page data; units are not stated, lower is assumed better).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 19.12 (Visual Studio 2017 15.5.5), x64 and x86, flags not stated; GCC 7.3 -O3 rows exist but the ICU column is 0 there (ICU not built under MinGW)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 library with optional compiled Unicode data, UTF-8/16/32 support and safe iterators with bounds checks in debug. The README lists the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm and the Line Breaking Algorithm as planned for future versions, so it does not yet cover bidi or line breaking, only word and grapheme segmentation (plus case, normalization and collation). Dual licensed Public Domain or MIT.
caveats: Category fit is weak: the benchmarked task is Unicode segmentation, a pre-step of text layout, not font shaping or rasterization, and the baseline is ICU rather than HarfBuzz or FreeType. Results use 2018-era toolchains (GCC 7.3, MSVC 2017), and the perf commits date from April 2023. The result file states no units, no CPU model, no ICU version and no description of the text sample; ICU was measured only under MSVC. The author calls his own perf test 'a mess', and the README claims only performance 'at least the same as other implementations'. Only the UTF-16 segmentation test exists because ICU cluster breaks do not support UTF-8.
found_via: WebSearch 'bidi line break grapheme library C benchmark faster than ICU FriBidi github' surfaced the repo; then read README (Performance section), perf/main.cpp and perf/result/segment_utf16.md

name: uniwidth
baseline: mattn/go-runewidth (the common Go terminal display-width library) and rivo/uniseg; ICU, HarfBuzz and FreeType are not involved
workload: StringWidth and RuneWidth on ASCII, CJK, mixed, emoji, flag, ZWJ and real-world TUI strings in a separate bench/ module.
claimed_speedup: bench/README on Intel Core i7-1255U (Windows, amd64): ASCII short 9 ns vs 107 ns (go-runewidth) and 165 ns (uniseg); ASCII long (228 chars) 340 ns vs 5,380 ns and 8,058 ns; CJK short 96 ns vs 347 ns and 379 ns; mixed short 173 ns vs 469 ns and 632 ns; emoji short 158 ns vs 380 ns and 534 ns; ZWJ strings about 1x vs go-runewidth (323 ns vs 326 ns); top-level README headline '3-46x faster than go-runewidth'.
compiler_and_flags: go test -bench=. -benchmem -count=5 -run=^$ in bench/ (library requires Go 1.25+; exact toolchain version not stated)
hardware: Intel Core i7-1255U, Windows, amd64
tradeoffs: Four-tier lookup tables plus 8-byte SWAR ASCII fast path with zero dependencies; allocates one []rune for medium and long non-ASCII strings; width of ZWJ and variation-selector sequences can differ from uniseg, which does full UAX #29 segmentation.
caveats: Own benchmark module with public code and a named CPU, but the Go toolchain version is not stated and results come from one Windows laptop; the top-level headline (3-46x, ASCII 15-46x) is larger than the measured table in bench/README (ASCII 12-24x, non-ASCII 2.4-4x, ZWJ about 1x), so quote the table. Baselines are Go libraries, not C++ HarfBuzz or FreeType, and display width is a text-layout primitive.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/wcwidth, then raw README and bench/README

name: uwcwidth
baseline: wcwidth (jquast/wcwidth, the standard Python terminal width library); cwcwidth also measured
workload: wcswidth of the string 'コンニチハ, セカイ!' in IPython %%timeit.
claimed_speedup: README: uwcwidth 41 ns vs wcwidth 1.73 us (about 40x) and cwcwidth 211 ns (about 5x); heading 'Performance: 40x faster than wcwidth'.

name: uWrap
baseline: canvas-hypertxt (JavaScript canvas text-wrapping library)
workload: Wrapping 100,000 random sentences into boxes of random widths between 50px and 250px using Canvas2D measureText; run from the demo page's DevTools console.
claimed_speedup: README headline '10x faster'. Table: Chrome 135 82ms vs 770ms (about 9.4x, derived from page data); Firefox 137 90ms vs 1660ms (about 18x, derived from page data); Safari 18.1 185ms vs 1430ms (about 7.7x, derived from page data). README also says it is better in memory use and more accurate.
tradeoffs: Under 2KB minified. Only the pre-line wrapping strategy is implemented; works most accurately for Latin text; does not handle Windows-style \r\n line breaks. It predicts row heights for virtualized lists and does not do shaping.
caveats: Baseline is a third-party canvas wrapping helper, not HarfBuzz or FreeType, and not a widely recognised incumbent; this is text wrapping, at the edge of the shaping and layout category. Browser versions are named but the machine is not. The README says the baseline is less accurate, so the two do not compute identical output. Memory claim has no numbers.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch (allowed_domains news.ycombinator.com) 'Show HN text layout engine paragraph line breaking bidi shaping fast written from scratch' surfaced the thread 'Show HN: uWrap.js' (item 43583478); repo README then opened.

name: xxUTF
baseline: ICU4C (unorm2 NFD normalization on UTF-8 input; also compared for NFC, NFKD, NFKC and case folding per README)
workload: NFD normalization of UTF-8 text in eight scripts (Arabic, Japanese, Chinese, Hindi, Russian, Latin, Hebrew, Korean; real text inputs under benchmarks/inputs), throughput in GB/s on an ARM NEON machine.
claimed_speedup: README states 'the fastest open source implementations of the supported algorithms' and shows only a bar chart (doc/neon_utf8_nfd.png). Approximate values read off that chart (not stated as numbers in the text): Arabic about 1.9 vs 0.5 GB/s, Japanese about 2.7 vs 0.8, Chinese about 4.1 vs 1.0, Hindi about 2.6 vs 0.7, Russian about 2.4 vs 0.5, Hebrew about 2.3 vs 0.6, Korean about 0.8 vs 0.25, Latin about 35 vs 0.35 GB/s (xxUTF vs ICU4C).
compiler_and_flags: Built with Zig 0.16.0, 'zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast' (README); benchmark runner is 'zig build bench'. ICU4C version and its build flags not stated.
hardware: Unnamed 'machine supporting ARM NEON'; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: C library distributed as a single-header amalgamation (callable from C++), no allocation, no libc dependency, UTF-8/UTF-16LE/UTF-16BE, NFD/NFC/NFKD/NFKC plus case folding, streaming helpers. Built for Unicode 17.0.0. README shows ARM NEON results and says not many instruction sets are supported yet (it claims to be fastest even in scalar mode). Build system is Zig 0.16.0. Input is assumed valid.
caveats: README publishes no numeric table, only a PNG chart for NFD on UTF-8 with NEON, so the numbers above are eyeballed from the image and approximate. The Latin bar (about 35 GB/s vs 0.35) is dominated by an already-normalized fast path and is not representative of text that needs decomposition. CPU model, compiler flags for ICU and ICU version are missing, which is why the tier is C and not A. The project calls itself alpha, with a security review still pending. Category fit is marginal (Unicode normalization and case folding, not shaping or rasterization); the baseline is ICU, not HarfBuzz or FreeType.
found_via: WebSearch 'C++ Unicode library case folding normalization "faster than ICU" "utf8proc" benchmark github'; README fetched via raw.githubusercontent.com, chart doc/neon_utf8_nfd.png downloaded and viewed, commits page opened.

name: libgrapheme
baseline: ICU, GNU libunistring and libutf8proc (UAX #29 grapheme, word and sentence segmentation, UAX #14 line break detection, case conversion, UTF-8 decode)
workload: Unicode text segmentation (grapheme clusters, words, sentences, line break opportunities) and case conversion on UTF-8 strings and codepoint arrays; the repo's benchmark/ directory times libgrapheme against libutf8proc on the Unicode conformance test strings.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. README: 'It is also way smaller and much faster than the other established Unicode string libraries (ICU, GNU's libunistring, libutf8proc).'
compiler_and_flags: Repo default config.mk: CC=cc, CFLAGS=-std=c99 -Os -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic; benchmark binaries link -lutf8proc; no published benchmark run
stars_or_usage: 15 stars on the author's GitHub copy; canonical repo is git.suckless.org/libgrapheme (blocked here); suckless library
tradeoffs: Freestanding C99 library, no libc needed at runtime, heavily compressed lookup tables generated from Unicode 17.0.0 data, about 400 KB per the suckless page snippet. Scope is segmentation, case mapping and bidi only: no normalization, no shaping, no collation, no locale handling (ICU covers all of those).
caveats: Tier D slot: claim is qualitative. The repo ships benchmark programs (benchmark/character.c compares grapheme_next_character_break against utf8proc_grapheme_break_stateful, and util.c prints the ratio) but no results, hardware or flags are published in the files I opened, and no ICU or libunistring benchmark exists in the repo. The suckless project page, where results may be listed, and git.suckless.org are blocked here. README conformance section still says Unicode 15.0.0 while the intro says 17.0.0. A verifier with a C toolchain can run make benchmark (needs libutf8proc) to turn this into tier A for the utf8proc comparison.

name: Pretext
baseline: Browser DOM text measurement (getBoundingClientRect, offsetHeight and the layout reflow they trigger)
workload: Measuring multiline text height and line breaks in the browser without DOM layout: prepare() once per text, then layout() as pure arithmetic over cached widths.
claimed_speedup: No numbers in the project README, which says 'Fast, accurate' and that it side-steps getBoundingClientRect/offsetHeight reflow, 'one of the most expensive operations in the browser'. Third-party list descriptions on the GitHub text-layout topic page call it '500x faster than browser layout' (bluedusk/awesome-pretext) and expo-pretext lists '~0.0002ms JS layout'; these are not measurements in the repo.
tradeoffs: Layout only: the browser still paints the text, and it reads font widths through canvas measureText, so correctness depends on the host font engine; no bidi levels or visual order; not a general CSS inline formatting engine; in a worker small emoji measure too wide in Chrome and Firefox on macOS. JavaScript, not usable from C++.
caveats: Tier D: the repo documents a harness and many internal before/after benchmarks (RESEARCH.md, bun harness bench) but no head-to-head DOM versus Pretext table was found in README, RESEARCH.md, DEVELOPMENT.md or thoughts.md; the 500x figure is a third-party tagline. Included as the one notable (50k stars) tier D entry; the verifier should look in pages/ or the harness for an actual DOM comparison. Baseline is not HarfBuzz or FreeType, and the work is text measurement and line breaking, not glyph shaping.

name: icey (HTTP server module)
baseline: Go net/http
workload: wrk -t4 -c100 -d10s against an empty-body 200 OK handler on one vCPU: icey single-threaded HTTP/1.1 keep-alive server versus a Go net/http keep-alive server (Node.js v20 and a hand-rolled libuv+llhttp C server also measured).
claimed_speedup: Keep-alive: icey 72,209 req/s at 1.43 ms average latency versus Go 1.25 net/http 53,878 req/s at 2.31 ms (README: 'outperforms Go's net/http by 34%'), Node.js v20 45,514 req/s at 3.56 ms, raw libuv+llhttp 96,088 req/s at 1.04 ms. Connection: close is parity: icey 14,330 req/s versus Go 14,723 req/s (Go marginally ahead), Node.js 9,309 req/s, raw libuv 18,468 req/s.
compiler_and_flags: C++ compiler not stated; built with cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DBUILD_PERF=ON -DENABLE_LOGGING=OFF. Baselines: go1.25.0, Node v20.19.5, wrk 4.1.0 [epoll]. Harness: src/http/perf/benchmark.sh, httpperf.cpp, go-server.go, node-server.js.
hardware: 11th Gen Intel Core i7-11800H @ 2.30GHz, 1 vCPU, Linux 6.8.0-106-generic x86_64
tradeoffs: Single-threaded libuv loop per server; multi-core scaling is one server per core with SO_REUSEPORT (the 'multi' variant, not part of the quoted comparison). LGPL-2.1+ licence. C++20. The HTTP module is one of about 16 modules (WebRTC via libdatachannel, TURN, Symple signalling, FFmpeg pipeline).
caveats: First-party benchmark with public harness and CPU stated, but the C++ compiler is not named, so it falls short of tier A. Server and wrk share the single vCPU, so the load generator competes with the server; one run, no variance reported. The handler returns an empty 200 with no routing, TLS or body, so this measures per-request framework overhead only. With Connection: close the claim disappears (Go 14,723 versus icey 14,330 req/s). Go server runs default net/http with goroutine-per-connection and no tuning. The project's headline claim ('lightweight libwebrtc alternative', media stack) has no numeric comparison: the README table against libWebRTC, libdatachannel and GStreamer is qualitative (build time 'Hours' versus 'Minutes', binary size '50MB+' versus 'Small'). This record therefore documents the HTTP module, not the media path; the listed baseline libwebrtc has no numbers.

name: ConvectionKernels (CVTT BC6H decoder)
baseline: bcdec (also AMD Compressonator cmp_core, DirectXTex, SwiftShader, Mesa in the same chart; BC6H unsigned decode only)
workload: Single-thread BC6H (unsigned) texture decode in Mpix/s, from aras-p's June 2022 bcn_decoder_tester harness decoding a set of DDS test images (ambientCG textures, Kodak, Poly Haven HDRI, WebP gallery) with ConvectionKernels ('convection') versus eight other BCn decoders.
claimed_speedup: BC6Hu decode, Mpix/s, labels printed in the chart PNGs (ratios derived from page data): Ryzen 5950X VS2022: convection 101 vs bcdec 85 (1.19x), swiftshader 70, mesa 57, dxtex 25, amd_cmp 9 (11x). Ryzen 5950X clang14: convection 105 vs bcdec 104 (1.01x, a tie), swiftshader 97, mesa 79, dxtex 34, amd_cmp 33 (3.2x). Apple M1 Max clang13: convection 149 vs swiftshader 143 (1.04x), mesa 84, bcdec 79 (1.89x), dxtex 37, amd_cmp 30 (5.0x). Convection is the top BC6H bar in all three charts. On BC7 decode it is slower than bcdec and bc7enc_rdo (VS2022: convection 124 vs bcdec 142 vs bc7dec_rdo 621; M1 Max: 157 vs 220 vs 517).
compiler_and_flags: Chart titles name VS2022, clang14 (Windows) and clang13 (Apple). Public harness aras-p/bcn_decoder_tester builds Windows with CMake preset x64-release = RelWithDebInfo plus /Ob2 (CMakeLists.txt); the macOS build flags are not stated.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5950X (Windows, VS2022 and clang14 charts); Apple M1 Max (macOS clang13 chart); 1 thread
tradeoffs: Stand-alone SPMD-style SIMD kernels extracted from Convection Texture Tools (CVTT); SIMD ops and 16-bit math; the API works on cvtt::NumParallelBlocks blocks at a time, so callers must pad partial batches. README lists BC6H as 'Experimental' and 11-bit EAC as 'Experimental'; BC7, BC1-5 and ETC1/ETC2 as complete; no ASTC or PVRTC. The faster-decode result is for BC6H only.
caveats: The result is about the decoder, not the encoder: the README makes only an unquantified claim ('very high quality at good speed') and no encode comparison against ispc_texcomp, bc7enc or Compressonator was found, so the lead's encoder baselines are untested here. The margin over bcdec is 1% on the clang14 chart and bcdec was an early-2022 snapshot that later moved on (the tester README lists a 2022-09-15 bcdec commit), so a re-run is needed. Per-run flags are inferred from the CMake preset, not printed on the charts; the blog post text was blocked in this environment (aras-p.info EGRESS_BLOCKED), so figures come from the chart PNGs in aras-p/aras-p.hugo (bcn-decode-win-vs2022.png, bcn-decode-win-clang14.png, bcn-decode-mac.png), whose bar labels are printed numbers. name: ffpng
baseline: image-rs/image-png v0.18.1 (Rust PNG decoder with fdeflate, built with --features=unstable); the same harness also times libpng + zlib, libspng, stb_image and libdeflate-backed inflate, but the README publishes no libpng or libspng numbers
workload: PNG decode of the whole QOI benchmark suite (2848 images in 13 categories), single core pinned at real-time priority with boost off, geometric mean MP/s and per-image ratio against image-png, output checked byte for byte.
claimed_speedup: Overall 1.115x faster than image-png on a Ryzen 7950X (356.3 vs 319.5 MP/s geomean) and 1.204x faster on a Ryzen 9950X3D (352.6 vs 292.8 MP/s); faster in all 13 categories, from 1.024x (photo_wikipedia, 9950X3D) to 1.827x (screenshot_web, 9950X3D). README says decode speed is about 3% ahead on dense photographs.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 16.1 (7950X run) and gcc 16.2.1 (9950X3D run) targeting x86-64-v3 (AVX2, BMI2, PCLMUL); image-png at target-cpu=x86-64-v3 on Rust nightly (1.98.0-nightly c1b22f44c for the follow-up); clang builds run about 10% slower per README
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X and Ryzen 9 9950X3D, one isolated core (isolcpus, nohz_full), taskset plus chrt -f 99, CPU boost off
tradeoffs: Single header ffpng.h, C99, libc plus immintrin.h only. Decode only (no encoder). Requires x86-64-v3 (AVX2, BMI2, PCLMUL; Intel since 2013, AMD since 2017); not portable to ARM. Output is fixed to 8-bit samples (EXPAND and STRIP_16: 16-bit truncated to the high byte). Handles all PNG color types, depths and interlacing.
caveats: The win is over the previous state of the art (image-png), not over libpng; the README says the harness times libpng, libspng and stb_image but does not print their numbers, so the libpng speedup is not stated on the page. 16-bit PNGs are truncated to 8 bits, the same semantics as image-png (EXPAND and STRIP_16) but not libpng default output. Corpus (QOI benchmark suite) is not vendored. Absolute throughput requires core isolation and boost off. Very new repository (first commit 2026-06-23). Source header carries an SPDX MIT tag and a copyright line but the repository has no LICENSE file.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/image-decoder sorted by recently updated (description 'faster than image-png on the QOI corpus'); README cites the image-rs blog post 'fastest PNG decoder in the world' (post itself not opened)

name: fpng
baseline: libpng
workload: Lossless 24/32bpp PNG encode, and decode of fpng-produced PNGs, single-threaded, on the QOI benchmark suite (QOIR harness) and on 303 GPU-texture test images (fpng README).
claimed_speedup: README text: about 23x faster compression and 2.5-3x faster decompression than libpng (decompression only on fpng-compressed PNGs). QOIR benchmark: fpng encode 192.16 MPixels/s vs libpng 5.49 (about 35x, derived from page data) and decode 148.19 vs 56.18 (about 2.6x, derived from page data); output files about 1.29x larger than libpng (CmpRatio 0.3115 vs 0.2423, derived).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 10.2.1 (Debian Bullseye); QOIR script/run_full_benchmarks.sh builds the adapters with -Wall -O3 -march=native; the libpng and libwebp under test are the Debian Bullseye system builds; fpng's own README: MSVC 2019, gcc/clang need -msse4.1 -mpclmul -fno-strict-aliasing
hardware: Intel Core i5-10210U @ 1.60GHz (author's desktop machine), single-threaded; fpng README: Xeon E5-2690 3.00 GHz
tradeoffs: Encoder writes standards-conformant PNG readable by any decoder, but the fast decoder only accepts PNGs written by fpng (returns FPNG_DECODE_NOT_FPNG otherwise). 24/32bpp only. SIMD (SSE4.1 plus PCLMUL for CRC and Adler) is x86 only. Output about 29% larger than libpng. Single source file, no dependencies. README recommends Wuffs for decoding untrusted PNGs.
caveats: fpng's own README table has no libpng row, so the libpng ratios are a text claim there; the libpng numbers above come from the QOIR author's harness, which uses Debian's libpng at its default level. Decoder speed advantage applies only to fpng-encoded files; README says Wuffs is within about 10% on those.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'fast lossless image codec faster than libpng PNG encoder decoder github fpng fpnge benchmark' surfaced the codec; numbers from the QOIR benchmark page

baseline: libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2 (AVX2, single thread) for JPEG; Wuffs for PNG

Single-threaded nitrojpeg 103 ms versus libjpeg-turbo 107 ms, about parity. On a Core i7-1260P (Linux) 5.4 ms parallel versus 32.3 ms on one thread. PNG on the i9: nitropng parallel 45.5 ms versus Wuffs 180 ms, about 4x (derived); libpng is not in the PNG table.

hardware: Intel i9 13th gen, 8 cores / 16 threads, macOS (exact SKU not stated); also Apple M1, Xeon E3-1245 v5 and Core i7-1260P (Arch Linux)
stars_or_usage: 0 stars; 82 commits, earliest visible commits dated 2026-09-27
tradeoffs: Baseline sequential JPEG only (progressive JPEG is left to libjpeg-turbo or the OS decoder); 8-bit non-interlaced PNG only; plain C with pthreads and AVX2 or NEON, but the loop bodies are clang blocks so it needs clang with -fblocks (GCC is not supported); uses every core for a single image, which helps latency but not total throughput of a batch; output is claimed bit-identical to libjpeg-turbo (checked by the author's bench/verify).

Very new repository with no stars and a single author's benchmark. The i9 SKU is not named (the i7-1260P run is a different image set). The PNG baseline is Wuffs, not libpng. libjpeg-turbo gets no restart-marker parallelism because camera JPEGs lack restart markers.

name: libfacedetection (Highway-optimized facedetect_hw_cnn and Rust crate)
baseline: libfacedetection original C++ implementation (facedetect_cnn, AVX2 build with _ENABLE_AVX2) from the same repository
metric: latency and throughput (ms per image / FPS)
workload: CNN (YuNet) face detection on the repo's images/cnnresult.png resized to 640x480, 320x240, 160x120 and 128x96, 128 iterations after 5 warmups, single thread and 28 external caller threads.
claimed_speedup: README 'Highway Optimized Version' table, single thread, original AVX2 vs Highway AVX2 hybrid: 640x480 33.42 ms / 29.92 FPS vs 8.48 ms / 117.89 FPS (about 3.9x, derived from page data); 320x240 7.70 ms vs 2.14 ms (about 3.6x, derived); 160x120 1.49 ms vs 0.53 ms (about 2.8x, derived); 128x96 0.88 ms vs 0.32 ms (about 2.8x, derived). External multi-thread 640x480: 4.56 ms vs 2.44 ms (about 1.9x, derived); 128x96: 6750.38 FPS vs 19047.05 FPS. Versus the original default/scalar build, 640x480 65.66 ms vs 8.48 ms (about 7.7x, derived). Rust crate libfacedetection_rs vs original C++ AVX2, 640x480 single thread: 35.93 ms vs 8.73 ms (about 4.1x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 19.40.33821.0 (Visual Studio 17 2022), CMake Release; original built with the _ENABLE_AVX2 macro, Highway AVX2 targets with /arch:AVX2 per highway/CMakeLists.txt, Highway 1.3.0; Rust 1.95.0 release profile with runtime AVX2 dispatch. Benchmark: highway/benchmark/hw_resolution_benchmark.cpp, command fdt_hw_resolution_benchmark.exe images\cnnresult.png 128 28.
hardware: Intel Core i7-14700KF, 20 cores / 28 logical processors, Windows, max clock 3400 MHz as reported by Windows
tradeoffs: Highway path is a separate C API (facedetect_hw_cnn, own result buffer size) beside the untouched original; it is built per instruction set with no runtime dispatch and needs the Highway 1.3.0 dependency. The public API uses thread-local workspaces, so scaling comes from calling it from several threads with one result buffer per thread. ARM Linux is untested for the Highway version and AVX512 rows are N/A on the test CPU. The Rust crate (libfacedetection_rs 0.1) has a safe API and runtime AVX2 dispatch but no published C ABI.
caveats: Baseline is the project's own original implementation, not an external incumbent: no comparison against OpenCV FaceDetectorYN, dlib, MTCNN, RetinaFace or any other detector appears in the README, opencv_dnn/ (deployment demos only), COMPILE.md or the Rust report. All numbers are first-party and the Highway section is recent (2026). The benchmark times the detector only (cv::resize happens outside the timed loop) and prints a face count per detector but does not assert output parity; the Rust section says its table is not for result-buffer parity or accuracy. Origin AVX2 differs between the two README tables (33.42 ms vs 35.93 ms at 640x480), about 7 percent run-to-run spread. PR #383 (merged 2026-06-28) fixed a SIGSEGV in five Highway kernels that used aligned Load/Store on a 16-byte-aligned std::vector (faults on AVX2+ with glibc); the fix switched to LoadU/StoreU and its performance effect is not stated; the README numbers come from MSVC on Windows. Domain note: this is CNN inference for face detection and could instead be filed under numerics-and-science / autodiff-and-ml-kernels. The older README tables (i7-7820X AVX2/AVX512, Raspberry Pi 4B) have no baseline.

name: PNG XL (PXL)
baseline: libpng (decode into raw RGBA pixels)
workload: Decoding the 24 Kodak lossless photographs from in-memory compressed bytes straight to a raw pixel buffer, single thread, median of 15 repeats per file, summed over the 24 files (bench/rawdec); also size-versus-decode-speed charts on photographs and synthetic stills against libpng, QOI, WebP, JPEG XL and AVIF.

Photographs: PXL about twice libpng speed (libpng 98.6 MB/s vs PXL 200-276 MB/s) at 85.6% of source PNG size. Synthetic stills: PXL 485 MB/s vs libpng 309 MB/s, but WebP wins both axes there (570 MB/s, 44.6%). On a real PSP-3008 (333 MHz) three of four filters beat libpng by 2.8-3.5x while the adaptive filter only ties.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 16.1.1 / 16.2.1, CMake Release build (-O2, later -O3), no -march=native; libpng 1.6, zstd 1.5.7 (docs/BENCHMARKS.md).
hardware: Intel Pentium B960 @ 2.20GHz, 2 cores, 15.2 GiB RAM (docs/BENCHMARKS.md); also a real PSP-3008 at 333 MHz.
stars_or_usage: 7 stars; used by the repo's own Qt image plugin, Dolphin thumbnailer and FFmpeg module

Files are 85.5% of PNG on photographs but JPEG XL and WebP compress better; decoder is 174 KB .text versus libpng's 210 KB. Single-threaded decode; PNG files must be converted to PXL first.
caveats: Descends from Zpng (catid/Zpng, already catalogued). The comparison is format versus format: libpng decodes the original PNG while PXL decodes a .pxl file re-encoded from it (13.6 MB versus 15.9 MB total), so it is not two decoders on identical bytes. Benchmarked on a 2-core Pentium B960. README states libjxl and libavif were given no worker threads, QOI is about 16% faster than PXL on 24 of 24 files, and an earlier README chart overstated PXL by about a third before all outputs were forced to RGBA8. language: x86-64 assembly (GNU as, Intel syntax) with a C test and benchmark harness

Drop-in for the four qoi.h symbols (qoi_encode, qoi_decode, qoi_write, qoi_read) with no algorithmic change, so the format and compression ratio are the same as qoi.h. Like qoi.h, qoi_decode may read a few bytes past the end on a truncated stream.
