tradeoffs: Custom non-PNG format that needs Zstd (bundled in the repo). C API plus command-line tool, about 500 lines. Works best on photographic images. Author calls it experimental and does not expect others to use it.
caveats: No commits since 2018. README timing is one image on Windows with no compiler flags stated; the A tier rests on the QOIR harness, which uses an adapted copy of ZPNG. QOIR notes ZPNG is competitive with or better than QOIR on photographic subsets.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'fast lossless image codec faster than libpng PNG encoder decoder github fpng fpnge benchmark' surfaced the codec; numbers from the QOIR benchmark page
Named in nigeltao/qoir README (opened) from WebSearch 'fast PNG decoder encoder faster than libpng SIMD library site:github.com'; opened Zpng README and the Image-Compression-Benchmark README

name: CharLS
baseline: Pillow PNG encoder and Pillow JPEG 2000 plugin (in Image-Compression-Benchmark); the README compares against the original HP JPEG-LS code, JPEG-XR and JPEG 2000
workload: Lossless compression and decompression of 585 CLIC2021 RGB 24-bit images (4.1 GB), single-threaded, total time and total size, using the CharLS-based pillow-jpls 1.3.2 plugin.
claimed_speedup: Image-Compression-Benchmark (CLIC2021, units not stated on page, presumably seconds): JPEG-LS compress 72.237 and decompress 66.567 vs JPEG2000 319.912 and 275.398 (about 4.4x and 4.1x faster, derived from page data) and vs PNG (optimize=False) 334.791 and 33.677 (4.6x faster compress but about 2x slower decompress); JPEG-LS total size 1931584595 vs JPEG2000 1992860964 and PNG 2003016524 bytes. CharLS README: 'about twice as fast as the original HP code, and beats both JPEG-XR and JPEG 2000 by a factor 3'.
compiler_and_flags: Python 3.9 with Pillow 10.1.0 and pillow-jpls 1.3.2 (CharLS wheel build flags not stated)
hardware: Intel Core i7 12700H, 16GB DDR4-3200, Windows 10
tradeoffs: JPEG-LS (ISO/IEC 14495-1) is a lossless/near-lossless codec with low complexity; decode is about twice as slow as Pillow's PNG decode in the cited suite. README notes Hewlett Packard patents on JPEG-LS (licensed free for conformant implementations; some may have expired). No SIMD: speed comes from templates and traits.
caveats: Weak fit to the listed baselines: none of libjpeg-turbo, libpng, libwebp or libavif is directly compared, and Pillow's PNG codec uses zlib rather than libpng. The suite measures a Python wrapper (pillow-jpls, which PyPI says is based on CharLS), so Python overhead is included. The README's own 'twice as fast as HP code' claim cites a page on imagecompression.info that was not opened and is dated. Another JPEG-LS-family row ('JPEG-LS-ext') is a different codec and is not counted here.
found_via: github.com/topics/image-compression?l=c%2B%2B (team-charls/charls listed); opened README, LICENSE.md, commits page, the Image-Compression-Benchmark README and the pillow-jpls PyPI page

name: HALIC (High Availability Lossless Image Compression)
language: unknown (binaries only; README says built with GCC and Clang)
baseline: libwebp lossless (Pillow 10.1.0, method 1) and PNG (Pillow 10.1.0, optimize=False)
workload: Total compress and decompress time and compressed size on CLIC2021 (585 RGB images, 4.1 GB) and GDCC2020 (100 RGB images, 1.0 GB) in the Image-Compression-Benchmark shootout, all codecs single-threaded.
claimed_speedup: CLIC2021: HALIC 1,473,481,803 bytes, 22.187 s compress, 28.447 s decompress versus WebP lossless m1 1,496,478,650 bytes, 720.160 s, 37.044 s (about 32x faster compress, 1.3x faster decompress, 1.5% smaller, derived) and PNG optimize=False 2,003,016,524 bytes, 334.791 s, 33.677 s (about 15x compress, 1.18x decompress, 26% smaller, derived). GDCC2020: HALIC 4.780 s compress and 5.426 s decompress versus PNG optimize=False 152.321 s and 11.545 s (about 32x and 2.1x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated: most codecs are prebuilt Windows .exe files in the benchmark's codec folder, WebP and PNG run through Python 3.9 with Pillow 10.1.0; commands are listed in the README (PNG: Image.open('in.pnm').save('out.png', optimize=False))
hardware: Intel Core i7-12700H, 16 GB DDR4-3200, Windows 10; every codec single-threaded, SIMD allowed
tradeoffs: Binary releases only (Windows and Linux executables), PPM and PNM input, ANS (FSE) entropy coder with independent blocks, multithreading only from version 0.7 on. Compression ratio is behind JPEG XL, EMMA and NBLI; the 'HALIC fast' variant trades size for speed and failed to decompress one gray test image (zone_plate.pnm) in the benchmark.
caveats: The repository holds only README, LICENSE (MIT) and .gitignore; the benchmark's own format table marks HALIC as not open source, so the source cannot be inspected or rebuilt, and has_code is false even though the licence file says MIT. The numbers come from prebuilt executables with no flags. The PNG baseline is Pillow's zlib-based codec, not libpng. On tiny images PNG decodes faster (Kodak: PNG optimize=False 0.484 s versus HALIC 0.615 s), so the decode win shows only on large images. The author's own README charts carry no numbers.
found_via: Image-Compression-Benchmark README (WangXuan95/Image-Compression-Benchmark), found by WebSearch 'Image-Compression-Benchmark RunBenchmark.py github'

name: JPEGDEC (bitbank2)
baseline: TJpgDec (via Bodmer/TJpg_Decoder) and picojpeg (via Bodmer/JPEGDecoder); libjpeg-turbo and stb_image not compared
workload: Decode of one 280x240 baseline JPEG held in memory on an ESP32-S3 (with PSRAM), timed with millis() around the library's decode call, with and without drawing to a TFT; JPEGDEC, Bodmer/TJpg_Decoder, Bodmer/JPEGDecoder and Espressif ESP32_JPEG compared.
claimed_speedup: Decode-only ms from the atomic14 table: Bodmer/JPEGDecoder (picojpeg) 108, Bodmer/TJpg_Decoder (TJpgDec) 55, bitbank2/JPEGDEC 32 (older version, struck through), JPEGDEC new SIMD-enabled version 23, ESP32_JPEG 20. Derived from page data: JPEGDEC is 1.7x faster than TJpgDec (55/32) and 2.4x with the new version (55/23); 3.4x and 4.7x faster than picojpeg (108/32, 108/23). Decode plus draw: TJpg_Decoder 64, JPEGDEC 38 (old) or 29 (new), ESP32_JPEG 37. The JPEGDEC README itself gives only per-MCU timings for its own code (tulips 640x480 test image: Cortex-M7 at 600 MHz 29,592 us full decode, Apple M1 992 us at 1/8 scale) and unquantified claims ('performs better than anything else available', 'cropping function that's faster than JPEGTRAN').
compiler_and_flags: PlatformIO espressif32 / Arduino framework with -Ofast (platformio.ini); GCC version and library versions not pinned.
hardware: ESP32-S3 (esp32-s3-devkitc-1, PSRAM enabled); clock speed not stated
tradeoffs: Baseline JPEG only (grayscale or YCbCr Huffman); progressive files are handled only as DC-only thumbnails (the decoder forces 1/8 scale and decodes the first scan). Aims at no more than 18K of RAM for baseline decode when output goes straight to an LCD (comment in jpeg.inl; README says 20K minimum). Callback design: caller supplies draw function, 2048-pixel internal buffer. Built-in 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 scaling, crop, Exif thumbnail, Floyd-Steinberg dithering; SIMD color conversion on ESP32-S3, Arm NEON and x86 SSE2.
caveats: Evidence is an independent but small one-image, one-run-per-library demo (millis() resolution, no repeats, no stated clock, no pinned compiler or library versions); each library uses its own callback so the work per call is not identical; Espressif's ESP32_JPEG was faster in decode-only (20 vs 23 ms). Comparison against desktop libjpeg-turbo, stb_image and the lead's '1/8-scale progressive in about 18 KB' claim has no published numbers anywhere found. The repo's own wiki (Home page only) has no benchmark; the README chart (perf.jpg) shows only JPEGDEC on different boards. Newest numbers in atomic14's repo are dated 2024-04-07. A search snippet of an esp32.com thread (blocked here) also compares rom tjpgd.h and JPEGDEC but could not be read.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/bitbank2/JPEGDEC (README, jpeg.inl, perf.jpg); WebSearch 'JPEGDEC vs TJpg_Decoder decode time ms comparison issue benchmark ESP32 tjpgd' surfaced github.com/atomic14/esp32-jpeg-perf-tests

name: meshoptimizer (vertex codec used as a lossless float-image compressor)
baseline: OpenEXR ZIP compression (zlib), also compared with EXR PIZ, RLE, HTJ2K and libjxl lossless
workload: Lossless compression of 10 floating-point EXR images (3122 MB total, half and float, up to 37 channels), split into 16K-pixel chunks compressed in parallel; compression ratio versus GB/s, 3 runs.
claimed_speedup: The author's conclusion: 'mesh optimizer is very impressive ... very far ahead of others towards top right of the chart'. Approximate readings of the Ryzen 5950X chart: decompression about 8 GB/s versus about 2.4 GB/s for EXR ZIP (about 3.3x, derived) at compression ratios of about 1.9 to 2.03 versus 1.87 for ZIP; compression about 1.3 to 1.8 GB/s versus about 1.2 GB/s for ZIP. JPEG-XL and HTJ2K are slower; the README says EXR HTJ2K decompresses at 2x slower than ZIP.
compiler_and_flags: Release cmake builds: Visual Studio 2022 v17.14 on Windows, Xcode clang 16 on Mac; OpenEXR 3.4.0, libjxl pre-v0.12 (029cec4), meshoptimizer v0.25, zstd 1.5.7 fetched via FetchContent
hardware: Windows AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (16 threads); Mac MacBook Pro M4 Max
tradeoffs: Not an image format: the benchmark wraps meshoptimizer's vertex-data compression (vertex size set to the pixel size, padded to a multiple of four) in a custom chunked container written by the benchmark author, so there is no interoperability. Code size +26 KB (+431 KB with zstd) versus +308 KB for EXR HTJ2K and +6017 KB for JPEG-XL.
caveats: The figures are read off chart images, not text. Test images are mostly noisy path-traced renders and could behave differently on natural images, as the author notes. It is a test harness by Aras Pranckevicius, not a supported meshoptimizer image feature, and meshoptimizer's own purpose is mesh optimization, so it may be catalogued under other categories. Both sides are multithreaded.
found_via: Shootout sweep: aras-p/test_exr_htj2k_jxl, found via the 'OpenJPH vs OpenJPEG' WebSearch results

name: OpenJPH (HTJ2K encoder and decoder)
baseline: OpenJPEG (JPEG 2000 Part 1)
workload: Single-image decode time in the dicom-codecs shootout on three DICOM test images (8-bit color US, 12-bit gray MR, 16-bit gray CT); each codec decodes its own encoded stream, one iteration.
claimed_speedup: Decode: openjph 4.09 ms versus openjpeg 24.73 ms (8-bit color US), 1.43 ms versus 15.65 ms (12-bit gray MR), 1.53 ms versus 22.27 ms (16-bit gray CT), about 6x, 11x and 15x (derived from page data). Kakadu, which is proprietary, is faster still at 1.13, 0.51 and 0.64 ms.
hardware: Apple MacBook Pro M1 Pro
stars_or_usage: 296 stars; packaged in several distributions per the README's repology badge
tradeoffs: Implements High-Throughput JPEG 2000 (Part 15, ITU-T T.814) only, with Part 1 wavelet and coding features reused; it cannot read ordinary Part 1 JPEG 2000 files, so adoption needs HTJ2K-encoded data. The HT block coder trades some compression ratio for speed.
caveats: The two codecs decode different codestreams (HTJ2K for OpenJPH, JPEG 2000 Part 1 or HTJ2K for OpenJPEG depending on the test file, not stated), so part of the gap is the format rather than the library. One iteration per case, no compiler or flags, and the dicom-codecs repository calls itself WIP (10 stars). The OpenJPH README itself publishes no numbers and only links third-party papers (Kakadu ICIP 2019, blocked here).
found_via: WebSearch 'OpenJPH vs OpenJPEG vs Kakadu HTJ2K encode decode speed benchmark comparison' led to dicom-codecs/dicom-codecs

name: @napi-rs/image
baseline: sharp (Node.js binding over libvips with libwebp and libavif)
workload: One EXIF JPEG with orientation applied, resized to width 225 and encoded to WebP (quality 75) or AVIF (quality 70, 4:2:0), work submitted concurrently up to the CPU count.
claimed_speedup: Default thread pool: WebP 202 ops/s vs sharp 169 ops/s, AVIF 26 vs 24 ops/s. UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=10: WebP 431 vs 238 ops/s (README: 'The 1.8x ratio applies only to the recorded WebP pipeline with a thread pool of 10'), AVIF 36 vs 32 ops/s.
compiler_and_flags: node bench/bench.mjs (benchmark script in the repo); Node.js and package versions were not recorded with the results.
hardware: Apple M1 Max, macOS 12.3.1, arm64
tradeoffs: Rust native addon for Node.js (plus a WebAssembly build) that resizes, converts and optimizes JPEG, PNG, WebP, AVIF; HEIC not available in WASM. API differs from sharp. It is a Node.js packaging of native image codecs rather than a new codec design (README: Rust-powered image processing), so it may fold into the libwebp/libavif entries.
caveats: README labels the table 'historical results ... not a new benchmark of 1.15.0'; Node and package versions unrecorded; single input image; equal numeric quality settings do not guarantee equal visual quality or file size across encoders (README says so). The 1.8x win applies to one configuration; the other three configurations are 1.08x to 1.19x (derived from page data). Baseline is sharp, not libwebp or libavif directly.

WebSearch: 'fast PNG OR JPEG OR WebP encoder Rust OR Zig OR Nim crate "faster than libpng" OR "faster than libwebp" OR "faster than libjpeg-turbo" benchmark README' returned image.napi.rs; opened github.com/Brooooooklyn/Image, its README and commits page.

name: Accelerating JPEG Decompression on GPUs (Weissenberger and Schmidt, HiPC 2021)
baseline: libjpeg-turbo (CPU) and NVIDIA nvJPEG (GPU)
workload: GPU JPEG decompression that locates codeword boundaries at arbitrary bitstream positions so independent chunks decode in parallel; compared on A100 and V100 GPUs against libjpeg-turbo and nvJPEG (also nvJPEG with the A100 hardware decoder).
claimed_speedup: From search-result snippet of the arXiv abstract (arXiv:2111.09219, paper page not opened): outperforms libjpeg-turbo (CPU) and nvJPEG (GPU) by up to 51x (34x) and 8.0x (5.7x) on A100 (V100), and up to 3.4x over nvJPEG with the dedicated hardware decoder on A100.
hardware: NVIDIA A100 and V100 GPUs (per snippet)
tradeoffs: Needs an NVIDIA GPU and PCIe transfers; implements an important subset of the JPEG standard, not all of it. Presented at HiPC 2021 (peer reviewed). Related author repos on github.com/weissenberger (gpuhd, multians) cover GPU Huffman and ANS decoding, not a JPEG decoder.
caveats: Snippet only: arXiv, ACM and IEEE are blocked here, so the numbers are from search-result text and I could not read the paper or find its code (the author's GitHub profile lists gpuhd, multians, bzip2gpu and HIPSW4 but no JPEG decoder). Tier capped at C, has_code false.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'JPEG decoder faster than libjpeg-turbo SIMD GPU paper github' and '"Accelerating JPEG Decompression on GPUs" Weissenberger Schmidt github code'

name: astc-encoder (astcenc)
baseline: astcenc 1.7 (earlier major series of the same encoder; no third-party baseline opened)
workload: Compression performance (MTex/s) versus PSNR across Arm's test image sets (LDR, HDR, normal map and grayscale images) at 4x4, 5x5, 6x6 and 8x8 block sizes for the -thorough, -medium and -fast presets, astcenc-avx2 2.0 versus astcenc 1.7 (relative-performance chart in the 2.x changelog).
claimed_speedup: Values read off the relative-performance chart image (approximate, the changelog text gives no numbers): astcenc-avx2 2.0 versus astcenc 1.7 at about the same PSNR (delta about 0 to -0.2 dB for nearly all points): -thorough about 2.1-3.1x, -medium about 1.7-3.8x (most points 2.2-3.5x), -fast about 1.3-4.0x (most points 1.9-3.4x). Later series on the same CPU: 4.0 -thorough versus 3.7 about 1.2-1.75x at near-equal PSNR (chart). Text claims in the current README and 5.x changelog: each step from SSE2 to SSE4.1 to AVX2 gains about 15%, and the reference C build (ASTCENC_ISA_NONE) is about 3.25 times slower than the SSE2 build.
compiler_and_flags: astcenc-avx2 binary (AVX2, SSE4.2, POPCNT, F16C); compiler and optimization flags are not stated on the changelog pages. Repo CMake uses -flto=auto for GCC and -ffp-model=precise with -ffp-contract=on for Clang in non-invariant builds.
hardware: Intel Core i5-9600K at 4.2 GHz, 6 threads (stated at the top of each changelog page)
stars_or_usage: 1.3k stars, 286 forks; official Arm ASTC reference-quality encoder; latest series 5.7.0 (August 2026)
tradeoffs: Quality presets (-fastest to -exhaustive) trade compression time against PSNR. Multiple prebuilt ISA variants (SSE2, SSE4.1, AVX2, NEON, SVE 128 and 256, RISC-V vector backend). Codec library API is not binary compatible across versions. Builds are bit-exact across platforms by default; the NO_INVARIANCE option gives up to 5-20% more speed for up to 0.2 dB lower quality (4.0 changelog). 2.0 changed the command line and added a library API.
caveats: The baseline is the project's own scalar 1.7 release, and the 2.0 gain mostly reflects adding SSE2, SSE4.2 and AVX2 SIMD paths, so it is a self-comparison from 2020, not a comparison with a rival encoder (the 2.0 changelog lists the SSE2, SSE4.2 and AVX2 paths as new features of the 2.x series). The 1.7 to 2.0 comparison is only on tag 3.7 and earlier (the main branch changelogs start at 4.x), and the numbers are in chart images, so the ranges above are my visual readings with about 0.1x uncertainty, not tabulated values. Compiler and flags are not stated, and charts are first-party, so tier C. Arm's public test harness (Test/astc_test_image.py, documented in Docs/Testing.md) can regenerate relative charts. A WebSearch result snippet mentions an Arm Khronos presentation (ASTC_Arm.pdf) benchmarking astcenc against ISPC TexComp ASTC on the Kodim suite at 6x6 on an i5-9600K; www.khronos.org is blocked here, so I could not read it and recorded no numbers from it. The lead's '2-4x over 1.7' is supported only for 2.0 on -medium and -fast, with -thorough closer to 2-3x.

name: bc7e (Binomial BC7 encoder, ISPC)
baseline: Intel ispc_texcomp (Fast ISPC Texture Compressor)
workload: BC7 texture encoding at matched average quality (PSNR or SSIM) against the ispc_texcomp library and its profiles.
claimed_speedup: 'usually around 2-3x faster vs. ispc_texcomp at the same average quality (as measured by PSNR or SSIM), and up to ~8x faster vs. ispc_texcomp's "slow" profile'
compiler_and_flags: ISPC compiler 1.82 (1.10.0 bundled) with sse2, sse4, avx, avx2 targets per the README build command; benchmark flags not stated
stars_or_usage: 182 stars; used inside bc7enc_rdo and todds
tradeoffs: Needs the ISPC compiler. Deterministic (does not use approximate SSE instructions, unlike ispc_texcomp). Repository archived by the owner on 2026-01-28; the bc7enc_rdo README says bc7e.ispc was ported to plain C++ (basisu_bc7e_scalar.cpp in basis_universal) and that the newer bc7f is faster still.
caveats: The page gives claims only: no benchmark table, hardware, image set or flags. The same 2-3x claim for Basis BC7 appears in the bc7enc README, so this is first-party only.

name: bc7enc (rgbcx BC1 and bc7enc16 BC7 encoders)
baseline: libsquish (BC1 cluster fit); Intel ispc_texcomp (BC7); also AMD Compressonator and DirectXTex CPU BC7
workload: Encoding 31 images (Kodak corpus plus others) to BC1 and BC7, comparing total encode time and average PSNR at matched quality settings (multithreaded with OpenMP).
claimed_speedup: BC1 'prioritized cluster fit' is 3-4x faster than traditional cluster fit as in libsquish (SSE2) at the same or slightly higher average quality; rgbcx BC1 is faster than AMD Compressonator and libsquish at the same quality. BC7 perceptual (luma PSNR): ispc_texcomp slow 355.4 s 48.6 dB vs bc7enc16 38.3 s 49.6 dB (9.3x faster, derived from page data); ispc_texcomp fast 41.5 s 48.0 dB vs bc7enc16 20.8 s 49.3 dB (2.0x faster, derived from page data). BC7 non-perceptual: DirectXTex CPU default 9485.1 s 45.6 dB vs bc7enc16 36 s 46.0 dB (263x faster, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated; multithreaded with OpenMP; ispc_texcomp called with 64 blocks at a time using AVX instructions
hardware: dual Xeon workstation (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: The BC7 encoder here supports only modes 1 and 6 for RGB (plus modes 5 and 7 for alpha) and is scalar, not vectorized, so it will not match full-mode encoders on every texture; the author points to bc7e and bc7enc_rdo for best BC7 quality. Single-source C/C++ with no dependencies; archived 2026-01-28.
caveats: The README says most timings are for the original release (the latest bc7enc16.c is 8-27% faster when mode 1 is enabled). The CPU model and compile flags are missing. In the non-perceptual ultrafast row ispc_texcomp is faster (1.9 s vs 3.8 s at 42.7 dB), so the win is not uniform. Dual-licensed: choose MIT or public domain (no patent grant for the public-domain option). DirectXTex run used a locally patched pbit bugfix.
found_via: WebSearch 'BC7 encoder fast SIMD faster than Compressonator OR ISPC Texture Compressor OR NVTT benchmark github C++' surfaced richgel999/bc7enc and BinomialLLC/bc7e; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: bc7enc_rdo
baseline: Intel ispc_texcomp (BC7 slow, basic, fast and ultrafast profiles); also Microsoft DirectXTex CPU BC7 encoder
workload: Total BC7 encode time and average PSNR (perceptual REC709 luma PSNR, and plain RGB PSNR) over 31 images (kodim corpus plus others), multithreaded with OpenMP, encode time only, bc7enc16-lineage encoder (modes 1 and 6 only, not vectorized) versus ispc_texcomp profiles (called 64 blocks at a time, AVX) and DirectXTex.
claimed_speedup: Perceptual metric: ispc_texcomp slow 355.4 s at 48.6 dB versus bc7enc16 uber0/max_partitions 64 38.3 s at 49.6 dB (9.3x faster and 1.0 dB higher, derived from page data); ispc_texcomp basic 100.2 s at 48.3 dB versus 20.8 s at 49.3 dB (4.8x, derived); ispc_texcomp fast 41.5 s at 48.0 dB versus 20.8 s at 49.3 dB (2.0x, derived); ispc_texcomp ultrafast 1.9 s at 46.2 dB versus 8.9 s at 48.4 dB (bc7enc16 about 4.7x slower, derived). Non-perceptual RGB PSNR: ispc_texcomp slow 355.4 s at 46.8 dB versus 29.3 s at 45.8 dB (12.1x faster, derived, but 1.0 dB lower) and versus 51 s at 46.1 dB (7.0x, derived); ispc_texcomp fast 41.45 s at 46.09 dB versus the latest bc7enc16 41.42 s at 46.03 dB (parity, README says 'just as fast as ispc_texcomp fast'); ispc_texcomp ultrafast 1.9 s at 42.7 dB versus 3.8 s at 42.7 dB (bc7enc16 2x slower). DirectXTex CPU default (no 3-subset modes) 9485.1 s at 45.6 dB versus bc7enc16 uber1/max_partitions 64 36 s at 46.0 dB (about 263x, derived); DirectXTex mode-6-only 466.4 s at 41.9 dB versus 6.7 s at 42.8 dB (about 70x, derived).
hardware: Dual Xeon workstation (CPU model not stated), OpenMP multithreaded (thread count not stated); ispc_texcomp used AVX instructions
stars_or_usage: 282 stars, 62 forks; encoder lineage also in bc7enc and bc7enc16
tradeoffs: Per the LICENSE file the repo's own code is MIT or Unlicense (public domain, no patent grant), the bundled bc7e.ispc is Apache-2.0 and LodePNG is zlib-style. No third-party dependencies for the encoder (C++11, drop-in files rgbcx.cpp, bc7enc.cpp, ert.cpp). Builds with cmake; SUPPORT_BC7E=TRUE adds bc7e.ispc and needs Intel's ISPC compiler. bc7enc.cpp is the 4-mode non-ISPC encoder with optional reduced-entropy mode; bc7e.ispc supports all modes but not reduced entropy. RDO post-processing (ert.cpp) works with any block format, tuned for Deflate, LZHAM or LZMA, and the README claims 10-50% size reductions after LZ compression. The README now points to bc7f as an even faster analytical alternative.
caveats: These tables are no longer in the current README (checked: the 2026 README has no benchmark tables); they are in the 2021-02-13 README at commit 0db1ba2, inherited from bc7enc16, so they describe the predecessor encoder (modes 1 and 6, no SIMD), not the current bc7enc_rdo or its bundled bc7e.ispc. The README says most timings are for the original release, and later versions are about 8-27% faster at the same quality. The README names only 'a dual Xeon workstation' and OpenMP; no CPU model, compiler, flags or thread count is given, so tier C (and the DirectXTex ratios of about 70x and 263x are implausibly large for an unstated setup, and the README notes it used a locally patched DirectXTex build, so cap at C). The perceptual win is measured with the encoder's own optimization target (weighted YCbCr luma PSNR), and the non-perceptual RGB result trades 1.0 dB for speed. The ultrafast profile is faster in ispc_texcomp. The old README also claims the BC1 encoder is 3-4x faster than libsquish cluster fit with SSE2 and faster than AMD Compressonator, with no numbers. Commits since at least 2021-09-13 in the visible history are all README edits (latest 2026-07-31, bc7f note), so the code itself looks unchanged for years (status stale). The lead's check of README tables against bc7e and Compressonator found nothing in the current README; a WebSearch snippet suggests a Compressonator-versus-bc7e comparison exists elsewhere but I did not open it. Blog posts that may hold newer numbers (richg42.blogspot.com) were not opened.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/richgel999/bc7enc_rdo (current README had no tables; found the benchmark section in the README history, commit 0db1ba2, via the README commit list at /commits/master/README.md)

name: Efficient Compression Tool (ECT)
baseline: zopfli (and gzip -9); the published benchmark is gzip/deflate on enwik8, not PNG
workload: Compressing enwik8 (100,000,000 bytes) into gzip format at ECT levels 1-9 versus gzip -9 and zopfli with 1, 5, 15 and 30 iterations.
claimed_speedup: ECT -3 35,014,543 bytes in 16.2 s vs zopfli -i15 34,966,078 bytes in 3m 59.9s (14.8x faster at 0.14% larger, derived from page data); ECT -2 35,019,440 bytes in 14.8 s vs zopfli -i5 34,983,757 bytes in 2m 12.0s (8.9x derived); ECT -9 34,937,781 bytes in 3m 17.9s vs zopfli -i30 34,961,453 bytes in 6m 30.6s (smaller and 2.0x faster, derived); ECT -1 36,493,257 bytes in 3.5 s vs gzip -9 36,475,811 bytes in 5.8 s.
compiler_and_flags: clang on macOS 12.5 (flags not stated); ECT v0.9.2
hardware: Intel i7-7700HQ
tradeoffs: Optimizer for PNG, JPEG (bundles mozjpeg), GZIP and ZIP files; needs nasm and a recursive clone. Multithreading can be turned off at CMake time.
caveats: The README publishes no PNG or JPEG timings; the benchmark is deflate output on text, so this probably belongs under general lossless compression rather than image codecs. Mismatch flagged for the orchestrator. Single run table, old version (0.9.2).
found_via: Recalled as a known PNG/JPEG optimizer while checking PNG deflate kernels (no search query); github.com repo page, commits page and README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: etcpak
baseline: NVIDIA in-driver ETC2 decoder (decompression only; no competing compressor is timed)
workload: ETC1, ETC2, BC1, BC3 and BC7 compression and decompression of a real-life RGBA 16K x 16K atlas, single-threaded (ST) and multithreaded (MT).
claimed_speedup: Title claim 'The fastest ETC compressor on the planet'. Ryzen 9 7950X compression: ETC1 797 Mpx/s ST, 9613 Mpx/s MT; ETC2 356/6378; BC1 5730/10174; BC3 2437/8568; BC7 12.1/225. Decompression ETC2 599 Mpx/s single-threaded vs 'Nvidia in-driver ETC2 decoder can do only 42.5 Mpx/s' (14x, derived from page data).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X; also Intel i7 1185G7 and Apple M3 Max in the same README
stars_or_usage: 331 stars; README says it is used in production builds by millions of users
tradeoffs: Quality is explicitly not the goal ('best suited for rapid assets preparation during development, when graphics quality is not a concern'). Handles ETC1, ETC2, BC1-BC7 and decoding; Benchmarked on x86 (Ryzen, Intel) and Apple M3 Max.
caveats: The compression benchmark lists no competing encoder, so the 'fastest' claim is unverified here; the only named competitor figure is the NVIDIA driver decoder. The quality comparison image is hosted on imgur, which I did not open. Compiler and flags not stated. Weak entry kept for the keep-and-document rule.
found_via: WebSearch 'etcpak fast ETC BC texture compressor benchmark site:github.com'; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: fNBLI (NBLI lossless image codec)
baseline: libpng (via Pillow 10.1.0) and libwebp lossless (via Pillow)
workload: Single-threaded lossless compression and decompression of the CLIC2021 training set (585 RGB 24-bit images, 4 GB) and six other datasets, in the author's Image-Compression-Benchmark shootout.
claimed_speedup: NBLI README (CLIC2021): fNBLI 94.8 MB/s compress and 149.1 MB/s decompress, 29.79% smaller than optipng PNG; Pillow PNG 12.2 and 121.5 MB/s (5.13% larger than optipng); WebP -5 3.7 and 82.8 MB/s (22.53% smaller than optipng). Shootout totals, CLIC2021: fNBLI 43.164 s compress, 27.450 s decompress, 1,337,587,020 bytes vs Pillow PNG (optimize=False) 334.791 s, 33.677 s, 2,003,016,524 bytes and Pillow WebP lossless m5 1112.134 s, 49.442 s, 1,475,908,700 bytes (derived: 7.8x faster encode and 1.2x faster decode than PNG, 26x faster encode and 1.8x faster decode than WebP, with smaller files).
compiler_and_flags: NBLI README build: g++ -O3 -static (MinGW or Linux); the shootout ran the prebuilt fNBLI.exe, which needs AVX2; compiler of that binary not stated
hardware: Intel Core i7 12700H, 16GB DDR4-3200, Windows 10, single-threaded with SIMD allowed
tradeoffs: Custom non-PNG format for 8-bit gray and 24-bit RGB; GPL-3.0 (copyleft); fNBLI needs AVX2. The slower prototype NBLI (-g, 14.7 MB/s compress, 17.0 MB/s decompress) compresses to -30.37% but decodes far slower than PNG. Includes PNG and PNM input.
caveats: Author-run benchmark of the author's own codec; PNG and WebP go through Python Pillow (including process and interpreter overhead per file), not the C libraries directly. The fNBLI source directory src/fNBLI exists (commit 'make fNBLI opensource', 2026-07-18) but the README still links fNBLI.exe and the shootout's format table still marks fNBLI as not open source, so the benchmarked binary may not match the repo source. Compiler flags for the benchmarked binary unknown, hence tier C.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'lossless image compression paper code released outperforms PNG WebP JPEG XL ... SIMD' surfaced NBLI and the Image-Compression-Benchmark shootout

name: Gamut (QOI and QOIX codecs in the D image library)
baseline: PNG via stb (the README row 'PNG (stb)', presumably stb_image and stb_image_write); not libpng
workload: Decode and encode speed in Mpixels/s and bits per pixel on '8-bit color images' for PNG (stb), QOI and QOIX (Gamut's QOI derivative with better predictors plus an LZ4 stage); dataset and machine not stated.
claimed_speedup: README 'Why QOIX?' table (decode mpps / encode mpps / bits per pixel): PNG (stb) 89.73 / 14.34 / 10.29693; QOI 201.9 / 150.8 / 10.35162; QOIX 179.0 / 125.0 / 7.93607. QOIX vs PNG (stb): 2.0x faster decode, 8.7x faster encode, 23 percent fewer bits per pixel (all derived from page data). README text: 'QOIX and QOI generally outperforms PNG in decoding speed and encoding speed.'
tradeoffs: D library (DUB package), nothrow @nogc @safe and usable with -betterC; no C API or C bindings found, so not directly callable from C++. QOIX is a custom format whose bitstream 'may change between major Gamut tags', so it is not a storage format. QOIX is slower than QOI (179.0 vs 201.9 Mpps decode) in exchange for smaller files. Optional WebP and JPEG XL decoders add BSD-3-Clause code (configuration 'boost+mit+bsd3'); dub.json declares 'BSL-1.0+MIT'.
caveats: Table has no hardware, dataset, compiler or flags, and the repo has no benchmark folder (only a convert tool with a --time option), so it is not reproducible from the repo. The win comes from the QOI and QOIX formats, not from a faster PNG or JPEG codec; the baseline is stb's PNG path, not libpng, libjpeg-turbo, libwebp or libavif. Low notability and a single self-measured table.
found_via: Hacker News web search 'Show HN lossless image compression faster than PNG smaller and faster' surfaced the QOI threads; thread pages cannot be opened here, so the QOI topic page github.com/topics/qoi led to this repo. README, LICENSE and dub.json read via github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com.

name: gif_load
baseline: giflib 5.2.2 (also stb_image)
workload: Wall-time decode of every frame of 6 synthetic animated GIFs (320x240 x100, 640x480 x200, 1920x1080 x150; flat shapes and incompressible noise), file read into RAM with read() or mmap(), cold and warm page cache.
claimed_speedup: Warm cache: 1.3x-1.7x faster than giflib and 1.4x-2.5x faster than stb_image (e.g. 1080p shapes 668 ms vs giflib stream 1149 ms vs stb_image 1829 ms). Cold cache: 1.3x-1.5x vs giflib on the 3 shape GIFs but 0.83x-0.85x (slower) on the 3 noise GIFs. Author says the 1.3x-1.5x cold claim also holds on real giphy GIFs. Peak memory: one frame plus a 16 KB code table versus giflib slurp 296 MB at 1080p.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.5 -O2, Linux 6.4
hardware: CPU model not stated (RAM latency 128 ns, 8 GB/s sequential read, EXT4 cold disk read 342 MB/s)
tradeoffs: Whole file must be in memory before decoding (cannot overlap I/O with decode, which is why cold noise cases lose to giflib). Callback API, header-only, under 300 lines, no libc dependency apart from realloc. Interlaced GIFs are the caller's job to unwind (giflib's DGifSlurp does it). Public-domain dedication (no patent grant).
caveats: The README says 'take everything below with a grain of salt' and that the harness is not published, so the numbers are not reproducible from the repo; synthetic GIFs only; best of two runs. Does not claim to beat stb_image's memory-heavy approach on anything but speed and memory.
found_via: github.com/topics/gif?l=c page listed hidefromkgb/gif_load as 'slim, fast'; README Performance section read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: giflib-turbo
baseline: giflib
workload: GIF LZW decoding through the unchanged giflib API; the decoder uses the output image buffer as the LZW dictionary instead of a linked-list string table.
claimed_speedup: Per search-result snippet of the author's blog post and a repo summary (not opened, see caveats): about 5x faster than giflib on images with a low compression ratio and more than 20x faster on well-compressed images. The repo README itself says only 'A faster drop-in replacement for GIFLIB' with identical function names, parameters and output.
stars_or_usage: 39 stars; drop-in for giflib, which is packaged in vcpkg and Conan
tradeoffs: Uses more RAM than giflib (the author's own description: 'It uses more RAM, but you get more speed'); the README lists possible security vulnerabilities and CPU incompatibilities as not yet tested, and says it may take a long time before big projects adopt it.
caveats: Snippet only: the numbers come from a WebSearch snippet of the author's blog post 'A Big Memory GIF Decoder' (bitbanksoftware.blogspot.com, 2021-03, blocked by the egress proxy and not opened) and of a deepwiki summary (also blocked); the github.com repo page and README carry no numbers, test.c is the only test file and no benchmark script is visible. No CPU, compiler, flags or test images known. Search-summary text also mentioned '2.5x to 30x' overall, which could not be confirmed. Only decoding is claimed. Last commit March 2024 and 10 commits in total.
found_via: giflib is a vcpkg and Conan port; WebSearch 'giflib-turbo GIF decoder faster than giflib SIMD github' surfaced the drop-in replacement; repo page and commits opened on github.com

name: Goofy (realtime DXT1/ETC1 encoder)
baseline: stb_dxt (ryg DXT1, STB_DXT_NORMAL); also rgbcx 1.08, icbc 1.0 and rg_etc1 1.04
workload: Single-thread compression speed in megapixels per second and RGB-PSNR on a test image set (README examples show Kodak kodim17, kodim18 and Lena) using each encoder's fastest or lowest-quality setting.
claimed_speedup: Goofy DXT1 1429 MP/s at 37.02 dB vs rgbcx v1.08 level 0 60 MP/s (40.85 dB), ryg stb_dxt 43 MP/s (40.82 dB), icbc v1.0 24 MP/s (41.00 dB); Goofy ETC1 1221 MP/s (36.30 dB) vs rg_etc1 v1.04 3 MP/s (40.87 dB). Ratios derived from page data: about 24x vs rgbcx, 33x vs stb_dxt, 60x vs icbc, 407x vs rg_etc1.
hardware: i7-7820HQ 2.9 GHz, single thread, fastest of 128 runs
tradeoffs: Speed over quality by design: about 37.0 dB RGB-PSNR for DXT1 versus roughly 40.8-41.0 dB for the compared encoders (only 3.6 dB above the downsample-to-RGB565 baseline at 33.39 dB). One heuristic, DXT1 and ETC1s only, poor on normal maps; DXT5 and ETC2 alpha are future work. Header-only, needs SSE2 (NEON not implemented).
caveats: Compiler and flags are not given. Test code and data are in the repo (test-data and test-results folders) but I did not open them. The comparison is a speed-quality trade, not equal quality: the compared encoders produce 4 dB higher PSNR. The author compares each tool at its fastest setting.
found_via: github.com/topics/texture-compression?l=c%2B%2B page led to SergeyMakeev/Goofy; README read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Grok JPEG 2000 codec
baseline: OpenJPEG (JPEG 2000); also Kakadu (proprietary, via GDAL JP2KAK)
workload: GDAL workflows reading JPEG 2000 imagery: Spot 6 on network storage, Spot 6 on local storage, and a Pleiades region read, using 16 threads and a GDAL release build.
claimed_speedup: README table (Grok JP2Grok vs Kakadu JP2KAK vs OpenJPEG): Spot 6 (Network Storage) 35.17 s vs 344 s vs 85 s; Spot 6 (Local Storage) 26.92 s vs 30.57 s vs 52.09 s; Pleiades (Region) 0.74 s vs 1.41 s vs 4.28 s.
compiler_and_flags: GDAL release build (compiler and flags not stated)
hardware: Fedora 42, 16 threads (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Strong copyleft: AGPL v3 (network use triggers source obligations), a poor fit for permissive-license projects. Adds HTJ2K, random-access sub-image decoding with TLM and PLT markers, a multi-level tile cache and S3 access, which are features of the whole GDAL workflow measured. Reported to have started as an OpenJPEG fork (per third-party descriptions seen in search snippets); GitHub does not mark it as a fork.
caveats: JPEG 2000 is outside the listed baselines (libjpeg-turbo, libpng, libwebp, libavif); OpenJPEG is the widely used open-source incumbent. First-party end-to-end GDAL timings that include I/O, caching and region reads, not codec-only throughput. CPU model, compiler flags and the benchmark inputs are not given in the README. Kakadu's 344 s network-storage result is far above its 30.57 s local result, which suggests an I/O-pattern effect rather than codec speed (my inference).
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'HTJ2K OpenJPH OpenJPEG Kakadu encoding decoding speed benchmark faster open source library'
WebSearch 'JPEG 2000 HTJ2K codec C++ "faster than OpenJPEG" github' (result listing Grok); opened README, LICENSE and commits page

name: ICBC (high quality SIMD BC1 encoder)
baseline: squish 1.15 and stb_dxt 1.09 (also RGBCX 1.12 and AMD CMP_Core 4.0.4855)
workload: Average PSNR of BC1 encoders against encode time on the Kodim and Waterloo image sets, several quality levels per encoder.
claimed_speedup: Chart only (time axis unlabeled, values read off the chart image and approximate): at the top quality point (PSNR about 30.9) ICBC-AVX512 takes about 5.5 time units versus about 20.6 for RGBCX and about 19.3 for ICBC-Scalar; squish sits at about 7.4 units for PSNR about 30.43 and AMD CMP at about 14.6 units for PSNR about 30.25.
stars_or_usage: 131 stars; the BC1 encoder used by NVTT
tradeoffs: BC1 (DXT1) only, single header, SIMD variants up to AVX-512; quality levels trade encode time for PSNR.
caveats: The result is a PSNR-versus-time chart with no hardware, compiler or time unit stated, and the numbers above are approximate readings of the picture. The speed lead appears at the highest quality settings; at low quality ICBC, RGBCX and stb are close. The README itself says RGBCX is most likely a better choice for a well supported, actively developed library, and RGBCX is already catalogued. Last commit 2022-11-09.
found_via: Texture-compressor shootout search; opened castano/icbc README and doc/kodim-chart.png

name: ImageZero
baseline: PNG (implementation not named; presumably libpng)
workload: Lossless compression and decompression of 24-bit PPM files, natural photos.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Compared to PNG, it compresses 24 bit PPM files about 20 times faster, and decompresses to PPM about 2 times faster, while the compression rate is nearly as good as PNG for natural photos.'
tradeoffs: Own format and API (README calls it 'early work in progress'; neither format nor API fully outlined). Works on 24-bit RGB only; README says it is not suited for flat computer-generated graphics or grayscale images.
caveats: Only a README paragraph: no benchmark code, images, CPU, compiler, flags or PNG library version, so the baseline is inferred (low confidence). Repository has had no commits since 2013, so the comparison predates modern libpng and zlib-ng. Found in the GitHub topic listings for image-compression and image-decoder; I did not open a second benchmark page.
found_via: github.com/topics/image-compression?l=c%2B%2B and github.com/topics/image-decoder?l=c%2B%2B (cfeck/imagezero listed as 'Fast Lossless Color Image Compression Library'); opened the README and commits page

name: intel-tex-rs-2 (intel_tex_2)
baseline: intel-tex-rs-2 main before PR #50, i.e. the vendored Intel ISPCTextureCompressor kernels built with ISPC 1.20 (the PR does not compare against a separately built Intel ispc_texcomp binary)
workload: Single-threaded texture block encode time per format and preset on a 256x256 image (criterion benchmark: bc1, bc3, bc4, bc5, bc6h and bc7 presets, bc7 opaque and alpha, etc1), plus a full 4096x4096 texture (examples/lambertian.jpg) across all presets.
claimed_speedup: PR #50 (merged 2026-09-28) title: BC6H 1.8-3.1x, BC7 2.1-6.2x and ETC1 6.1x faster; BC1-BC5 unchanged. Per-row examples (256x256, 1 thread): bc7_opaque/basic 51.07 ms to 20.14 ms (2.54x) and bc7_alpha/basic 68.44 ms to 13.18 ms (5.19x) versus main on ISPC 1.20; versus PR #49 (the same kernels rebuilt with ISPC 1.31) bc7_opaque/basic 49.37 ms to 20.14 ms (2.45x) and bc7_alpha/basic 68.21 ms to 13.18 ms (5.18x); bc6h/fast 3.10x, bc7_alpha/slow 6.18x, etc1 6.06x; 2.35x total across all presets at 4096x4096.
compiler_and_flags: ISPC 1.31 (LLVM 23) after PR #49, Apple CPU targets pinned (apple-a14 for macOS builds); Rust release profile lto = true, opt-level = 3, codegen-units = 1 (Cargo.toml); harness is criterion (cargo bench -- --save-baseline main, then --baseline main) as described in the PR text.
hardware: Apple M5 Max (ARM64 NEON), 1 thread; x86, Windows, Linux and Android binaries were regenerated but not benchmarked
stars_or_usage: 17 stars, 3 forks; published on crates.io as intel_tex_2 0.5.0
tradeoffs: Rust bindings over prebuilt ISPC kernels (ISPC and libclang only needed with --features ispc to regenerate; binaries for macOS, iOS, Android, Linux and Windows are committed in the repo). Speedups came from removing per-lane gathers (NEON has no gather), inlining helpers, hoisting subset work and sharing work between modes, which also made fully inlined kernels much slower to compile (generate-binaries CI jobs went from about 2/3/4 minutes to 17/23/45 minutes on macOS/Linux/Windows). Quality: PSNR change within 0.0001 dB for BC1, BC3 and BC7, worst single image -0.006 dB (BC6H); ETC1 final commits changed tie-breaking so about 10% of blocks differ with equal or better PSNR. Kernels derive from the discontinued Intel ISPCTextureCompressor, now vendored from Traverse Research's fork. ASTC is listed as pending in the README.
caveats: The lead's framing (2.1-6.2x faster than Intel ispc_texcomp) is not what the PR measures: the baseline is the crate's own previous main, which is the Intel kernels built with ISPC 1.20, so the gain is against an older build of the same lineage. Only Apple Silicon was measured, and much of the gain comes from avoiding gathers that are expensive on NEON, so the x86 gain is unknown (PR #51 says the same about its own estimator changes). I could not find the criterion benchmark code in the repository tree (no benches/ directory on main; PR #50 has two commits, 'Update vendor to the fork's ARM64 performance work' and 'Regenerate binaries with the optimized kernels'), so the numbers are not reproducible from the repo as read; hence tier C, not A. PR text was read through a page summarizer on two separate fetches that agreed on the headline figures and sample rows; treat per-row values as quoted, not verbatim copies. The repo commits page for main still showed 2026-07-01 as latest while the PR list shows PRs #49, #50 and #51 merged 2026-09-28 (last_commit uses the merge date). Related same-day evidence at https://github.com/Traverse-Research/intel-tex-rs-2/pull/51 (BC7 bc7e-style partition ranking, opaque presets 1.04-1.73x faster than the post-#50 state on 24 Kodak images, Apple M5 Max, 1 thread; on a 4K texture the PR says bc7e is slower than the new kernel at every comparable quality level, e.g. veryfast 2.38 s vs 1.05 s at 51.27 dB and basic 8.84 s vs 5.21 s); this could be a stronger third-party-baseline entry once the harness is public.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/Traverse-Research/intel-tex-rs-2/pull/50 (plus /pull/49, /pull/51, repo page, README.md, Cargo.toml, .gitmodules)

name: jpeg-rusturbo
baseline: image crate JPEG encoder (jpeg-encoder) and decoder (zune-jpeg) as used by the Rust image crate; not libjpeg-turbo
workload: Encoding RGB to 4:2:0 JPEG at q=80 for 1592x1124, 1080p and 4K, single thread and auto threads; decoding the resulting JPEG to RGB on synthetic and natural-like images.
claimed_speedup: Encode 4:2:0 4K single thread: Apple M-series 13.41 ms vs 67.61 ms for image (5.04x); Intel Xeon Platinum 8272CL 57.27 ms vs 320.93 ms (5.60x). Encode with threads=auto 4K: 6.83 ms vs 68.47 ms (10.02x) on Apple M, 46.77 ms vs 320.95 ms (6.86x) on Xeon. Decode 4K natural-like: 5.93 ms vs 7.00 ms (1.18x) Apple M, 28.01 ms vs 34.26 ms (1.22x) Xeon; decode at 1592x1124 on Xeon is parity or slightly slower (0.97x to 0.98x).
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench with release profile lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1; SIMD build (AVX2 / NEON) versus force-scalar feature; rustc version not stated.
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8272CL @ 2.60 GHz, 4 vCPU (AVX2); Apple Silicon M-series developer laptop, 8 cores (exact model not stated), NEON.
stars_or_usage: 0 stars; crates.io jpeg-rusturbo 0.9.2 with about 7.8k downloads
tradeoffs: Rust crate with unsafe SIMD kernels (AVX2 and NEON only, AVX-512 and SVE explicitly not planned). Encoder handles baseline and progressive, RGB/gray/CMYK, EXIF/ICC pass-through; decoder handles baseline and progressive Huffman. Optional rayon threading.
caveats: No comparison with libjpeg-turbo or mozjpeg: the baseline is the Rust image crate, whose encoder is scalar, so the 5x to 10x encode win says nothing about libjpeg-turbo. Decode is at rough parity with zune-jpeg (the BENCH.md says so itself). Methodology is one timed batch of 50 iterations after 3 warm-ups with no statistical filtering; Apple M CPU model and rustc version not stated; decode numbers are retained from an older campaign.
found_via: WebSearch: 'pure Rust image decoder faster than libpng libjpeg-turbo libwebp benchmark github' snippet mentioning jpeg-rusturbo, then crates.io API and github.com/naoto256/jpeg-rusturbo plus BENCH.md.

name: jpeg4py (Python libjpeg-turbo wrapper)
language: Python (cffi bindings over the C library libjpeg-turbo)
baseline: Python Pillow Image.open().tobytes() and scipy.misc.imread() JPEG decoding
workload: Decoding JPEG files into numpy arrays through the TurboJPEG API (tjDecompress2), single-threaded and multithreaded.
claimed_speedup: README: 'about 1.3 times faster than Image.open().tobytes() and scipy.misc.imread() in a single thread and up to 9 times faster in multithreaded mode.'
tradeoffs: Decode only (tjInitDecompress, tjDecompressHeader2, tjDecompress2); needs libturbojpeg installed separately. The multithreaded gain comes from releasing the GIL, not from a faster decoder. Python binding, so not usable directly from C++.
caveats: Wrapper of libjpeg-turbo, which is already catalogued, so this duplicates that entry. README was written for Python 2.7/3.4 on Ubuntu 14.04 and names no CPU, library version or benchmark script; the comparison targets are Pillow and scipy of that era. Repository is abandoned (last commit 2018-02-23).
found_via: PyPI JSON API scan (pypi.org/pypi/jpeg4py/json: 'libjpeg-turbo cffi bindings and helper classes'), then repo page and commits on github.com

name: LERC (Limited Error Raster Compression)
baseline: zlib deflate level 9 (labelled 'LZW' in the benchmark document; called through compress2)
workload: Tile-by-tile (1024 max tile) encode and decode of float and 16-bit integer geospatial rasters (4600x4300 float TIFFs, DTED-1 1201x1201 and DTED-2 3601x3601 int16 elevation, multi-band 11/16-bit satellite imagery) against zlib level 9.
claimed_speedup: Lossless 16-bit DTED-2 (MaxZError 0): average encode 231 ms vs 2484 ms and average decode 51 ms vs 130 ms for zlib-9 (about 10.8x and 2.5x, derived from page data). Float rasters (MaxZError 0.01): average encode 0.3 s vs 8.1 s, decode 68 ms vs 424 ms. Multi-spectral lossless: average encode 2.4 s vs 30.5 s, decode 0.7 s vs 1.8 s; the document says 'the much faster encoding speed of 5-10x'. README: encode about 20-30 ms and decode about 5 ms per megapixel per band.
stars_or_usage: 215 stars; vcpkg port lerc and Conan recipe lerc; README says it is used in Esri software
tradeoffs: Special-purpose raster codec for 16-bit and larger or float data with a bounded per-pixel error (MaxZError); lossless only for integer types with MaxZError 0 and only slightly better ratio than zlib there. The README itself says PNG can compress 8-bit data better.
caveats: Benchmark document is from February 2016 and states no CPU, compiler or flags. The baseline is zlib deflate level 9 (not libpng or a tuned PNG encoder). The lossy LERC settings (MaxZError 0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 2, 4, 5) are not the same task as lossless zlib, so only the MaxZError 0 columns are like for like. Not a general photographic codec.
found_via: vcpkg port scan (microsoft/vcpkg ports/lerc, description 'rapid encoding and decoding for any pixel type'), then README link to doc/LercBenchmarks_Feb_2016.pdf

name: libjpeg-turbo
baseline: IJG libjpeg (libjpeg 6b reference)
workload: JPEG compression and decompression on systems with common CPU architectures, SIMD-accelerated Huffman and DCT paths.
claimed_speedup: README: 'generally 2-6x as fast as libjpeg, all else being equal'; on systems without SIMD support it 'can still outperform libjpeg by a significant amount' thanks to optimized Huffman coding.
tradeoffs: Drop-in libjpeg API and ABI plus the simpler TurboJPEG API; SIMD per architecture (x86, ARM and others); the README lists performance pitfalls: decompression can drop by as much as 20% (still far above libjpeg) for JPEGs with restart markers, and compression can drop by as much as 40% when the fast integer forward DCT is used at JPEG quality 98 to 100.
caveats: First-party claim with no published methodology, so tier C; this category's own baseline list already names libjpeg-turbo, so it is recorded here against the IJG libjpeg incumbent. Independent runs I opened show it ahead of newer decoders: jpeg-nitro's README table has libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2 at 124 ms per image versus stb_image 175 ms and Wuffs 159 ms on an Intel i9, and google/decoder-benchmarks-for-rust has turbojpeg at 84.25 ms versus jpeg-decoder at 126.2 ms on a 2000x3000 image. Neither run uses IJG libjpeg as the baseline.
found_via: Opened libjpeg-turbo README after the 'faster than libjpeg-turbo' search; checked its ChangeLog for other speed numbers

name: libjpeg-turbo-rs
baseline: libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2 (decode) and 3.2.0 (encode)
workload: JPEG decode of 64x64 to 3840x2160 images at 4:2:0, 4:2:2, 4:4:4, quality 75, and encode at 640x480 to 1920x1080, Rust vs C in microseconds per image, on x86_64 AVX2 and Apple M1 Pro.
claimed_speedup: README decode table, Intel i5-10400 vs C libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2: time ratios 0.77x (320x240 4:2:0), 0.87x (1280x720 4:2:0), 0.90x (1920x1080 4:2:0), 0.93x (2560x1440), 0.88x (3840x2160), but 1.23x (64x64) and 1.05x (640x480 4:2:0), i.e. about 3 to 23% faster on most sizes. Encode on Zen 3 and Zen 4 runners: stock build is 1.05 to 1.10x C 3.2.0's time at 1080p (slower); the target-cpu=native i5-10400 build is 2 to 7% faster than C 3.1.2. Apple M1 Pro: 0.99 to 1.07x of C.
compiler_and_flags: stock `cargo build --release` (portable runtime dispatch) for decode and the portable encode table; RUSTFLAGS=-C target-cpu=native for the supplementary i5-10400 encode table; rustc and C build flags not stated
hardware: Intel Core i5-10400 @ 2.90GHz (turbo off); AMD EPYC 7763 (Zen 3) and Zen 4 GitHub runners; Apple M1 Pro
tradeoffs: Pure-Rust port of libjpeg-turbo with NEON, AVX2, SSE2 and WASM SIMD128 kernels, byte-for-byte cross-validated against C in CI; ships C ABI shims (TurboJPEG 3 and libjpeg-compatible) so C++ can link it. MSRV 1.87. Lossless transforms and progressive supported.
caveats: First-party harness, tiny project (9 stars); the commit page credits Claude as co-author on recent commits. Decode wins are 3 to 23% and mixed (small images lose); the stock portable encoder is slower than C on 1080p, only a target-cpu=native build wins. Compiler versions and C libjpeg-turbo build flags are not stated, so tier C. On Apple M1 Pro it is not faster than C.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'SIMD JPEG encoder decoder AVX2 AVX-512 NEON faster than libjpeg-turbo github open source 2025'

name: libqoi
baseline: qoixx (wx257osn2/qoixx)
workload: Encoding and decoding a 640x480, 30 fps webcam stream inside ROS (robotics framework), reported by a third-party user.
claimed_speedup: Issue #1 (2022-07-24): 'About 20% faster to encode and about 30% faster to decode' than qoixx.
hardware: Intel i7-10875H @ 2.30GHz x 16, as written in the issue.
stars_or_usage: 9 stars; proposed for ROS image_transport_plugins in PRs #103 and #104
tradeoffs: README: work in progress, compliant with QOI v1.0, based on the phoboslab reference implementation; expect API breaks. Only 5 commits.
caveats: One informal third-party comment: no benchmark code, compiler, flags, qoixx version, image content or repeat counts, and the stream is a live webcam so the numbers are end-to-end in a ROS node. Not a comparison against libpng or the listed incumbents. The ROS PR #103 text (https://github.com/ros-perception/image_transport_plugins/pull/103) adds only that QOI kept a 640x480 30 fps stream at 30 fps where PNG dropped to 3 fps, with CPU at 28 percent for compression and 13 percent for decompression against PNG above 100 percent; it does not say which QOI library produced those figures. No benchmark in the repo (tools/ holds only unix_compile.func). Last commit September 2022.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/ShadowMitia/libqoi issue #1 and README; ROS PR #103 as context

name: lodepng-turbo
baseline: libpng
workload: Baseline PNG decompression using SIMD filters and libdeflate in place of zlib (no workload described).
claimed_speedup: README: 'On x86 and x86-64 or ARM systems, lodepng-turbo is twice as fast as libpng, but it may be slower elsewhere.' No numbers beyond 'twice as fast'.
tradeoffs: Hacked lodepng with libdeflate (git submodule, builds with gcc/clang and GNU make) plus 'depng' prediction routines for unfiltering; accelerates decoding only. Implements both the lodepng API and a TurboPNG API. README itself warns it 'may be slower elsewhere'.
caveats: No benchmark program, methodology, CPU, compiler or data in the repository; the single ratio is first-party. Repository has had no commits since January 2019, so numbers predate current libpng (which has its own SIMD) and libdeflate. The predecessor repository kanryu/simd_lode_png states a goal of 5x libpng but contains no measurements.
found_via: WebSearch 'fast PNG decoder encoder faster than libpng SIMD library site:github.com' (result kanryu/lodepng-turbo); opened README and commits page

name: lowzag
baseline: libjpeg-turbo (progressive coefficient array memory); also ROM TJpgDec for decode time on ESP32
workload: Progressive JPEG decode at 1/2, 1/4 and 1/8 scale of a 12-megapixel 4:2:0 image (peak allocation), plus decode time of progressive lowzag versus baseline TJpgDec on an ESP32-S3 at 240 MHz for 800x480, 1600x1200 and 4000x3000 test cards.
claimed_speedup: Memory at 12 MP: lowzag 36.2, 19.6, 6.8 and 3.4 MB at scales 1/1, 1/2, 1/4 and 1/8 against libjpeg 36.1 MB at every scale (about 10.6x less at 1/8, derived from page data); with an 800x480 crop 3.4 to 2.3 MB. Decode time on ESP32-S3: 4000x3000 5.7 s vs 9.1 s for ROM TJpgDec baseline JPEG, 1600x1200 1.75 s vs 1.95 s, 800x480 0.63 s vs 0.46 s (slower).
hardware: ESP32-S3 at 240 MHz (timing table); memory numbers are allocation sizes, not tied to a CPU
tradeoffs: Progressive JPEG only, portable C99, decodes at 1/2, 1/4 or 1/8 scale without allocating the full coefficient array (keeps only the low-frequency corner its reduced IDCT needs); cropping and cancellation supported; ESP-IDF component. No arithmetic coding, CMYK or lossless JPEG; 8-bit, 1 or 3 components. Development is on a private GitLab with GitHub as mirror.
caveats: Memory numbers compare two different quantities (lowzag's own info.peak_alloc versus the coefficient array size libjpeg-turbo requests, computed from its JBLOCK size), as the README itself notes; process peak RSS is said to track both. The speed table is single measurements from one board and not reproducible on a host. This is a memory win, not a speed win: at 800x480 baseline TJpgDec is faster. Commit history shows an AI co-author. The README statement that mozjpeg, stb_image, Go image/jpeg and Rust jpeg-decoder also size progressive coefficient storage from the source dimensions comes from reading their source, not from measurement.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/image-decoder sorted by recently updated ('Progressive JPEG decoder optimized for low memory')

name: MANGO image codecs
baseline: libpng and libjpeg (version not stated in README; possibly libjpeg-turbo)
workload: Decode and encode time in milliseconds of one 2560x1600 and one 4833x5875 PNG, and one 5184x3456 and one 2560x1600 JPEG, against libpng, lodepng, stb, spng, fpng, Wuffs and libjpeg, toojpeg.
claimed_speedup: README table, 2560x1600 PNG: mango decode 3.2 ms vs libpng 57.3 ms (about 18x, derived from page data) and encode 57.2 ms vs 820.5 ms (about 14x, derived). 4833x5875 PNG: decode 53.7 vs 379.5 ms, encode 287.0 vs 14051.3 ms. JPEG 5184x3456: decode 23.3 vs libjpeg 197.8 ms (about 8.5x, derived), encode 18.5 vs 70.1 ms (about 3.8x, derived). JPEG 2560x1600: decode 3.2 vs 32.9 ms, encode 4.3 vs 16.3 ms.
hardware: 11th Gen Intel Core i7-11800H @ 2.30GHz (PNG tables); Intel Core i9-8950HK @ 2.90GHz (JPEG tables)
tradeoffs: Large C++20 graphics library (vector math, SIMD abstraction, virtual filesystem, Vulkan text) with image codecs inside, not a standalone codec. Mango's PNG encode output is larger than libpng's (3531 KB vs 2843 KB on the first image) and its JPEG output is slightly larger than libjpeg's.
caveats: First-party table with no compiler, flags or thread count stated, and the libjpeg version is unstated (the 90 MP/s libjpeg decode speed suggests an optimised build, but this is not confirmed). Mango's decode may use multiple threads; not stated. In both PNG tables the mango output size equals the quoted input file size (3531 KB and 33598 KB), so the input PNGs may themselves be mango-produced, which could favour its decoder. README quotes a sceptical comment from libspng's author.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: web search 'github image codec faster than libjpeg-turbo OR faster than libpng ...' surfaced LibMango as a JPEG codec faster than libjpeg-turbo; README opened
Prior knowledge of C++ image libraries (not surfaced by a search query); opened the t0rakka/mango github.com page, README, license and commits page

name: mozjpeg-rs
baseline: mozjpeg (C encoder, libjpeg-turbo fork with trellis quantization)
workload: Encoding a 2048x2048 (4 MP) image 30 times with trellis quantization (AC + DC) and with Huffman-optimized baseline settings.
claimed_speedup: README: trellis modes 'produce 0.05-0.80% smaller files than C mozjpeg while being 6% faster at 2048x2048'. Table: Trellis (AC + DC) 197 ms vs 210 ms for C mozjpeg ('6% faster'); Baseline (huffman opt) 42 ms vs 9 ms for C mozjpeg ('4.6x slower').
compiler_and_flags: cargo test --release --test bench_2k -- --nocapture, 'release mode with AVX2/NEON'; rustc version and RUSTFLAGS not stated.
tradeoffs: Safe Rust (#![forbid(unsafe_code)]) using the archmage safe-SIMD layer; encoder only. Output is byte-identical to C mozjpeg for baseline and progressive modes; trellis output differs slightly (smaller) unless TrellisMode::MozjpegExact is chosen. Optional fast_color(true) gives about 40% faster RGB to YCbCr at the cost of exact parity.
caveats: The speed win exists only for trellis quantization and is 6% on one image size; the faster-baseline case is 4.6x slower than C mozjpeg (README admits the entropy-coding gap). No CPU model, compiler version or flags beyond 'release'. Baseline is mozjpeg, not libjpeg-turbo or libpng.
found_via: WebSearch: 'mozjpeg pure Rust port benchmark faster than mozjpeg libjpeg-turbo encoder github' returned github.com/imazen/mozjpeg-rs; opened repo, README and commits page.

name: msf_gif
language: C (single header, compiles as C99 or C++98)
baseline: gif.h (Charlie Tangora's single-header encoder, named gif_h in the timings file) and jo_gif
workload: GIF encoding time on the author's test animations in the separate msf_gif-testing repo (workload size not stated in the timings file).
claimed_speedup: README: 'uses SSE where available to encode at hundreds of megabytes a second, several times faster than comparable gif libraries'. timings.txt in msf_gif-testing: jo_gif ~425 seconds, gif_h ~75 seconds, msf_gif ~14 seconds, msf_gif simd ~8 seconds, msf_gif threaded ~4 seconds, msf_gif simd threaded ~2 seconds (about 5x vs gif_h and 30x vs jo_gif, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Uses one fixed constant-quality palette-and-dither scheme per frame instead of adaptive quantization; delta encoding between frames for smaller files. SSE on x86 only (NEON listed as a TODO). Public domain, also available under MIT.
caveats: The timings file is a four-line note with no hardware, input set, compiler or flags, so it is a bare first-party number; it does not say which gif.h the label gif_h refers to (presumably Charlie Tangora's). A gifski comparison is a TODO in the author's notes. The mix of MIT and public-domain dedication carries no patent grant.
found_via: github.com/topics/gif?l=c page listed notnullnotvoid/msf_gif; README plus the linked msf_gif-testing repo timings.txt read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: mtpng (parallel PNG encoder with C API)
baseline: libpng
workload: Re-encoding a dual-4K screenshot PNG at default options, single-threaded and multi-threaded, compared with libpng built by gcc and clang.
claimed_speedup: docs/perf.md old data (MacBook Pro 13in 2015, Core i7 3.1 GHz, Linux x86_64): libpng gcc 850 ms, libpng clang 900 ms, mtpng 1 thread 555 ms (1.5x vs libpng gcc, derived from page data), 2 threads 302 ms (2.8x derived), 4 threads 248 ms (3.4x derived). README: single-threaded about 30-40% faster than libpng (Rust 1.29.0, Sept 2018), 'multiple threads consistently beats libpng by a lot'. 2026 data lists only mtpng times (e.g. Apple M3 Max 23 ms at 16 threads, 237 ms at 1 thread; Ryzen 9 5950X 25 ms at 32 threads, 301 ms at 1 thread).
compiler_and_flags: cargo run --release (Rust); libpng built with gcc or clang, versions and zlib not stated
hardware: MacBook Pro 13in 2015, 5th-gen Core i7 3.1 GHz, 2 cores plus Hyper-Threading (libpng comparison); several newer machines for mtpng-only timings
tradeoffs: Encoder only; input must be pre-packed pixels. Compression ratio is a tiny fraction worse than libpng at the default 256 KiB chunk size (closer with larger chunks). Files under 128 KiB uncompressed see no threading gain. Rust library with a C API that the README says is still unstable; pulls libz_sys. Small-file and ancillary-chunk support needs work.
caveats: perf.md itself says '@fixme how did I measure those libpng times? need to recreate that', so the libpng baseline numbers are from 2015-2018 and unverified; the 2026 section has no libpng column. Third-party libpng version and zlib build are unstated.
found_via: github.com/topics/png-encoder page listed brion/mtpng; README and docs/perf.md read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: nativewebp
baseline: Go standard library image/png encoder at png.BestCompression
workload: Encoding five images from Google's WebP lossless gallery with the lossless-only nativewebp encoder at nativewebp.BestCompression versus image/png at png.BestCompression, reported in ns/op together with output size.
claimed_speedup: README: encoder is 'approximately 50% faster' than the standard Go PNG encoder and produces smaller files. Per image (PNG ns/op vs nativewebp ns/op): 42,945,049 vs 35,413,726 (17% faster, 21% smaller file); 98,509,399 vs 42,626,779 (57% faster, 24% smaller); 178,205,535 vs 96,800,750 (46% faster, 19% smaller); 29,088,555 vs 19,877,708 (32% faster, 26% smaller); 63,423,995 vs 27,813,126 (56% faster, 14% smaller).
compiler_and_flags: Go benchmark (ns/op); Go version and flags not stated.
tradeoffs: Pure Go, no cgo or libwebp. Encodes only lossless WebP (VP8L) and animations; decoding is a wrapper around golang.org/x/image/webp. Not a lossy encoder.
caveats: README calls it 'a quick benchmark': five gallery images, no hardware or Go version, no benchmark code location named. The comparison is against Go's own PNG encoder, not libwebp, libpng or any C codec, so it does not show nativewebp beating libwebp (which compresses and encodes differently).
found_via: GitHub: opened github.com/HugoSmits86/nativewebp directly while checking Go WebP libraries (Go row of the any-language assignment); read README and commits page.

name: nvavif-py
baseline: Pillow with pillow-avif-plugin (libavif/libaom decode) and software AV1 encoders (libaom, rav1e, SVT-AV1) for encode
workload: Decoding a 5184x3456 AVIF to a NumPy array including disk read, and encoding AVIF with NVIDIA NVENC versus software AV1 encoders.
claimed_speedup: README decode table: nvavif_py.decode_file() ~80 ms vs Pillow (pillow-avif-plugin) ~360 ms (a second table says 320 ms), OpenCV ~280 ms, imageio + av ~400 ms; 'nvavif_py is 3-4x faster than standard tools'. Encode: NVENC 'milliseconds per image' versus software 'dozens of seconds per image', '200x'.
tradeoffs: PyO3 Rust extension wrapping dav1d (decode, fixed-point YUV to RGB, rayon), rav1e (CPU encode fallback) and NVENC AV1 hardware encode via ffmpeg-next; GPU encode needs an RTX 40/50-series (Ada Lovelace or Blackwell) card. Pillow save plugin included.
caveats: Numbers have no stated hardware, library versions, thread counts or method, and the two README tables disagree (320 ms vs 360 ms for Pillow). Single commit ('init'), zero stars. The decode gain is mostly a backend choice (dav1d, multithreaded) versus a plugin the README says uses libaom, so it is largely a dav1d wrapper effect, and the NVENC 'dozens of seconds versus milliseconds' encode comparison is hardware versus software at unmatched quality settings. Likely folds into the dav1d, rav1e and libavif entries.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/avif-decoder listing flagged imbecility/nvavif-py ('High-performance Python library for encoding/decoding AVIF images using hardware acceleration'); opened repo, README and commits page.

name: opencodecs
baseline: imagecodecs (Python wrappers over libjpeg-turbo, libpng, libwebp, OpenJPEG, libjxl and others) and tifffile for TIFF reading
workload: One codec operation per row at identical settings against imagecodecs 2026.8.16, on 4096x4096 uint16 and 2048x2048 RGB crops, median over fresh alternating processes; plus TIFF read of tifffile-written files against tifffile.
claimed_speedup: TIFF read versus tifffile on Linux: 4.2x (tiled deflate+predictor, 1 reader), 10.0x with 8 readers, 13.2x (3072x3072 uint8, 144 tiles, deflate, 8 readers). Versus imagecodecs: PNG RGB uint8 level 6 encode 3.45x (Mac) and 3.68x (Linux), JPEG quality 90 encode 2.68x (Mac) and 3.91x (Linux), JPEG decode 1.56x (Mac) and 1.80x (Linux), JPEG 2000 lossless threaded 4.66x to 8.05x, JPEG XL threaded 2.30x to 10x, BC7 decode 4.09x to 11x; TIFF LZW decode about 3x.
compiler_and_flags: wheels built as the project's CI wheels (flags not listed); benchmark script bench/bench_vs_imagecodecs.py
hardware: 20-core Apple silicon Mac, 64-core x86-64 Linux workstation (one 4-core group pinned) and a 4-core x86-64 Windows laptop; exact CPU models not stated
tradeoffs: Python package with 39 compiled codec extensions; most codecs wrap system or vendored C libraries (libjpeg-turbo, libwebp, OpenJPEG, vendored libjxl 0.11.2), so C++ users get the algorithmic parts only through the extension sources. Own kernels for LZW, PackBits, BC1 and BC7 decode. Parallel by default for JPEG 2000 and JPEG XL.
caveats: Many of the speedups come from threading by default versus a single-threaded baseline call (rows are marked 'opencodecs threaded'), from libdeflate under PNG (versus zlib), and from lower Python dispatch overhead. README lists many rows at 0.8x to 1.0x (zstd, brotli, lz4, WebP, QOI, JPEG-LS) and PNG decode 0.80x on Windows and 0.99x on Linux, so it is not a blanket win. Benchmark code is public, but CPU models are not named so the tier stays C. Linux JPEG XL lossy decode differs from imagecodecs output by 1 in about a third of values. Repository page shows 463 commits total and a v0.6.0 release on 2026-10-03.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/jpeg-xl sorted by recently updated ('Native, parallel, cloud-aware image codecs for scientific imaging'), README Performance section

name: oss-nvjpg
baseline: libjpeg-turbo
workload: Baseline JPEG decode to an RGB surface, 720x1080 (70 KiB file) and 3200x1800 (1.6 MiB file), average of 1000 iterations, on a Tegra X1 (Aarch64 Cortex-A57 at 2.091 GHz).
claimed_speedup: NVJPG hardware decoder: 2.036 ms vs libjpeg-turbo 6.127 ms (70 KiB image) and 15.997 ms vs 66.341 ms (1.6 MiB image); ratios about 3.0x and 4.1x (derived from page data). Also listed: stb_image with NEON 16.512 and 158.474 ms, Python-pillow 11.688 and 114.918 ms, nanoJPEG 48.299 and 531.575 ms.
hardware: Nvidia Tegra X1 SoC, Aarch64 Cortex-A57 at max 2.091 GHz (hardware JPEG block NVJPG)
tradeoffs: Drives the Tegra X1 hardware JPEG block (NVJPG) through the Host1x interface, so it only runs on Tegra X1 class devices (for example Nintendo Switch homebrew with devkitA64). Baseline JPEG only: progressive and arithmetic coded files return an error. Hardware YUV to RGB conversion and downscaling by up to 8. Requires C++20. GPL-3.0 limits reuse in permissive projects.
caveats: First-party README table only; no compiler, flags or libjpeg-turbo version stated, and the README does not say whether a timing harness ships in the repo. Two test images only. The speedup comes from dedicated hardware, not a better software algorithm, so it does not transfer to other CPUs. The libjpeg-turbo build is presumably NEON-enabled but this is not stated.
found_via: WebSearch 'GPUJPEG OR nvImageCodec JPEG decode throughput vs libjpeg-turbo images per second github benchmark' surfaced the oss-nvjpg reference; README opened on github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com

name: oxipng
baseline: OptiPNG
workload: Lossless PNG optimization of single test images (d3js.org.png, powertoys.png) by an independent blog comparison; wall-clock time and size reduction at default and maximum levels.
claimed_speedup: From the blog, via search snippet: d3js.org.png default level oxipng 0.764 s for 29.14% reduction versus optipng 2.638 s for 25.42% (about 3.5x faster, derived); powertoys.png oxipng 0.266 s for 17.62% versus optipng 0.960 s for 5.85% (about 3.6x faster, derived); at maximum settings oxipng --opt max --zopfli 28.896 s for 30.25% versus optipng -o 7 -strip all 32.800 s for 25.53%.
tradeoffs: Rust command-line tool and library (not a C or C++ API); multithreaded by design, the README says it began as a Rust rewrite of OptiPNG to add multithreading. Optimizes existing PNG/APNG files, it is not a general encoder. Higher levels and --zopfli are slow.
caveats: Snippet only: op111.net is blocked from this environment, so the numbers are copied from a search-result summary and not checked against the page; the oxipng README links the blog as an independent benchmark 'with permission by the author'. Hardware, versions and flags unknown. The speed gain is largely multithreading versus single-threaded OptiPNG, and it is also a better optimizer at the same level, so the comparison mixes time and size.
found_via: WebSearch 'oxipng and friends: A comparison of PNG optimization tools'; oxipng README Benchmarks section links the blog

name: Pfim
baseline: FreeImage, DevIL and ImageMagick (native C/C++ libraries driven through .NET wrappers), plus managed Targa/DDS decoders (TargaImage, ImageFormats, StbSharp, TgaSharpLib)
workload: Decoding one 120x120 image stored as 3 Targa variants (24-bit RLE, 32-bit RLE, 32-bit raw) and 4 DDS variants (32-bit, DXT1, DXT3, DXT5), measured with BenchmarkDotNet as mean time per decode.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Pfim is hands down the fastest targa decoder. More than 10x faster than the closest competitor'; for DDS 'one of the fastest if not the fastest', first everywhere except DXT5 where it is 1% slower. From TargaBenchmark-report.csv (Mean column, unit not printed, BenchmarkDotNet default is ns): 24bit-rle.tga Pfim 5,083.1 vs FreeImage 65,756.5 vs DevILSharp 47,792.0 (about 12.9x and 9.4x, derived from page data); 32bit.tga Pfim 3,655.9 vs DevILSharp 52,740.6 (about 14.4x, derived from page data). DdsBenchmark-report.csv: 32bit.dds Pfim 1,569.2 vs DevILSharp 115,072.4; dxt1.dds Pfim 46,734.1 vs FreeImage 75,354.5; dxt5.dds Pfim 93,732.4 vs FreeImage 92,683.4 (Pfim slightly slower).
compiler_and_flags: BenchmarkDotNet; CSV columns show Runtime=Clr, Jit=RyuJit, Platform=X64; release build flags and .NET Framework version not stated in the numbers file.
tradeoffs: .NET library that decodes only Targa (TGA) and DirectDraw Surface (DDS) files; no PNG/JPEG/WebP. Returns raw pixel data with optional pooled allocator, so display needs extra glue (System.Drawing, ImageSharp, WPF samples in the README).
caveats: One 120x120 test image per format, so per-call fixed costs dominate. The CSV carries no CPU model. DevIL, FreeImage and ImageMagick are called through .NET wrapper libraries, so interop overhead is included in their times. README claim 'more than 10x faster than the closest competitor' does not hold for 24bit-rle.tga against DevILSharp (9.4x, derived from page data). Competitor versions are from the 0.10.0 era (DevIL 0.2.19, FreeImage 4.3.6, ImageMagick 7.12.0). Baselines are not libjpeg-turbo/libpng/libwebp/libavif, so the result says little about mainstream codecs.
found_via: GitHub: opened github.com/nickbabcock/Pfim (C# row of the any-language assignment) and its analysis/ directory (TargaBenchmark-report.csv, DdsBenchmark-report.csv).

name: pngenc
baseline: libpng 1.6 (with zlib)
workload: Encode one 1920x1080 24-bit image to PNG in three low-compression modes (uncompressed, Huffman-only, RLE).
claimed_speedup: README table (ms, libpng 1.6 vs pngenc 1 thread vs pngenc multi-threaded): Uncompressed 9 vs 0.8 vs 0.2; Huffman Only 82 vs 7.3 vs 1.2; RLE 84 vs 30 vs 4. README says 'up to an order of magnitude faster' at the same compression rates in those modes.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X
tradeoffs: Encoder only. Supports only uncompressed, Huffman-only and RLE modes (full LZ77 is 'N/A'), so it does not replace libpng at default compression levels. Needs OpenMP for the multi-threaded numbers; tested with gcc/mingw, clang and MSVC. Author calls it a hobby project; the CRC32 code is adapted from Mark Adler under a zlib-compatible license.
caveats: Single first-party table, one image and one CPU; compiler, flags and benchmark harness are not stated. The comparison is against libpng's low-effort strategies (Z_HUFFMAN_ONLY, Z_RLE) which the README itself calls a valid trade-off. No libpng-at-default-level comparison is given for any mode that pngenc supports.
found_via: WebSearch 'fast PNG decoder encoder faster than libpng SIMD library site:github.com' (result GregorBudweiser/pngenc); opened readme.md, LICENSE and commits page

name: PngEncoder (Java)
baseline: javax.imageio PNG writer (ImageIO, JDK built-in encoder)
workload: Encoding BufferedImages to PNG at the default compression level 9: a random 1024x1024 image, a 2121x350 logo and a 4900x6000 fashion photograph, reported as images encoded per second.
claimed_speedup: README: 'About 5 times faster than ImageIO (on a computer with 8 logical cores)'. Table (images encoded per second, PngEncoder vs ImageIO): random1024x1024 36.324 vs 5.150 (7.1x), logo2121x350 127.034 vs 24.857 (5.1x), looklet4900x6000 0.159 vs 0.029 (5.5x). Lowering the compression level adds up to 2.3x more speed at the cost of about 2.5x larger files (level 1) according to the README speed-versus-size table.
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark source is PngEncoderBenchmarkPngEncoderVsImageIO.java in the repo; JDK version and JVM flags not stated (project targets Java 8).
hardware: A computer with 8 logical cores (CPU model not stated).
stars_or_usage: 46 stars; used in production at Looklet per README
tradeoffs: Pure Java; speedup comes mainly from multithreaded DEFLATE over blocks, so output is about 2% larger than ImageIO at the same level. Optional predictor encoding and indexed output give smaller files at a speed cost. Encoder only.
caveats: Speedup is almost entirely multithreading: README says a single-core machine will not see a significant gain. CPU model, JDK version and warm-up method are not stated, and the benchmark is the project's own. Baseline is the JDK ImageIO writer, not libpng; the Java wrapper fpng-java (not reported here) reports much larger gains over ImageIO by calling the native fpng library.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Java image codec library faster than ImageIO benchmark PNG JPEG WebP encoder decoder github "faster than"' returned github.com/pngencoder/pngencoder.

name: ptpng
baseline: libpng with zlib-ng 2.2.4 (ZLIB_COMPAT); for the encoder also stock zlib level 6 and zlib-ng level 6
workload: PNG decode (27 cases across native, RGB8 and RGBA8 output) and encode (nine generated fixtures: gradients, graphics, noise) on five CI platforms, median of alternating rounds.
claimed_speedup: README: decoder geometric-mean speedup over libpng + zlib-ng 2.2.4 across 27 cases is 1.80x Linux x64, 1.64x Windows x64, 1.59x Linux ARM64, 1.62x macOS ARM64 and 1.46x Windows ARM64 (30 Sep 2026 run). Encoder (after 1 Oct change) averages 2.25-2.98x stock zlib level 6 and 1.14-1.52x zlib-ng, with files at most 2.4% larger than zlib-ng level 6.
