compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build; nightly workflow matrix uses gcc, clang and MSVC cl (versions not stated); PERFORMANCE.md quotes -O3 for paired runs and MSVC /O2 for one local run
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (Windows x64 runner, four logical CPUs) for the 30 Sep snapshot; Intel i7-1355U for local runs; Neoverse-N2 for Linux ARM64 (PERFORMANCE.md)
tradeoffs: No LICENSE file found at the repo root (raw.githubusercontent.com returned 404 for LICENSE, LICENSE.md and LICENSE.txt) and the README has no license section, so reuse rights are unclear. Single-threaded; library calls must be serialized across threads (shared tables and dispatch state). Encoder writes non-interlaced PNG without palette, packed-sample or metadata support. C11 core with a header-only C++17/20 wrapper; AVX2/SSE2 on x86 and NEON on ARM64.
caveats: Very new repository (0 stars; commit activity visible from 2026-09-24 and PERFORMANCE.md is titled 'September-October 2026'); numbers change nightly and the README says compare ratios only within a run. Fixtures are synthetic (gradients, graphics, random noise) and the project itself says they do not establish a fastest-in-the-world claim. Decoder loses on some Windows cases (26/27) and the new encoder loses to zlib-ng level 6 in several fixtures (for example 0.76x on photo_rgb8 in the local i7-1355U table per PERFORMANCE.md). Compiler versions are not stated, so a verifier who finds them in CI logs could promote this to tier A.
found_via: WebSearch 'fast PNG decoder encoder faster than libpng SIMD library site:github.com' (result bojosos/ptpng); opened README, PERFORMANCE.md, CI workflows and commits page

name: pyspng (Python libspng wrapper)
language: Python (pybind11 extension over the C library libspng)
baseline: Python Pillow PNG loading (libpng with zlib)
workload: Loading uncompressed (PNG compression level 0) PNG files into numpy arrays, aimed at machine-learning datasets.
claimed_speedup: README and PyPI page: 'Synthetic benchmarks indicate pyspng to be roughly 2-3x faster in loading uncompressed PNGs than the Python Pillow library.'
stars_or_usage: 12 stars; PyPI package pyspng (a fork, pyspng-seunglab, adds progressive decoding)
tradeoffs: Decode only, no image manipulation. Python binding, so not directly usable from C++; the C++ route is libspng itself. LICENSE file is BSD-3-Clause text taken from the pybind11 template.
caveats: Thin wrapper of libspng, which is already catalogued, so this mostly duplicates that entry; the claim is only about uncompressed PNGs and names no CPU, compiler, Pillow version or benchmark script (none is visible in the repo). Treat as supporting evidence for libspng rather than a separate codec.
found_via: PyPI JSON API scan of image-codec packages (pypi.org/pypi/pyspng/json: 'Fast libspng-based PNG decoder'), then the repo page and commits on github.com

name: PZP (Portable Zipped PNM)
baseline: libpng (PNG decode through OpenCV cv2.imread)
workload: Load time of 500 COCO val2017 panoptic segmentation label maps (3-channel uint8 RGB, varying resolutions), in-process, best of 3 passes, libpzp.so called through Python ctypes with USE_COMPRESSION, USE_RLE and USE_PALETTE flags versus cv2.imread.
claimed_speedup: PNG total 1141.2 ms (2.282 ms per image) vs PZP 500.6 ms (1.001 ms per image): 2.28x faster load; files 4.1 MB as PNG vs 2.0 MB as PZP (52% smaller).
tradeoffs: Not PNG: a custom container (PNM pixel data wrapped in a compact binary header, ZSTD or LZ4, optional delta filter, palette indexing, inter-frame delta, multi-frame with audio) that needs libzstd and liblz4 and has no interoperability with PNG tools. Header-only C with Python ctypes bindings; 8-bit and 16-bit grayscale and RGB only. GPL-3.0.
caveats: First-party numbers with no CPU model, compiler or flags, and the harness is a Python script comparing a ctypes call against cv2.imread (OpenCV overhead is in the PNG column). The dataset is segmentation label maps with few distinct colors, which favour zstd with palette and RLE; the README itself gives this as the best case. The README credits the speedup to zstd decoding faster than zlib plus a flat layout, not to a faster PNG decoder. An optional SIMD (SSE2 and AVX2 prefix-scan) RLE decode path exists (compile-time INTEL_OPTIMIZATIONS) but is not what the headline number isolates. Not compared with fpng, Wuffs or libspng, which decode PNG much faster than libpng.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/image-compression sorted by recently updated with C filter (README headline '2.28x faster to load than PNG')

name: qoi (qoi-rust)
baseline: QOI reference C implementation (phoboslab/qoi qoi.h, commit 8d35d93)
workload: Encode and decode of 2846 PNG images from the QOI benchmark suite (1.32 GPixels, 4.46 GB of raw pixels), single run per codec.
claimed_speedup: Decode 427.4 Mp/s versus 282.9 Mp/s for qoi.h and encode 290.0 Mp/s versus 225.3 Mp/s (1477.7 versus 978.3 MB/s decode, 1002.9 versus 778.9 MB/s encode), about 1.5x decode and 1.3x encode (derived from page data).
hardware: Apple M1 laptop
stars_or_usage: 129 stars; published on crates.io as qoi
tradeoffs: Pure safe Rust (unsafe forbidden), no_std support; usable from C++ only through FFI, there is no C API in the README. Same QOI format and compression ratio as the reference.
caveats: First-party numbers with the suite public but no compiler, flags or rustc version, and one machine (Apple M1). Compares only against the QOI reference, not against libpng, so it says nothing about the category baselines. The README says it is the fastest of the Rust QOI crates but gives no table for the others.
found_via: WebSearch 'QOI encoder decoder AVX2 SIMD faster than reference qoi benchmark github results'

name: qoixx
baseline: qoi.h (reference QOI implementation, phoboslab/qoi)
workload: QOI encode and decode of the QOI benchmark suite (grand total, 20 iterations), ms and megapixels per second, on seven CPUs.
claimed_speedup: README: on Intel Core i9-10900 (g++ 11.1.0) qoi decodes in 2.2389 ms (207.326 mpps) and encodes in 2.5434 ms (182.504 mpps) vs qoixx 1.3477 ms (344.431 mpps) and 1.5255 ms (304.280 mpps), about 1.7x faster in both directions (derived from page data); similar gains on Ryzen 7 2700X, Ryzen 7 3800X, Ryzen 9 3950X, AWS Graviton3, Kryo 585 and Apple M1 Max.
compiler_and_flags: g++ versions listed per CPU, 11.0.0 to 12.0.0 (11.1.0 on the i9-10900); optimization flags not stated
hardware: Intel Core i9-10900; AMD Ryzen 7 2700X; Ryzen 7 3800X; Ryzen 9 3950X; AWS Graviton3; Qualcomm Kryo 585; Apple M1 Max
tradeoffs: Single-header C++20 QOI codec with SIMD encoder (AVX2, SVE or NEON, scalar fallback via QOIXX_NO_SIMD). Decoder is optimized scalar and 'with some input, original implementation is faster'. Output size is identical to qoi.h (463 KB total). Decoder built with MSVC is not fast per the FAQ.
caveats: Baseline is qoi.h, not libpng/libwebp, so this only qualifies indirectly: see the QOI entry for qoi.h vs libpng (about 27x encode, 3.4x decode in nigeltao/qoir's run). Optimization flags and benchmark program are not stated in the README; first-party numbers.
found_via: github.com/topics/image-compression?l=c%2B%2B (wx257osn2/qoixx listed as 'Single Header Quite Fast QOI Implementation written in C++20'); opened README, LICENSE and commits page

name: rapid-qoi
baseline: qoi crate 0.4 (a Rust QOI encoder/decoder; it is the 'qoi' column in the benchmark source bench/src/main.rs). Not libpng, libjpeg-turbo, libwebp or libavif.
workload: In-memory QOI encode and decode of the RGBA pixels of the qoi_benchmark_suite PNG images (qoiformat.org), 5 runs per directory, grand total over the suite.
claimed_speedup: README grand total (ms, qoi vs rapid_qoi): Intel i9 decode 2.009 vs 1.404 (1.43x faster, derived from page data) and encode 2.706 vs 2.520 (1.07x, derived); Apple M1 decode 1.676 vs 1.100 (1.52x, derived) and encode 2.088 vs 1.836 (1.14x, derived). Throughput in Mpps (qoi vs rapid_qoi): i9 decode 231.01 vs 330.72, encode 171.52 vs 184.23; M1 decode 277.01 vs 421.99, encode 222.26 vs 252.77. README text: 'one of the most efficient implementations of QOI encoder and decoder'.
compiler_and_flags: Run with 'cargo run --release -p bench -- [iterations] [path]' (Rust release profile); rustc version and flags not stated. The Intel results directory is named benches/intel-msvc, suggesting a Windows MSVC toolchain.
hardware: 'Intel i9' (exact model not stated) and 'Apple M1'
tradeoffs: no_std and no unsafe, tiny crate (0.8 s clean build on an i9, per README). Rust crate only; no C API or C bindings found, so it is not callable from C++ without writing a wrapper. QOI itself compresses worse than PNG and is limited to 8-bit RGB/RGBA.
caveats: The only comparison is against another QOI implementation, so it says nothing about libpng or libjpeg-turbo. Encode gain is small (7 to 14 percent). In the repo's own benches/m1/rapid.md (the same run that produced the rapid_qoi row) the qoi column reads decode 1.161 ms vs rapid_qoi 1.100 ms (about 5 percent faster) and encode 1.614 ms vs 1.836 ms (rapid_qoi 14 percent slower), so the README's M1 row mixes numbers from benches/m1/reference.md and rapid.md. The README i9 rapid_qoi row (1.404 / 2.520 ms) also differs slightly from benches/intel-msvc/rapid.md (1.447 / 2.582 ms). The README labels the baseline as the 'Reference implementation' phoboslab/qoi, but the current bench source calls the qoi crate; the reference.md outputs may come from an older bench version. CPU model of the i9 and compiler flags are missing. A decoder correctness fix ('clamp QOI_OP_RUN split to remaining output length', 2026-06-29) landed after the README numbers were written.
found_via: Hacker News web search 'Show HN lossless image compression faster than PNG smaller and faster' surfaced the QOI threads ('QOI: Lossless Image Compression in O(n) Time', 'QOI'); thread pages cannot be opened here, so the QOI topic page github.com/topics/qoi led to this repo. README, benches reports and bench source read via github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com.

name: refreshed-astc-encoder
baseline: Mali GPU Texture Compression Tool astcenc binary (32-bit) and ARM astc-encoder official repo build (64-bit, 2015 era)
workload: ASTC compression time of turret_diffuse_map.png at five speed presets (veryfast to exhaustive).
claimed_speedup: 'about 2x faster than the Mali TCT binary and about 1.5x faster than the one from official repo'. Table (seconds, Mali TCT / astcenc / refreshed): veryfast 0.41/0.39/0.19; fast 1.04/0.86/0.40; medium 6.11/4.36/3.20; thorough 22.90/14.98/11.54; exhaustive 52.56/30.99/25.23. Derived from page data: 1.23x-2.15x vs official astcenc and 1.91x-2.60x vs Mali TCT across the five presets.
hardware: Intel Core i5 760
license: ARM ASTC Codec End User Licence Agreement (license.txt, not OSI)
stars_or_usage: 1 star (fork chain: ARM-software/astc-encoder, then Kirpich30000, then abusenius)
tradeoffs: Drop-in replacement for the Mali TCT astcenc binary; claims some quality improvement too. Based on the 2015 astcenc 1.x code line, so the speedup is relative to a very old reference encoder.
caveats: Historical: current ARM astc-encoder 4.x and 5.x are a rewrite with SIMD and are far faster than the 2015 code, so this fork is mainly useful as an example of optimizing the old reference encoder. Single image, one CPU, no flags. Licence is a custom EULA, so treat as reference only. An identical README is in the abusenius/refreshed-astc-encoder fork.
found_via: WebSearch 'ASTC encoder fast compression speed vs astcenc reference github C++ benchmark Mpix/s' surfaced abusenius/refreshed-astc-encoder; upstream Kirpich30000 repo page opened

name: rusty_gif
baseline: FFmpeg 8.1.2 GIF encode via palettegen/paletteuse (dither=none, high-quality path) and FFmpeg's GIF decoder
workload: Encode of 8 real-content frames (CIF to 1080p) with content-routed quantization versus FFmpeg's palettegen/paletteuse; pinned CPU time, interleaved A/B, 15 rounds; PSNR scored against the FFmpeg result. Decode workload not described.
claimed_speedup: README: 1.5-2.5x faster encode at higher PSNR on 8/8 benchmark frames (0.40-0.67x of FFmpeg's CPU time, PSNR +0.2 to +4.1 dB, 15/15 paired wins per frame); decode 'up to 2.5x faster' with no table or workload.
hardware: Not stated.
tradeoffs: #![forbid(unsafe_code)] throughout; LZW is the external pure-Rust weezl crate. The quantizer is output-changing (exact palette up to 256 colours, k-means up to 65,536, budget NeuQuant above) so palettes differ from upstream gif and from FFmpeg; RUSTY_GIF_Q_POLICY=upstream reproduces the pre-fork output byte for byte.
caveats: The speedup comes from a cheaper quantizer, not a faster LZW coder, and the quality side is judged by PSNR, which the k-means step is built to minimize. Not reproducible from the repo: the pinned ABBA harness is referenced in UPSTREAM-CHANGES.md ('see repo bench notes') but is not in this repo, whose examples/ holds only encode_bench.rs (times rusty_gif alone, single frame, and depends on the rusty_alloc-api 1.1.6 dev-dependency) and stage_profile.rs; CPU, compiler flags, FFmpeg build and thread settings are not given; decode claim has no numbers; no comparison against giflib or the listed baselines. Performance fork of image-rs/image-gif (gif 0.14.2 plus color_quant 1.1.0), which has no benchmark data in its page. Kept as a first-party claim, tier C.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/Remade-With-Rust/rusty_gif README, UPSTREAM-CHANGES.md, Cargo.toml and examples/encode_bench.rs; sibling of rusty_jpeg

name: rusty_jpeg
baseline: FFmpeg 8.1.2 native MJPEG encoder and decoder (not libjpeg-turbo)
workload: Encode: 40-frame 1920x1080 4:2:0 clip at about 680 KB per frame to MJPEG at matched output size with fixed Huffman tables on both sides. Decode: one photographic still stream-copied to 300 frames, both arms discarding output. One pinned core each, CPU time, paired interleaved runs.
claimed_speedup: No speedup: README states parity with FFmpeg. Encode median 0.96x (N=41, z -3.59, ours output 3.1% smaller); decode median 1.02x (N=31, z -0.18, inside noise). WHYS.md gives the ratio as FFmpeg time over ours, so encode is about 4% slower and decode about 2% faster. CHANGES.md says earlier claims of 1.19x-1.45x faster were small-N artifacts and were withdrawn.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. Cargo.toml has no custom release profile; default features enable AVX2/SSE4.1 kernels with runtime detection (NEON on aarch64). FFmpeg run with -threads 1 per WHYS.md.
hardware: CPU model not stated; one pinned core; the author notes the test box drifts about 15 percent. Harness scripts in WHYS.md are PowerShell (.ps1).
stars_or_usage: 1 star; README claims 2,784 active installs (RAG Converter runs it as WebAssembly)
tradeoffs: no_std plus alloc builds for ESP32-class chips; x86 AVX2 DCT and SSSE3 IDCT kernels are not bit-identical to the scalar twins (plus or minus 1 LSB); trellis quantization is off by default because it costs +144% encode time; optimized Huffman tables give -7.4% size for 2.09x encode time; chroma is box-averaged on downsample, so output differs from FFmpeg's. IJG attribution clause applies to the forward-DCT files.
caveats: Not faster than the baseline: the project's own final standing is parity, and its encode test (N=41) reads about 4% slower. Checks asked for in the lead: threads, one pinned core and ffmpeg -threads 1, but WHYS.md records that the 'single-threaded' ours arm was silently multithreaded until it was repaired (and an earlier 'decode faster' reading came from extra cores); timer is pinned CPU time; decode input bitstream and per-frame checksums are identical across arms per WHYS.md, while encode outputs differ (matched size only, no output hash comparison). Reproducibility is poor: the paired.ps1 and paired2.ps1 harness scripts are not in the repo tree (examples/ holds decode_bench.rs and others), the CPU and rustc settings are missing, and FFmpeg is a different baseline from libjpeg-turbo. WHYS.md also documents several void measurements and a trellis cost claim off by 46x. The crate is a vendored merge of jpeg-decoder 0.3.2 and jpeg-encoder 0.7.0 (vstroebel) with its own AVX2 and fused decode-IDCT changes; not a GitHub fork. Kept as a flagged entry.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/Remade-With-Rust/rusty_jpeg README, CHANGES.md and WHYS.md (raw.githubusercontent.com)

name: rusty_png
baseline: FFmpeg 8.1.2 PNG decoder and encoder (libavcodec)
workload: PNG decode to rgb24 on 5 admissible images, end-to-end PNG encode from raw pixels (CLIC professional photographs, Derf/xiph video frames) and output size on 9 real graphics (screenshots, charts, diagrams, logos), measured in on-core CPU cycles on one pinned core with ABBA interleaving.
claimed_speedup: README: decode per core '2.55-2.89x faster (median 2.60x)' than FFmpeg; encode wall clock multi-core '2.11-3.06x faster, 0.1-0.2% smaller' (parallel feature, multi-core against FFmpeg's single-threaded encoder); encode per core 0.94-1.05x on CLIC photographs and 0.86-0.91x on Derf video frames (parity to slower); graphics size -6.1% (was +115.6%).
compiler_and_flags: Optional features zlib-rs (on by default) and parallel; compiler version and flags not stated in the README (WHYS.md holds the measurement history).
hardware: 'The same machine', one pinned core each; CPU model not stated.
stars_or_usage: 1 star; README reports 995 active installs through a browser-based file converter
tradeoffs: Performance fork of image-png 0.17.16 for use inside the remade_ffmpeg_rs project: swaps miniz_oxide for flate2's pure-Rust zlib-rs backend, adds multi-threaded DEFLATE for a single image, adaptive filtering for graphics, and memory reductions. Pure Rust, no C.
caveats: Baseline is FFmpeg's PNG codec, not libpng. The decode win is most likely inherited from upstream image-png (already listed) rather than fork changes; the README does not separate the two. The 2-3x encode figure compares multi-core to FFmpeg's single-threaded encoder, and per-core encode is parity or about 13% slower on video frames. Cycle counts exclude process launch; CPU model, rustc version and flags are not stated; Repo created 2026-08-01 by importing a crate from remade_ffmpeg_rs.
found_via: WebSearch: 'fast PNG OR JPEG OR WebP encoder Rust OR Zig OR Nim crate "faster than libpng" ...' returned the repo title 'Decodes 2.7-2.9x faster than FFmpeg'; opened repo, README, commits page.

name: rusty_webp (remade_ffmpeg_rs crates/rusty_webp)
baseline: libwebp (default lossless effort m4, driven through FFmpeg 8.1.2's libwebp encoder); decode rows are against FFmpeg's native VP8/VP8L decoder, not libwebp
workload: Pinned single-core child CPU time, ABBA-interleaved pairs (N = 21-31, null-arm floor 5% or less), on a real-content corpus (Derf video frames 1080p to 8K, screen captures, alpha, odd sizes): lossless VP8L encode versus libwebp m4, plus lossy and lossless WebP decode versus FFmpeg.
claimed_speedup: Lossless encode: '1.6-2.8x faster than libwebp's default effort (m4)' at '+4...13%' size on photos (smaller than libwebp m0 on every corpus image) and 'up to 39% smaller' than m4 on screen or repeated content. Decode versus FFmpeg: lossy (VP8) 8K '1.24-1.29x faster, bit-exact'; lossless (VP8L) 8K '~2.15x faster'.
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, #![forbid(unsafe_code)], lossless VP8L encode and VP8/VP8L/animated decode, native YUV 4:2:0 output; no lossy (VP8) encoder. The encode speed comes with larger files than libwebp m4 on photographs (+4 to 13%). Lives as one crate in the remade_ffmpeg_rs monorepo (crates/rusty_webp), also published as the rusty_webp crate.
caveats: First-party, and the WebP harness is not in the repo: tools/bench has a generic pinab.py but no WebP script, docs/benchmarks.md covers VP9 only (Intel Core i7-14650HX), crates/rusty_webp/examples holds only decode_bench.rs, and the Derf corpus is not shipped; compiler, flags and CPU for the WebP rows are unstated. The libwebp baseline is reached through FFmpeg's libwebp wrapper, not cwebp. Decode wins are against FFmpeg's decoder; the upstream image-webp README says its decode is 70-100% of libwebp. The fork's NOTICE.md records that the first version was 16-23x faster at encode but produced 35-53% larger files, so the 1.6-2.8x figure is a size/speed trade chosen after tuning. Repository shows AI-assistance (CLAUDE.md, .claude directories); the rusty_webp path has two commits, both 2026-08-12 (repo-wide last commit 2026-10-05). This record shares repo_url with the existing remade_ffmpeg_rs record, so it needs a paper: id (for example paper:rusty-webp) when merged.
found_via: seed-record pass: lead text 'remade_ffmpeg_rs crates/rusty_webp'; github.com/Remade-With-Rust/remade_ffmpeg_rs crates/ listing, crates/rusty_webp/README.md and NOTICE.md, docs/benchmarks.md, tools/bench listing, crates.io API for rusty_webp

name: TinyTIFF
baseline: libTIFF (libtiff 3.8.2 and 4.6.0)
workload: Writing many small uncompressed 16-bit frames (64x64, 10 to >100000 frames) and frames of 64x64 to 4096x4096 into one multi-frame TIFF, compared with libTIFF and with raw fwrite(), using the repo's tests/tinytiffwriter_speedtest program.
claimed_speedup: README: 'significantly faster than libTIFF, especially in writing large multi-frame TIFFs'; on an SSD 'still significantly (1.5-3x ...) faster than libTIFF' over frame count and 'faster than libTIFF by a factor of 1.5-5x' over frame size; on a hard disk libTIFF per-frame write time grows with frame count while TinyTIFFWriter stays close to fwrite().
compiler_and_flags: Release builds (32-bit on the Win10 run, 64-bit on the Win11 run); compiler and flags not stated
hardware: Ryzen 5 3600+, Win10, hard disk, libTiff 3.8.2; Ryzen 7 5800H, Win11, SSD, libTiff 4.6.0
tradeoffs: Basic TIFF only: uncompressed pixel data, limited tag set and pixel formats; the writer pre-reserves a fixed header block per frame. LGPL-3.0 licence.
caveats: Speedups are read from log-scale charts (PNG images) and quoted from README prose; the exact per-run numbers are not in text. The hard-disk run uses libTiff 3.8.2, a very old release, and a 32-bit build; only the SSD run uses libTiff 4.6.0. Write-side only: no read-speed comparison. The workload is many tiny frames, where libTIFF's per-directory overhead dominates; for few large frames the README says libTIFF is in the same range. Compiler and flags are not stated, so not tier A.
found_via: vcpkg port scan (microsoft/vcpkg ports/tinytiff, description 'Lightweight TIFF reader/writer library'), then raw README on raw.githubusercontent.com

name: wpd (WebP decoder)
language: Rust with x86 assembly, C ABI (wpd.h)
baseline: libwebp (libwebpdecoder built from the pinned Meson subproject)
workload: Decode time (hyperfine, 3 warmup, 20 runs, single thread, output to /dev/null with format conversion) of 7 test WebP files: lossy, lossy with alpha, lossless and animated, compared with libwebp and the image-webp crate.
claimed_speedup: README table (libwebp ms / wpd ms): lossy.webp YUV420P 180.40/173.56 = 1.04x; simplelf-lossy.webp 174.43/162.07 = 1.08x; anim_yuv.webp RGBA 190.90/169.18 = 1.13x; lossless.webp RGBA 195.75/111.27 = 1.76x; anim_rgb.webp 104.47/62.56 = 1.67x; a_lossy.webp YUVA420P 50.70/36.38 = 1.39x; anim_yuva.webp RGBA 494.37/374.46 = 1.32x. image-webp crate is slower than libwebp on the same files (e.g. lossless 231.50 ms, anim_yuva 776.54 ms).
compiler_and_flags: Meson release build (-Dbuildtype=release -Dtrim_dsp=false per README); compiler name and version not stated
tradeoffs: Decoder only. Needs the Rust toolchain plus nasm on x86 (Meson build). Assembly is on by default; building with -Denable_asm=false gives memory-safety guarantees at the cost of speed. C API in include/wpd.h, installs static and shared libraries plus wpd.pc, so it is callable from C++. Streaming and cropping/scaling options exist.
caveats: The README table does not name the CPU (it says 'CPU affinity above' but the machine line is gone), so the tier stops at C although scripts/bench.sh is public. Test files live in a separate repo (halidecx/wpd-test-data). Lossy gains are small (1.04x-1.08x); the larger wins are lossless and animation. The README was reformatted on 2026-10-01 and the benchmark commit is dated 2026-10-03, so the numbers are very fresh; a search snippet seen earlier in the session quoted larger ratios (2.38x-4.56x) that no longer appear on the page, so only the current README table is reported. libwebp threading is off in the default single-thread run (THREADS=1).
found_via: WebSearch 'libwebp faster alternative WebP decoder encoder SIMD "faster than libwebp" github' surfaced halidecx/wpd; README and scripts/bench.sh read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: zenjpeg
baseline: libjpeg-turbo (mozjpeg-sys 2.2 with nasm_simd, C+NASM)
workload: JPEG decode throughput on 10 CID22 photos (baseline 4:2:0 and progressive) and parallel decode of baseline JPEGs with restart markers (DRI) at 1024, 2048 and 4096 pixels, zenbench interleaved A/B runs.
claimed_speedup: README: baseline 4:2:0 decode 73.8 MiB/s (default Triangle upsampling) vs libjpeg-turbo 78.1 MiB/s (0.94x, slower) and 80.4 MiB/s with NearestNeighbor upsampling (1.03x); progressive decode 46 vs 34 MiB/s (1.35x faster); parallel decode with DRI: 1.56 vs 3.86 ms at 1024, 3.05 vs 15.8 ms at 2048, 8.74 vs 65.3 ms at 4096 (about 2.5x, 5.2x, 7.5x faster, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: cargo --release, default target, no -C target-cpu=native, runtime SIMD dispatch; rustc version not recorded in the benchmarks README
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (WSL2)
tradeoffs: AGPL-3.0 or paid commercial licence. Pure Rust, so C++ needs bindings. Baseline decode is slightly slower than libjpeg-turbo with libjpeg-compatible upsampling; the large win needs restart markers (DRI) and the parallel feature (multi-threaded versus single-threaded libjpeg-turbo). workload: README: JPEG encode and decode time per frame for a 16K DCI source image cropped or downscaled to HD (2 Mpix), 4K (8 Mpix), 8K (33 Mpix) and 16K (132 Mpix), RGB input, quality 75, non-interleaved, restart interval 24-36, average of 99 runs excluding the first, gpujpegtool -n 100.
claimed_speedup: No comparative speedup is claimed. README timings only: encode 4K 1.65 ms on RTX 4080, 1.71 ms on RTX 3080, 2.89 ms on RTX 2080 Ti, 3.16 ms on AMD RX 7600 via ZLUDA; encode 8K 6.33 ms (RTX 4080) and 16K 24.92 ms; decode 4K 1.46 ms (RTX 4080) and 8K 5.78 ms; on RTX 3080 8K encode 6.21 ms at quality 70 and 2.28 ms without PCIe transfers. compiler_and_flags: Recommended build cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native (optional -DUSE_NATIVE_CPU_ARCH=ON); the README says the RTX 4080 numbers were taken with cmake configured without those flags and that other measurements were made without a Release build type. CUDA toolkit and host compiler versions are not stated.
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 4080, RTX 3080, RTX 2080 Ti, GTX 1060M, GTX 580 and AMD Radeon RX 7600 via ZLUDA; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Needs an NVIDIA CUDA GPU (AMD only through ZLUDA). Baseline sequential-Huffman JPEG only, 8-bit; GPU Huffman encode and decode require restart markers (with restart interval 0 the CPU Huffman coder is used, because the README says one GPU thread would be very slow), so arbitrary JPEGs from cameras decode without GPU parallelism. Default timings include host-device PCIe transfers (8K encode 6.21 ms versus 2.28 ms without them on RTX 3080). First call has initialization cost (about 28.6 ms for 8K on RTX 3080 in the README). Larger images can run out of memory on small GPUs. COPYING is BSD-2-Clause; the README also says the code contains source provided by NVIDIA Corporation and is based on SiGenGPU.

The only comparison numbers found are two user issues from September 2020 (https://github.com/CESNET/GPUJPEG/issues/47 and https://github.com/CESNET/GPUJPEG/issues/48, read through a summarizer, no maintainer reply visible, GPU model and CUDA version not stated): on a random 8192-labelled image total time was 911.242 ms for GPUJPEG against 1608.21 ms for nvJPEG, but on a portrait with a uniform background it was 620.884 ms against 441.444 ms, so nvJPEG was faster, and the user noted GPUJPEG produced 16384 restart segments against 1 for nvJPEG. These are mixed, old and without methodology. Independent GPU decode papers (for example arXiv 2111.09219, which compares against libjpeg-turbo and nvJPEG) were found in a search snippet but arXiv is blocked here and they do not benchmark GPUJPEG in the snippet. A later check of the README against a CPU baseline is needed before listing it as faster than libjpeg-turbo.

name: jpegli
baseline: libjpeg-turbo
workload: None in the project's own docs. The README lists quality and feature improvements only. Third-party measurement (oximg issue #61): JPEG to JPEG resize pipeline, fit 512 px, quality 80, single thread, Zen 4.

Encoder does color conversion, subsampling and DCT in floating point, uses a JPEG XL style distance parameter, adaptive dead-zone quantization and XYB ICC support; decoder dequantizes to the Laplacian expectation and does IDCT, upsampling and color conversion in floating point with optional 16-bit or float output. The only numbers I found are third-party and point the other way for decoding: oximg issue #61 (https://github.com/oximg/oximg/issues/61, opened, Zen 4, measured 2026-09-30 to 2026-10-01, fit 512, quality 80) reports jpegli decoding 1.6-2.0x slower than libjpeg-turbo and, for encoding, upstream jpegli with default settings at +2.6% CPU and +10% bytes versus its baseline, and describes alternative jpegli baseline settings that cut encode cycles by about 12-17% (its own tuning experiment). name: mozjpeg
baseline: libjpeg-turbo
workload: None. The project documents compression speed as a deliberate cost of smaller files (trellis quantization, optimized Huffman tables, progressive scans with jpegrescan).
claimed_speedup: No speed advantage claimed. README-mozilla.txt states that with default settings mozjpeg is considerably slower than libjpeg-turbo or even libjpeg at compressing, that its performance is highly asymmetric (compression much slower than decompression) and that it is not suitable for real-time compression.
stars_or_usage: 5.7k stars, 435 forks; widely deployed in web image pipelines
tradeoffs: Speed and size trade-off versus libjpeg-turbo: slower compression by design in exchange for smaller files; decompression speed is the inherited libjpeg-turbo SIMD speed. Every mozjpeg improvement can be switched off at run time, in which case it behaves like libjpeg-turbo. Drop-in libjpeg API and ABI, strict superset of libjpeg-turbo features. Maintainers ask that non-mozjpeg-specific fixes go to libjpeg-turbo. Third-party estimates found (not measurements from this repo): libvips maintainer in https://github.com/libvips/libvips/discussions/2045 says libjpeg-turbo is perhaps 3x to 4x faster on x86 and mozjpeg can give up to perhaps 30% extra compression by adjusting parameters; a user report in https://github.com/mozilla/mozjpeg/issues/13 claims roughly 60% smaller output but almost 10 times longer compression than libjpeg-turbo, without versions, flags or machine.
caveats: No numbers in the project's own documentation, so tier D (notable, 5.7k stars). Versions: GitHub releases page lists v4.1.1 (August 15, 'Updated to libjpeg-turbo 2.1.3'; year not shown on the page), v4.0.3, v4.0.0 (libjpeg-turbo 2); the top entry of master's ChangeLog.md is 3.0.5, the inherited libjpeg-turbo changelog, whose speedup figures (for example 2-3.5x faster decompression than libjpeg) are libjpeg-turbo's, not mozjpeg's own. Last visible commit 2025-06-23 and several 2026 pull requests (for example #453, #455-#457) are open and unmerged, so maintenance is stale. The third-party numbers above were read through page summarizers and have no methodology. The entry is a size-efficiency tool rather than a speed win; it is useful as the baseline of the listed mozjpeg-rs and as a reference for the speed cost of trellis quantization.

name: MuPDF
baseline: poppler (pdftotext via libpoppler-cpp) and PDFium (pypdfium2)
workload: py-pdf/benchmarks: wall-clock time to extract the text of 14 pure (non-scanned) PDFs, and to extract their images, driven from Python through PyMuPDF (MuPDF), pdftotext (poppler) and pypdfium2 (PDFium).
claimed_speedup: Text extraction average 0.1 s for PyMuPDF against 0.3 s for pdftotext (poppler); per document 0.3 s against 1.0 s (GeoTopo-book) and 0.2 s against 0.8 s (1707.09725); pypdfium2 (PDFium) ties PyMuPDF at 0.1 s average. Image extraction average 0.5 s for PyMuPDF against 1.0 s for pypdfium2 (about 2x, derived from page data); poppler is not in the image row.
compiler_and_flags: not stated (PyMuPDF and pypdfium2 are prebuilt PyPI wheels, versions 1.28.2 and 5.13.0; pdftotext 0.86.1 built against the system libpoppler-cpp-dev)
hardware: Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-6700HQ CPU @ 2.60GHz
stars_or_usage: 3.0k stars on the GitHub mirror; backs PyMuPDF and is embedded in many viewers and tools
tradeoffs: AGPL-3.0 (commercial licence from Artifex for closed-source use), so copyleft applies to network services and products. The py-pdf numbers were taken through the PyMuPDF Python binding and pdftotext's Python binding, so both include Python call and string-copy overhead.
caveats: Independent suite (py-pdf organisation, BSD-3-Clause, runs the same script for every library; code public) but compiler and flags are not stated, so it is B not A. Times are rounded to 0.1 s, which makes the 0.1 s versus 0.3 s average coarse. The measured jobs are text and image extraction (parsing and interpreting content streams), not page rasterisation, so category rasterizers-2d is a best fit; the orchestrator may prefer a document-parsing category. First-party rendering evidence also exists: PyMuPDF docs Appendix 4 (https://github.com/pymupdf/PyMuPDF/blob/main/docs/app4.rst) report 150 DPI page rendering totals of 367.04 s for PyMuPDF against 646 s for XPDF pdftopng (rate 1.76) and 851.52 s for PDF2JPG across eight Artifex sample PDFs, and plain text extraction 8.01 s against 27.42 s for XPDF (3.42x); that page states no CPU or compiler and XPDF is poppler's ancestor rather than poppler, so it is tier C and was not used as the headline. PDF Association survey (pdfa.org, 2021) and an Alfresco blog compare MuPDF, poppler and PDFium rendering but both hosts are blocked here, so their figures were not read. Bindings (PyMuPDF, pypdfium2) are what the suite times, not the C libraries directly.

name: PDFium
baseline: Poppler (the pdftotext command-line tool, poppler 'pdftotext' row of py-pdf/benchmarks)
workload: Text extraction from 14 pure PDFs (7 to 134 pages) via the pypdfium2 binding of PDFium against the Poppler pdftotext command, in the independent py-pdf/benchmarks suite; page rendering is not measured.
claimed_speedup: Text extraction average 0.1 s for pypdfium2 (PDFium) against 0.3 s for pdftotext (Poppler), about 3x (derived from page data, times are rounded to 0.1 s). Per document: GeoTopo-book (117 pages) 0.2 s against 1.0 s, 1707.09725 (134 pages) 0.2 s against 0.8 s, 2201.00214 0.5 s against 0.7 s, 2201.00151 0.2 s against 0.3 s. pdftotext was never faster than pypdfium2 on any of the 14 documents. Text-quality score 95% (pypdfium2) against 90% (pdftotext).
compiler_and_flags: not stated (pypdfium2 5.13.0 is a prebuilt PyPI wheel carrying a PDFium binary; pdftotext is the distribution build of Poppler, no flags given)
hardware: Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-6700HQ CPU @ 2.60GHz
stars_or_usage: no GitHub star count (canonical repo is on googlesource); pdfium-binaries tracks it with release chromium/8086 (PDFium 157.0.8086.0) dated 2026-10-05
tradeoffs: Large C++ codebase with many bundled third-party dependencies (each carrying its own licence, per the pypdfium2 README), normally consumed through binary builds such as pypdfium2 or bblanchon/pdfium-binaries. Strong text extraction quality in the same suite (95% against Poppler's 90%).
caveats: Independent suite (py-pdf organisation, BSD-3-Clause, one script for every library, code public) but compiler and flags are not stated, so B not A. Not a like-for-like comparison: PDFium is driven in-process through the pypdfium2 ctypes binding (open document from bytes, get_textpage, get_text_range per page, plus Python post-processing), while Poppler is run as a subprocess (pdftotext -enc UTF-8 on a temp file written for each call), so Poppler's time includes process start and temp-file I/O, which inflates its figures on the small documents. Single run per document, no repeats, time.time(), times rounded to 0.1 s, so the 0.1 s against 0.3 s average is coarse. The measured job is text extraction (content-stream parsing and text layout), not page rasterisation, so category rasterizers-2d is a best fit (a sibling MuPDF record uses the same suite and category). The README lists pdftotext as the Python package 0.86.1 (libpoppler-cpp) but the benchmark code in library_code.py actually calls the pdftotext executable. PDFium licence taken from the list tag and the pypdfium2 README ('a BSD-style license'); pdfium.googlesource.com and its LICENSE file were not reachable from this environment. last_commit unknown for the same reason (activity inferred from pdfium-binaries releases and the pypdfium2 5.13.0 release of 2026-08-13). Other PDFium-versus-Poppler rendering comparisons exist (PDF Association 2021 Survey of OpenSource Solutions, Alfresco blog) but pdfa.org and hub.alfresco.com are blocked here and were not read.

name: Vello CPU (sparse strips renderer)
baseline: Skia (CPU pipeline) and Cairo; also Rust tiny-skia, raqote, AGG, JUCE
workload: Time for 1000 render calls of a single shape (rectangles, many-segment polygons, curves, strokes; solid/gradient/image paints) at sizes 8x8 to 256x256 on a 512x600 pixmap, single-threaded and 8-thread, in a fork of the Blend2D benchmark harness.
claimed_speedup: Thesis: Vello CPU 'outperforms nearly all other renderers, including Skia or Cairo, as the shape size increases'; Blend2D still wins in the vast majority of cases. Fill-Solid-RectU 256x256 single-threaded: Vello CPU 14.2 ms vs Skia 50.3 ms (about 3.5x faster, derived from page data) and Cairo 21.9 ms (about 1.5x faster, derived from page data) per 1000 renders; Blend2D 10.8 ms. At small sizes (8x8, 16x16) Skia, AGG and JUCE are faster in some tests. Multi-threaded 8T mode adds speedups up to about 4x on large shapes.
compiler_and_flags: Rust crates built with target-feature=+avx2 on x86 (no extra flags on ARM); build flags of the C++ baselines (Skia, Cairo, Blend2D) not stated in the thesis
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (8 cores, 16 GB) thesis results; Intel Core i9-14900K also run, per vello_chart manifest.json
tradeoffs: Rust crate (vello_cpu); C bindings exist in a separate repo (LaurenzV/vello_cpu_c) so C++ use needs FFI. Weak for very small shapes because of the fixed 4x4 tile size. Supports multi-threading and NEON/AVX2 SIMD.
caveats: Evidence is an ETH Zurich master's thesis (PDF checked into LaurenzV/master-thesis, read via raw.githubusercontent.com) by the Vello CPU author, so the benchmark is first-party for Vello CPU even though the harness is a fork of Blend2D's. Blend2D is faster in nearly all tests, so this is not a win over the category's best. Thesis reports M1 Pro only; interactive results for M1 Pro and i9-14900K live at laurenzv.github.io/vello_chart (blocked here, not opened; repo manifest.json read). The Vello repo README itself has no numbers. Thesis is not formally peer reviewed beyond the university examination, hence B.
found_via: WebSearch: 'sparse strips CPU GPU 2D vector graphics rendering Vello thesis benchmark Skia Blend2D'; then github.com/LaurenzV/master-thesis main.pdf

Mostly parity-level results on an old 2-core laptop CPU, with the project's own note that differences under about 2 ms are at the measurement floor; the Rust side runs in-process while the C++ side is a separate agg-render subprocess (render call only is timed). name: Blaze (aurimasg/blaze)
baseline: Blend2D, Skia (CPU), Apple CoreGraphics
workload: Multi-threaded CPU rasterization of large vector scenes (Paris-30k map, 4222x3474 px) and text, compared with Blend2D, Skia and CoreGraphics; each image rendered 500 times, 5 best and 5 worst dropped, remaining 490 averaged (per snippet of the author's article).
claimed_speedup: Search-result summaries of the author's article: Paris-30k (4222x3474, 50,681 layers) renders in 18 ms with Blaze vs 47 ms Blend2D, 190 ms Skia and 390 ms CoreGraphics (about 2.6x over Blend2D and about 10.6x over Skia, derived from snippet data); also described as around 20x faster than Core Graphics overall.  Snippet only.

Usable from C++ only by reusing the AGG-based device code, so this mainly counts as evidence that AGG-class scanline rasterizers beat Cairo in an R workload.

name: SFML
baseline: raylib (DrawTexture, C)
workload: Megabunny: draw one million identical static bunny sprites per frame for 100 frames in a 1000x1000 window, reported as millions of bunnies per second (gettimeofday around the draw loop).
claimed_speedup: SFML 12.4 mbunnies/s versus raylib (C) 9.6 mbunnies/s, about 1.29x (derived from page data). The same table shows SDL2 with the OpenGL renderer at 21.9, so SFML is about 0.57x of SDL2 (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: From the benchmark's run.sh scripts: g++ -O3 for the SFML program, gcc -O3 for the raylib and SDL2 programs; SFML, raylib and SDL versions and their own build flags are not stated.
tradeoffs: Object-oriented C++ multimedia API (window, 2D graphics, audio, network) on top of OpenGL, with bindings for C, .NET, Ruby and Python. Per-sprite draw calls through sf::RenderWindow; the project is mid-move to version 3 and 2.x no longer gets features.
caveats: Third-party hobby benchmark ('My results' in the README) with no CPU or GPU model, no library versions and no vsync or driver information, so it is tier C, not A. The README itself says the benchmark is not a good reason to choose a framework. The workloads are not identical: the SDL2 program draws 32x32 destination rects with SDL_RenderCopy, SFML and raylib draw the texture at its own size, and the raylib loop also calls DrawFPS each frame; the timer includes first-frame costs. The table labels SFML as language 'C' although the source is main.cpp. SFML loses to SDL2 in the same table, so this is only a win over raylib. No SFML-owned benchmark exists in the SFML repo (README, no benchmark directory). An old first-party SFML forum benchmark (2007, topic 43 on en.sfml-dev.org, AMD Athlon 64 X2 3800+ and GeForce 7800 GT) reported 303 versus 9 frames on 2000 static sprites and 277 versus 3 on 2000 rotating sprites against SDL 1.2; that page is blocked here, so those numbers are WebSearch snippet only, and SDL 1.2 is obsolete (a search snippet also says SDL2 beats SFML in a later benchmark except dynamic text).

name: stilus
baseline: golang.org/x/image/vector (the Go project's rasterizer) and gogpu/gg v0.52.5 CPU rasterizer
workload: Synthetic print-style scenes on an A3 landscape page at 150 dpi (2481x1754 px): 2,000 hatch lines and 20,000 short strokes. stilus strokes and fills directly; the x/image/vector run fills the outlines produced by stilus's own stroker, with one vector.Rasterizer sized to each outline's bounding box; gg runs with no clip.
claimed_speedup: README comparison table: 2 000 hatch lines: stilus 70 ms, x/image/vector 33 400 ms, gogpu/gg 14 800 ms; 20 000 short strokes: stilus 55 ms, x/image/vector 111 ms, gogpu/gg 2 090 ms. About 477x and 2.0x versus x/image/vector (derived from page data). Separate 'Numbers' table: stilus 1 core 67 ms (2 000 hatch lines at 0.35 mm) and 41 ms (20 000 short strokes), 4 cores 19 ms and 12 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Go (go.mod says go 1.24; toolchain version for the table not stated); `cd bench && go test -bench .`, comparison source is bench/compare_test.go (separate module)
hardware: 'Same machine' as the Numbers table: cloud Xeon @ 2.1 GHz (exact model not stated), minimum of 15 runs; some speed levers were measured on a Ryzen 7 5800H
tradeoffs: Pure Go, no cgo, no dependencies, builds for all GOOS/GOARCH including js/wasm; zero allocations after warm-up; sparse cost model (edge length plus covered spans); exact-area coverage like FreeType/AGG; optional AVX2/AVX-512 compositing under GOEXPERIMENT=simd; it is only the rasterizer core of a planned PDF renderer (no fonts, colour spaces or display lists).
caveats: The baseline is used in a way that favours stilus: x/image/vector's cost is proportional to the bounding-box area, so long diagonal hatch lines cost it a full box each, which explains the 477x ratio (above 50x, so capped at tier C). It is not compared against Skia, Cairo or Blend2D, so baseline_in_list is false; the README only checks quality against PDFium (mean deviation 0.3-1.5/255, SSIM at least 0.998). First-party, one author, synthetic scenes, CPU model not named exactly, Go toolchain version not stated for the comparison table; benchmark source was skimmed, not run.

name: scany (multi-threaded scanner, srwiley)
baseline: srwiley/scanFT ScanFT (Go port of the FreeType/golang freetype CL-AA gray antialiaser, same algorithm as FreeType ftgrays)
workload: Rendering SVG icons through oksvg and rasterx with ScanS (single thread) or ScanT (multi-thread) as the rasterx.Scanner; the repo's Go benchmarks (scant_test.go, scans_test.go) render a set of landscape icons and a gradient-heavy TestShapes6.svg (50 draws per run) at 1x and 5x scale with 1 to 32 threads.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. README: 'ScanS appears to be within 1 or 2 percent as fast as ScanFT'; 'If ScanT is run using a thread count of one it is around 10% slower than ScanFT or ScanS. However, as additional threads are added it will exceed the speed of the single thread implementations'; SVGs with gradients 'particularly benefit from using multiple threads'.
tradeoffs: ScanT starts three kinds of worker thread (cell splitting, cover and area, sweep) and a thread count of N starts N of each, all of which must be shut down with Close(); needs rasterx and oksvg; output via a Collector interface, only an image.RGBA collector is provided. Licensed MIT, while ScanFT is under the FreeType licence because it is a direct port of the C code.
caveats: No measured results anywhere in the repo or README, so the speedup is a prose claim (tier D). The benchmarks in scant_test.go and scans_test.go only vary ScanT's thread count and ScanS; the ScanFT and x/image/vector calls are commented out or absent, so none of the named baselines is timed. The README's own claim for single-threaded ScanS is parity (within 1-2 percent), not a win; only ScanT at several threads is said to be faster, with no hardware, Go version or crossover thread count. The lead's other baselines (golang.org/x/image/vector, scanx, FreeType ftgrays itself) are not compared; ScanFT is the nearest relative of ftgrays. Repository is one star, last commit 2022-01-17, 'go 1.17' module, so it is old and unmaintained. Kept at tier D because the instructions require a record for each listed project.

name: gopus (pure-Go Opus codec)
baseline: libopus 1.6.1 (C reference encoder and decoder, SIMD build)
workload: Matched C and Go encode and decode workloads in ns per sample per channel: CELT fullband 20 ms stereo 128 kbps, CELT 5 ms mono 64 kbps, SILK wideband 20 ms mono 32 kbps, Hybrid fullband mono 64 kbps and stereo 96 kbps encode; decode of 20,075 RFC test-vector packets as float32 and int16.
claimed_speedup: Go SIMD takes 2.5-28.7% less time than matched C SIMD in four of five encoder cases (for example SILK wideband 329.21 vs 462.01 ns/sample, Hybrid fullband mono 225.80 vs 253.40, CELT fullband 20 ms stereo 126.28 vs 129.50) and 14.6% more in the 5 ms CELT case; float32 decode 33.14 vs 35.90 (7.7% less), int16 decode 37.64 vs 38.83 (3.1% less). Scalar rows: Go scalar is slower than C scalar in 6 of 7 rows (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27.1 with GOAMD64=v3, GOEXPERIMENT=simd and PGO; C side GCC 13.3.0 with GOPUS_LIBOPUS_AMD64_TARGET=v3 (same x86-64-v3 target); each case three runs of at least 250 ms; reproduce with tools/encoderbenchcmp and tools/testvectorbenchcmp
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763
tradeoffs: Go-only (no cgo) so C++ use needs an FFI shim or a Go service; the win needs GOAMD64=v3 and GOEXPERIMENT=simd, a Go 1.27 toolchain feature, and PGO; the README says the Go build tracks libopus 1.6.1 for bit-exact and quality parity, with optional DRED, QEXT and OSCE builds behind build tags.
caveats: First-party harness, but the comparison tools are public and the revision (candidate 4b660d668) and toolchains are named. Results are a mix: Go is slower in the scalar table and in one SIMD encoder case, and the faster rows are 3-29% rather than multiples. Measures codec work only, not file I/O. The README states its own file-based bench-encode and bench-decode examples include opus_demo process start-up in the C timings and are only rough. The repo shows 3,296 commits; the benchmarks were not run by this agent. The fork hujm2023/gopus (0 stars) shows older CI numbers where Go is 1.3-1.7x slower than libopus; those were not used.

name: libopus-rs
baseline: libopus (Opus trunk commit 03647f524a40b05a1898522e92033810b58103c7)
workload: 48 kHz stereo CELT-only, 5 ms (240-sample) frames, maximum complexity, 16-bit and 24-bit PCM, CBR and constrained VBR at 192/256/320 kb/s; direct in-process encode and decode of 4 x 10 s excerpts, three alternating Rust/C rounds, median per source.
claimed_speedup: Encode 1.19-2.36% less time and decode 1.50-4.64% less time than trunk libopus in all 12 aggregate cells (e.g. 16-bit CBR 192 kb/s: encode 371.9 ms vs 380.9 ms, decode 95.3 ms vs 100.0 ms per 40 s of audio); Rust encoder 96.8-107.6x realtime, decoder 338-430x realtime.
compiler_and_flags: Rust release mode, ThinLTO, one codegen unit, -C target-cpu=native; C driver (tools/raw_celt_bench.c) built with -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native and linked against static libopus.a from the trunk commit; the final timing JSON records the build-flag fields as unknown because binaries were reused; compiler versions not stated.
hardware: GCP c4-highcpu-4, Intel Xeon Platinum 8581C, process pinned to CPU 2 with taskset
tradeoffs: Incomplete codec: only 48 kHz CELT-only raw frames are supported; no SILK, hybrid or Ogg Opus. Not a drop-in replacement for libopus, no C API, and encoder packets are not byte-identical to libopus. Encoder is marked experimental. Uses a private SIMD kernel path dependency crate.

The test corpus (SoundKit diverse-v1) is licensed local audio and is not stored in the repo, so the run is not reproducible as-is. The repository is archived and deprecated in favour of wavey-ai/soundkit (soundkit-opus/libopus-rs) per its README; that successor was not opened. name: opus-pure
baseline: libopus 1.6.1 (float build)
workload: Opus encode and decode of generated 48 kHz speech/music test signals, 20 ms frames, complexity 9, in-process, 8 s of audio per case, fastest of 12 passes, run through SILK, hybrid and CELT modes.
claimed_speedup: Encode 1.09-1.76x faster than libopus (SILK 1.09-1.12x, e.g. 218x vs 195x realtime for SILK NB 8 kb/s mono; CELT 128 kb/s 204x vs 116x realtime = 1.76x); decode slower or at parity, 0.84-1.02x of libopus (e.g. SILK NB 3432x vs 3958x realtime).
compiler_and_flags: Rust crate at cargo default release settings, no RUSTFLAGS, no -march=native (rustc version only stated as 1.88 or newer); libopus 1.6.1 built with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, OPUS_USE_NEON=ON with runtime dispatch, float build (also a fixed-point build for a second column); C compiler not named.
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (aarch64 NEON)
stars_or_usage: 2 stars; 19+ commits; on crates.io as opus-pure
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, no C API or FFI exposed (callable from C++ only by writing a wrapper); no dependencies; hand-written NEON/SIMD kernels for CELT. Decode is not faster than libopus. Chunk-parallel encode is lossy relative to serial encode. Ogg reader seeks only to the start.
caveats: Single machine (aarch64 Apple M1 Pro); x86 results are not given. SILK encode is a fixed-point port, so the harness reports a second table against fixed-point libopus where the ratio differs. The README states hybrid is not exactly like-for-like with either libopus build. The harness (cspeed.c, rspeed, run.sh) is in the repo, which is why this is tier A; the toolchain versions are not pinned.

name: opuspp
baseline: libopus 1.6.1 decoder (opus_decode_float), built with identical compiler and flags
workload: Decoding a 60 s mixed-audio stream (tones, noise, transients, orchestral music) encoded by libopus as 48 kHz fullband stereo, 10 ms CELT frames at 320 kb/s and encoder complexity 4; best of 7 passes pinned to one core, packet buffer flushed from cache before each pass. Other streams: 128 and 510 kb/s, 10% packet loss, complexity 0 and 2.
claimed_speedup: Like for like (same compiler and flags) opuspp is 1.27x to 1.48x faster than libopus at 320 kb/s (GCC Size 1.27x, GCC Balanced 1.48x, GCC Fast 1.43x, Clang Size 1.42x, Clang Balanced 1.46x, Clang Fast 1.42x); 1.09x to 1.50x across other bit rates, packet loss and encoder complexities. Five of six opuspp builds beat the fastest libopus build (GCC Fast) by 1.33x to 1.43x; GCC Size opuspp is slower than that build (0.88x).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 16.2 and Clang 22.1; Size: -Os, Balanced: -O2, Fast: -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -falign-loops=32 (libopus with OPUS_FLOAT_APPROX=ON and OPUS_FAST_MATH=ON, opuspp with OPUSPP_FLOAT_APPROX); all with -DNDEBUG -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections and -Wl,--gc-sections
hardware: One core of an AMD Ryzen 5 9600X
tradeoffs: Header-only freestanding C++23 decoder specialised to one stream type: CELT-only, fullband, 48 kHz stereo float output, 10 ms frames, prediction disabled, no pitch post-filter, no SILK, hybrid, FEC or DNN extensions. Bit-identical to libopus in strict-IEEE builds (47 encoder configurations, 300k-packet fuzz); the Fast profile is not bit-exact in either decoder. Smaller code (71-198 KB vs 98-236 KB static libopus) and decoder state (18.1 KB vs 26.6 KB), no heap or libm.
caveats: Brand-new repository written by Claude Code per its README (an AI-made port); benchmark is first-party and on one CPU (Ryzen 5 9600X), single synthetic 60 s stream; libopus reference built for the x86-64 baseline with SSE kernels per the verification doc. Only works for the narrow stream profile above, so it is not a general libopus replacement. Compiler versions (GCC 16.2, Clang 22.1) are as stated in the doc and were not independently checked. Results vary by a few percent between runs per the doc.

name: rav1d-safe
baseline: upstream rav1d (the Rust port of dav1d) built without assembly; against dav1d-derived assembly builds it is slower
workload: Still-image AV1 decode (12 inputs: photo and map at 1920x1080, 3840x2160, 7680x4320, minimum tiling and eight tiles, 8-bit 4:2:0 IVF) with 1, 4 and 8 workers; median of five paired repetitions per cell, geometric mean across inputs, MD5-checked against upstream and dav1d 1.5.3.
claimed_speedup: Checked rav1d-safe takes 0.680x the time of upstream rav1d without assembly with 1 worker (32.0% less decode time), 0.821x with 4 workers and 0.813x with 8 workers; for example photo-8k-min 231.4 ms vs 451.9 ms (0.512x). Against upstream rav1d with assembly the same page set shows checked rav1d-safe taking 1.8-8.6 times as long, and its README reports about 1.5x slower than the assembly build on 4K and 8K AVIF stills.
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.98.1 (LLVM 22.1.8), release, fat LTO, one codegen unit, unwind panics, RUSTFLAGS=-C llvm-args=-align-all-functions=4; upstream rav1d commit d3d1cd6 with default-features=false (bitdepth_8, bitdepth_16); rav1d-safe commit be5b244 checked features (no unchecked, c-ffi, asm)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7900X (24 logical CPUs)
license: BSD-2-Clause AND AGPL-3.0 (commercial licence also offered), per the GitHub licence panel
tradeoffs: Memory-safe AV1 decoder: replaces about 160,000 lines of assembly with checked safe Rust SIMD under forbid(unsafe_code), native Rust API (C API behind an optional c-ffi feature that implies unchecked). Strict mode by default rejects non-conforming streams that dav1d conceals. Fork of rav1d, which is a port of dav1d.
caveats: Not faster than dav1d or assembly-enabled rav1d: the author's own pages say 1.5-1.6x slower on stills and 1.8-8.6x slower in the 2026-09-07 assembly comparison (video, frame threading not enabled). The win is only against upstream rav1d with its assembly turned off (which still contains unsafe Rust), and it is on still-image fixtures from a two-source seed corpus; the page says this is not an ablation of SIMD and does not establish parity. Map-content cells are near 1.0x (up to 1.002x at 4K, 4 workers, eight tiles). Dual AGPL/commercial licensing may restrict reuse. The baseline is not in the FFmpeg, x264, Opus list.

name: soundkit (soundkit-opus)
baseline: libopus (Opus trunk commit 03647f524a40b05a1898522e92033810b58103c7, direct in-process C calls)
workload: Pure-Rust 48 kHz stereo CELT-only codec versus libopus: 5 ms (240-sample) frames, OPUS_APPLICATION_AUDIO, maximum complexity, 16-bit and 24-bit PCM, CBR and constrained VBR at 192/256/320 kb/s; four 10 s music excerpts, median of 3 alternating rounds with 7 repeats each, pinned to one CPU.
claimed_speedup: Encode: 1.19-2.36% less time than trunk libopus in all 12 aggregate cells (Rust 96.80-107.55x realtime; for example 16-bit CBR 192 kb/s 371.9126 ms versus 380.9057 ms, -2.36%). Decode, each implementation on its own packets: 1.50-4.64% less time, but the project withdrew this as the decoder gate; the same-packet 24-bit gate at 192 kb/s constrained VBR over 4 sources measured +0.51% (slower) on C packets, -0.30% on SoundKit packets, +0.10% combined, which the project calls native parity within noise. Perceptual score 4.5731 MOS-LQO versus 4.5724 for libopus trunk.
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.97.1 release profile, ThinLTO, one codegen unit, -C target-cpu=native; C driver tools/raw_celt_bench.c built with GCC 12.2.0 -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native against static libopus.a from trunk
hardware: GCP c4-highcpu-4, 4 vCPU Intel Xeon Platinum 8581C (Emerald Rapids), Debian 12 x86-64, process pinned to CPU 2 with taskset
stars_or_usage: 3 stars; successor of the listed libopus-rs (moved into soundkit-opus 0.13.x on 2026-08-25, history kept)
tradeoffs: Safe public Rust API with checked wrappers around private unsafe SIMD kernels (SAFETY.md); no libopus FFI. Scope is narrow: 48 kHz CELT-only fullband mono/stereo; decoder rejects SILK, hybrid, FEC and mode transitions; no packet-loss concealment; production target is 5 ms stereo at 192-320 kb/s. CBR packet bytes match libopus but constrained-VBR streams differ (350-527 bytes per 400 s). Wasm path is not at parity: CODEC.md (Node.js, full track, 20 ms frames) reports Rust wasm encode at 127-128x realtime versus 147.4x for C libopusjs at 48 kb/s and 81-82x versus 110.9x at 128 kb/s, with Rust wasm decode faster at 48 kb/s (377-380x versus 332.5x) and slightly slower at 128 kb/s.
caveats: Margin is small (1-2 percent) and covers encode only; decode is parity once both decoders read identical packets. One x86 host, no AArch64 or Wasm parity claim. The four 100 s licensed music sources are not in the repository (the runner accepts another corpus via --corpus), the libopus configure string was not recorded, the final timing JSON records build-flag fields as unknown because binaries were reused, and the raw result JSON stays local; the report gives SHA-256 hashes only. Benchmark code is public (soundkit-opus/tools/run_soundkit_flac_corpus.py, raw_celt_bench.c, run_native_celt_ab.py, run_same_packet_decode_ab.py), so tier A follows the literal rule, but a verifier may cap it at C because of the private corpus. First-party results. Other soundkit crates carry stronger first-party claims against FFmpeg and other baselines that could be separate records: soundkit-alac README reports 13.51% less elapsed time than FFmpeg C ALAC decoding at 16-bit and 11.58% at 24-bit (20-file corpus, same Xeon 8581C host, thin LTO, target-cpu=native, byte-exact PCM); README table also states soundkit-vorbis 8.65% less elapsed time per sample than libvorbis C and soundkit-mp3 2.17% less time per sample than minimp3 C.

name: aubio
baseline: audioread FFmpegAudioFile (decodes through an ffmpeg subprocess)
workload: Python audio-loading benchmark: time to decode a mono noise file (1 to 151 s long, 16 durations, one file per duration) into a numpy array with aubio.source (hop_size 1024) versus audioread's FFmpegAudioFile, librosa, soundfile and others; a second benchmark times metadata queries (samplerate, channels, samples, duration).
claimed_speedup: Numbers derived from the benchmark's results/*.pickle files in the repo (mean over the 16 durations, seconds for three consecutive loads; ratios derived from page data). Load to numpy, aubio vs audioread+ffmpeg: wav 0.064 vs 0.657 (about 10x), mp4 0.044 vs 0.101 (about 2.3x), mp3 0.068 vs 0.103 (about 1.5x), flac 0.067 vs 0.071 (about 1.06x, a tie). Versus librosa: mp3 0.068 vs 0.131 (about 1.9x), mp4 0.044 vs 0.111 (about 2.5x), wav 0.064 vs 0.289 (about 4.5x). Metadata-only queries, aubio vs audioread: mp3 0.0015 vs 0.098 (about 66x), flac 0.0015 vs 0.098 (about 66x), mp4 0.0030 vs 0.106 (about 35x), ogg 0.0046 vs 0.200 (about 44x), wav 0.040 vs 0.099 (about 2.5x). aubio is slower than other loaders in some rows: flac load 0.067 vs soundfile 0.045 and librosa 0.039; wav load 0.064 vs scipy 0.014; wav metadata 0.040 vs soundfile 0.0008.
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0-or-later, so copyleft for anything linking it. The fast decode path depends on the aubio build having libav (ffmpeg), libsndfile or CoreAudio enabled; the Python API streams hop-sized blocks (loop in Python), so very small hop sizes cost interpreter time. Python package is the code measured, not the C library alone.
caveats: Independent community benchmark (faroit/python_audio_loading_benchmark, 152 stars, last commit 2023-12-19), not run by the aubio project. The README only shows bar charts on a log time axis; the exact numbers above come from the results/benchmark_np_<ext>.pickle and benchmark_metadata_<ext>.pickle files in the repo, read with a restricted unpickler (no code executed). Hardware, CPU model, compiler and build flags are not stated ('our server'), and the aubio package's build configuration (which decoder backend) is not stated, so this falls short of tier A. Harness quirks: the stored time is the minimum over 3 repeats of timeit with number=3 (so seconds for 3 loads, not 1), and only the last file of each duration folder is recorded (one file per duration). The audioread baseline spawns an ffmpeg process per file, so aubio's win over it is largely process-spawn overhead rather than faster codecs; aubio itself decodes mp3/mp4 through libav when built with it. Versus libsndfile (soundfile) and scipy aubio is slower for wav and flac, so aubio is a competitive loader rather than the fastest one. aubio's own repo has only python/demos/demo_reading_speed.py with no published numbers, and its README makes no speed claim. The 'ffmpeg or standard codec' baseline is a Haiku guess; the row compared here is audioread's FFmpeg wrapper, not the ffmpeg library called from C.

name: GStreamer (gst-vaapi VA-API pipelines)
baseline: FFmpeg (libavcodec through OpenCV's VideoCapture/VideoWriter FFmpeg backend, CPU software codecs)
workload: OpenCV VideoCapture/VideoWriter benchmark on a 1920x1080 clip: frames per second decoding and encoding mpeg2, h264, h265 (decode only) and vp8 in mkv, mp4 and avi containers, GStreamer pipelines versus OpenCV's FFmpeg backend.
claimed_speedup: Encode with GStreamer + VA-API (gst-vaapi) vs FFmpeg backend: mkv/h264 193 vs 51 fps (x3.8), mp4/h264 194 vs 51 fps (x3.8), avi/h264 185 vs 50 fps (x3.7), mkv/vp8 124 vs 12 fps (x10.3), mkv/mpeg2 124 vs 106 fps (x1.2). Decode: mp4/h264 376 vs 169 fps (x2.2), avi/h264 373 vs 159 fps (x2.4), mp4/h265 391 vs 256 fps (x1.5), mp4/mpeg2 364 vs 258 fps. GStreamer with the libav plugin (CPU) also beat the FFmpeg backend on mp4/mpeg2 decode (343 vs 258 fps) and avi/mpeg2 (306 vs 243 fps), but lost on h264/h265/vp8 decode (e.g. mkv/h264 126 vs 158 fps).
compiler_and_flags: OpenCV built with cmake -DBUILD_EXAMPLES=ON -DWITH_GSTREAMER=ON -DWITH_FFMPEG=ON, make -j8; compiler, optimisation flags and GStreamer/FFmpeg/OpenCV versions not stated
hardware: Intel Core i5-6600 @ 3.30GHz, Intel HD Graphics 530 (Skylake GT2), Ubuntu 17.10
stars_or_usage: 3.3k stars on the GitHub mirror; used in many Linux media stacks
tradeoffs: Framework with plugin pipelines; speed here comes from the VA-API plugin offloading to the Intel iGPU, which needs Intel graphics, a VA-API driver and the gst-vaapi plugin. Hardware encoders trade compression efficiency and quality for speed; the page does not compare quality or bitrate. GStreamer's CPU path (gst-libav) wraps the same libavcodec as FFmpeg.
caveats: The win is a hardware-versus-software comparison (iGPU VA-API against CPU codecs in OpenCV's FFmpeg backend), not GStreamer's own code being faster. The measuring project is OpenCV, not GStreamer, so this is independent but narrow. The page is from the Ubuntu 17.10 era (Skylake iGPU) and states no OpenCV, GStreamer or FFmpeg versions, compiler flags, encoder settings, frame counts or run counts. The sample it links (samples/cpp/gstreamer_pipeline.cpp) returned 404 at the OpenCV repository HEAD, so the benchmark code was not reproducible from the page alone. gst-vaapi decode was slower than the FFmpeg backend for mkv input (e.g. h264 59 vs 158 fps) and CPU gst-libav was slower than FFmpeg on h264, h265 and vp8 decode. The upstream repository itself (GStreamer README, LICENSE) carries no benchmarks. The GStreamer repo license file is LGPL v2.1 text; SPDX taken as LGPL-2.1-or-later from the list entry.

name: Falcon audio codec
baseline: libopus 1.6.1 (float and fixed point), opusfile 0.12, libvorbis 1.3.7, Tremor (decoders)
workload: Library-level single-thread decode of an 18-file 48 kHz stereo corpus (11 real recordings plus 7 synthetic signals) from memory to PCM in 20 ms reads, with Falcon and Opus files at equal size and Vorbis at its own quality setting; total times real time over the corpus, plus 256 simultaneous stereo voices.
claimed_speedup: Falcon 1114x real time vs libopus 1.6.1 float 731x (Falcon time 0.66x of libopus), libopus fixed point 629x, opusfile 717x, libvorbis 879x (0.79x), Tremor 877x (0.79x) on an x86-64 laptop performance core; Apple M5 1551x vs libopus float 1056x (0.68x) and libvorbis 1297x (0.84x). Faster than libopus on 18 of 18 files on both CPUs; stb_vorbis 1154x is on par on x86-64 and 1.28x faster on M5. 256 voices: 291 ms vs libopus float 365 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Falcon: Rust release profile, fat LTO, one codegen unit, x86-64-v3 on x86-64 (MSVC-toolchain DLL on Windows); C decoders built with -O3, GCC 15.1 (MinGW-w64) -march=x86-64-v3 on x86-64 and Apple clang 17 on M5; libopus with default SSE4.1/AVX2 runtime dispatch, stack protector off; best of two passes, at least 10 runs and 1 s per file
hardware: Intel Core Ultra 9 185H laptop (Windows 11, thread pinned to one performance, efficiency or low-power efficiency core) and a MacBook Pro with Apple M5 (macOS 26)
tradeoffs: A different codec, not a drop-in decoder for Opus streams: Falcon is an MDCT codec whose decoder is deliberately light and whose quality comes from encoder-side work. Uses more memory per stream than libopus (about 320-345 KB of heap per stereo stream plus a copy of the compressed file, vs 27 KB for libopus) and voice start-up is slower (156 us vs 46 us). Includes a C/C++ API (falcon_capi) with falcon.h and falcon.hpp. Quality claim is on par with Opus on an 18-file corpus, not an independent listening test. Version 2 was redesigned to avoid specific patents.
caveats: First-party numbers on one laptop CPU and one Apple CPU. The C comparison program that links all decoders was not found in the repo (tools/ holds only eval and quality; falcon_capi/examples hold decode examples), so the table cannot be reproduced from the repo as far as opened. The README says earlier versions compared against FFmpeg's built-in Opus and Vorbis decoders by mistake and withdrew the old Vorbis figures; against FFmpeg's Vorbis decoder Falcon wins only 5 of 18 files. Raw libopus is fed pre-extracted packets (no Ogg parsing) while opusfile, vorbisfile and stb_vorbis include container parsing. Falcon is Opus-class quality at equal size per its own metrics, but speed compares a different codec at the same file size, not the same bitstream.

claimed_speedup: Input MB/s on the default input: amd64 (i7-1260P) go-flac 147 vs ffmpeg 128 (about 1.15x, derived from page data), libFLAC 229, SoX 194; arm64 (Cortex-A76) go-flac 51 vs ffmpeg 48 (about 1.06x, derived), libFLAC 76. Real-recording snapshot: 16-bit about 19 ms vs about 71 ms, 24-bit about 25 ms vs about 61 ms for ffmpeg flac (machine not stated). README: 'libFLAC's reference encoder remains about 1.5x faster'.
hardware: Intel i7-1260P (amd64) and Cortex-A76 (arm64); machine for the real-recording snapshot not stated
tradeoffs: Pure Go with no cgo, SIMD kernels (AVX2 on amd64, NEON on arm64) bit-identical to the scalar fallback. Stays bit-exact at 32-bit where the README says ffmpeg's FLAC encoder truncates to 24-bit. Go only, so C++ callers would need a c-shared build or a rewrite.
caveats: First-party claim. The benchmark script is public and CPU models are given, but the Go version, the ffmpeg version and build, and compiler flags are not stated, so tier C. The win over ffmpeg is modest on the controlled input (1.06x-1.15x) and go-flac is clearly slower than libFLAC (about 1.5x). The README text says go-flac beats ffmpeg on ratio, but its own table lists ffmpeg at 0.8519 and go-flac at 0.8523 (lower is smaller). name: HALAC (High Availability Lossless Audio Compression)
baseline: FLAC 1.5.0 (libFLAC) -8 and -5; the same release notes also list WavPack 5.9.0 -h, Monkey's Audio and OptimFROG
workload: Single-thread encode and decode of six BipTunia albums, 24-bit 44.1 kHz stereo, about 5.88 GB, release 0.5.4 notes; a separate 29-song 32-bit float set (about 2 GB) in release 0.4.8 notes.
claimed_speedup: Release 0.5.4 (Ryzen 9 9600X, single thread): HALAC -plus encodes in 11.578 s and decodes in 13.201 s with 4,232,751,891 bytes, versus FLAC 1.5.0 -8 at 50.802 s encode, 14.357 s decode, 4,243,522,638 bytes (about 4.4x faster encode, 1.09x faster decode, slightly smaller output; derived from page data). HALAC -normal: 7.200 s encode, 9.353 s decode, 4,268,470,589 bytes versus FLAC -5 at 15.857 s, 13.451 s, 4,265,600,750 bytes (about 2.2x faster encode at equal size, derived from page data). Release 0.4.8 float set: HALAC normal 3.050 s encode / 4.290 s decode, 1,381,439,835 bytes, versus OptimFROG fast 39.310 s / 32.179 s, 1,346,477,460 bytes, and WavPack fast 20.675 s / 13.914 s, 1,392,225,168 bytes.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for 0.5.4 (0.4.8 notes say 'Single Thread, AVX2')
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9600X (single thread)
tradeoffs: Uses ANS (FSE) entropy coding instead of Rice coding, trading a few percent of compression for speed; OptimFROG compresses better. Releases cover 16/24-bit and 32-bit float PCM and up to 128 channels. No SIMD/GPU in early versions, AVX2 and multithreading added from 0.4.3.
caveats: First-party release notes with numbers but no benchmark script, compiler or flags, and the audio test sets are not distributed, so tier C. The source in the repository is only version 0.1.9 (halac_encode/decode_v.0.1.9 plus an FSE folder); the benchmarked 0.4.x-0.6.x builds are release assets, so the measured code may not be what the repo source builds. Release pages show dates without a year in the fetched text. The 0.5.4 notes do not say whether HALAC ran multi-threaded. The FLAC decode gap is small (1.09x); the headline win is encode speed. Baseline FLAC is not in this category's baseline list.

claimed_speedup: Snippet only: 'QOA encodes 10x faster and decodes 7x faster than Opus'; '25.75 seconds to encode a 9807-second file, 5.7 times faster than MP3 encoding on an i7-6700k'; decoding faster than Opus on an i7-6700k single-threaded. The repo itself states only 'fast, lossy audio compression' with no numbers.
hardware: Intel i7-6700k (from search snippet)
stars_or_usage: 985 stars; supported in Godot 4.3, raylib, SerenityOS, Qmmp, OpenCubicPlayer

HN comment snippets say Opus is better in every way except complexity and CPU cost, and that QOA compresses less than MP3 and sounds worse. Best fit is games or microcontrollers that need cheap decoding. Single-header C/C++ API. Format has a 31 channel limit (latest commit message).
caveats: Numbers come only from Hacker News result snippets (the thread and the author's blog post were not opened; phoboslab.org, qoaformat.org and news.ycombinator.com are blocked here). The repo README and qoa.h contain no benchmark, so the verifier needs the blog post or a rerun. Compiler, flags and files are unknown. The README warns the implementation has not been fuzzed and must not be used with untrusted input. Ported implementations (qoa-fu, qoaudio, goqoa and others) are wrappers or ports of the same format.

name: remade_ffmpeg_rs
baseline: FFmpeg libavcodec native MP3 decoder and native AAC encoder; libvorbis
workload: MP3 decode of a 27.5-minute stream, decode-and-discard on the same physical cores, 15 pairs; AAC-LC encode of a 60 s stereo clip with frame-parallel encoding; Vorbis encode of stereo music on 24 cores.
claimed_speedup: MP3 decode 1.24x faster than FFmpeg on 1 core (1,952 vs 2,431 ms, 15/15 pairs) and 1.39x on 2 cores (1,017 vs 1,455 ms), at lower total CPU (1,875 vs 2,125 ms); AAC encode about 6x faster than ffmpeg's own AAC encoder via frame-parallel encoding (about 450x realtime; single-thread about 1.15x); Vorbis encode about 5.3x faster than libvorbis wall-clock (frame-parallel, 24 cores; per-thread about 1.4x behind libvorbis). Image side (not video-audio): PNG decode 2.55-2.89x faster than ffmpeg, lossy WebP decode 1.24-1.29x.
stars_or_usage: 6 stars; crates.io rusty_mp3 0.8.0 (42,200 downloads), rusty_aac 0.5.0, rusty_vorbis 0.1.1 point to this repo
tradeoffs: Pure-Rust 'FFmpeg remade' with permissive licences; codecs are also published as standalone crates (rusty_mp3, rusty_aac, rusty_vorbis, rusty_png, rusty_webp). Rust only. The AAC and Vorbis headline speedups come from multi-threaded frame-parallel encoding against single-threaded baselines. Video codecs are slower than the incumbents: VP9 decode about 0.16-0.21x of FFmpeg, VP9 encode about 0.3x at +36% bit rate, H.264 decode about 2x behind FFmpeg's native decoder, MP3 encoder about 0.7-1.1 ODG behind LAME on average (1.4-1.8 on transients).
caveats: First-party; hardware, compiler and flags are not stated for the audio rows and no benchmark script was seen on the opened README. The README itself notes an earlier CLI-to-CLI comparison had MP3 decode 1.20x behind and was corrected to a matched-core comparison. The repo carries CLAUDE.md and .claude directories (AI-assisted). The crates rusty_mp3, rusty_aac, rusty_vorbis share this repo URL, so any standalone listing needs a paper: id to avoid duplicates. Only the README text was read; the code was not.

name: rivet-h26x (rivet-h26x-codecs)

workload: Decode of 720p Big Buck Bunny encodes (cabac3.264 H.264 723 frames, a CAVLC H.264 clip, hevc6.265 and wpp10.265 H.265 1200 frames), process-tree CPU seconds and frames per wall second, 1 thread pinned to one core and all threads, best of five, both decoders materialising every frame.
claimed_speedup: All threads on the wavefront H.265 clip wpp10.265: 1963 fps vs libavcodec 1774 fps (+10.7%); single-thread on that clip 1.938 CPU s vs 1.906 s (1.02x libavcodec's time, parity). Non-wavefront H.265 hevc6.265 all threads 1288 vs 1387 fps (-7.1%), single-thread 1.12x libavcodec's CPU time. H.264 single-thread costs 1.46-1.55x libavcodec's CPU time; H.264 all-thread fps 2169 vs 2119 (CABAC) and 3116 vs 3063 (CAVLC) are +2.4% and +1.7%, which the README says are within its 4% noise floor.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for either decoder; libavcodec version not stated; SIMD rungs selected at run time (AVX-512 tier on this CPU), regenerate with tools/benchmark.py (which no longer runs FFmpeg)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X 16-Core Processor, 32 hardware threads, AVX-512 rung, machine 17% busy before the run; single-thread rows pinned to core 29
license: Open Encoding Attribution License v1.0 (source-available, royalty-free with commercial attribution; not OSI-approved; no SPDX id confirmed)
stars_or_usage: 0 stars; crates.io rivet-h26x 0.2; 515 commits; moved from the rivet-transcoder organisation to safewords on 2026-10-03
tradeoffs: Pure-Rust H.264 and H.265 decoders (no C, no build script, one dependency) with frame and wavefront threading and a run-time SSE2-to-AVX-512 and NEON kernel ladder; bit-exact on 204 JVT and 196 JCT-VC conformance streams; also an in-progress encoder. Source-available licence with an attribution requirement, so it is not freely copyable under an OSI licence.

The README says the ratio column is good to about +-5% between sessions and that the earlier table put wpp10.265 at 0.96x before an unchanged-code re-run gave 1.02x. The libavcodec rows are a 2026-09 record, since the tooling no longer runs FFmpeg. Whether libavcodec was pinned to equal threads on the all-threads rows is not stated beyond 'every thread'.
