name: ropus (Rust port of libopus)
baseline: libopus 1.5.2 (C reference, with its hand-tuned SSE4.1/AVX2 dispatch)
workload: Encode and decode time ratio Rust over C on ten WAV vectors (SILK narrowband and wideband noise, Hybrid noise, CELT noise, sine, sweep, square, TTS speech, stereo music), harness amortising codec construction, medians of five sweeps (tools/bench_sweep.sh --iters=30).
claimed_speedup: x86-64 ratios Rust/C (below 1.0 means Rust faster): encode SILK NB noise 0.97x, SILK WB noise 0.96x, Hybrid noise 0.97x, CELT sweep 0.96x; decode CELT square 0.92x, SILK NB 0.95x, CELT FB mono noise 0.98x, CELT sine 0.99x; means 1.06x encode and 1.01x decode (slightly slower overall). The README says Rust encode is faster than C on five vectors and decode faster or at parity on six.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler version and C flags not stated in the README; Rust build targets x86-64-v3 (AVX2, FMA3, BMI1/2) per the README CPU-target note; harness is tools/bench_sweep.sh driving the ropus-compare binary
hardware: Intel i7-14700KF under WSL2 (x86-64 table); Apple M1 Pro (second table, where decode is slower, for example SILK NB 1.30x and SILK WB 1.50x); earlier Ryzen 9 9950X3D baseline kept in a journal
license: BSD-3-Clause (the repo LICENSE is the upstream Xiph libopus licence text; the README says to refer to the upstream project licence)
tradeoffs: Rust port of libopus 1.5.2 including DNN features (LPCNet, FARGAN, DRED) with a C ABI shim (capi/) that exposes the libopus API, plus a differential FFI harness that compares byte-for-byte against the C reference; builds the C reference from a pinned xiph/opus checkout. Larger binary because of an embedded 8.78 MB weights blob.
caveats: Parity rather than a win: mean encode ratio is 1.06x (slower) and mean decode 1.01x on x86-64, and decode is 1.3-1.5x slower on some Apple M1 Pro rows. The README says earlier runs measured decoder construction cost, not steady-state decode. Single desktop CPU, compiler flags not given, first-party. The repo carries CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md (AI-assisted). Recorded because a few vectors are faster than the C baseline; the honest summary is roughly equal speed.

name: ruopus
baseline: libopus 1.6.1 (SIMD-enabled C)
workload: In-process Opus encode and decode of a generated 6 s mono speech/music-like 48 kHz signal in 20 ms frames, one core, expressed as times realtime (benches/vs_libopus.rs).
claimed_speedup: Decode faster than SIMD libopus on speech: SILK wideband 16 kb/s 2095x vs 1171x realtime (1.79x), hybrid fullband 32 kb/s 1199x vs 850x (1.41x); CELT fullband 64 kb/s 1389x vs 1566x (0.89x, slower). Encode at matched complexity 0 is at parity (0.99-1.00x); against libopus default complexity 10, SILK wideband 16 kb/s encode 703x vs 221x (3.18x).
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench --bench vs_libopus --features std; release profile opt-level=3, lto=fat, codegen-units=1 (Cargo.toml); libopus 1.6.1 reached through the opus FFI crate against the system libopus, so its build flags are not stated.
hardware: one core pinned to a single performance core; CPU model not stated

caveats: CPU model and OS not stated. The 3.18x encode figure compares a ruopus encoder with no complexity-dependent slowdown against libopus at complexity 10, so the work is not equal; at matched complexity 0 encode is at parity. CELT decode is slower than libopus. Benchmark signal is synthetic. Benchmark harness is public (benches/vs_libopus.rs) but flags of the linked libopus are unknown.

baseline: libopus (C reference encoder); also FFmpeg's native Opus encoder
workload: Single-thread encode of 300 s and 150 s clips driven as processes, reporting the slope t(300 s) minus t(150 s), pinned to one core, CPU time, ABBA-interleaved, 31 reps, with a null arm; split by coding path verified from TOC bytes (CELT 48 kHz speech at 32k, CELT 48 kHz stereo music at 128k, SILK 16 kHz speech at 16k).
claimed_speedup: CELT speech 436x realtime vs libopus 291x (1.50x faster, FFmpeg native 310x); CELT stereo music 213x vs 133x (1.60x faster, FFmpeg native 71x); SILK 139x vs 145x (0.96x, libopus 4% ahead). Frame-parallel encoding adds wall-clock speedup on top. Quality: mean BD-ODG -0.015 vs libopus over 13 core classes (parity), +1.532 vs FFmpeg's native Opus encoder.

name: rusty_flac
baseline: FFmpeg 8.1.2 native flac encoder and decoder (libavcodec)
workload: Single-core CPU-time comparison on a 180 s 44.1 kHz stereo music clip (guitar, piano, vocal): encode at -compression_level 8 and decode of an FFmpeg-encoded stream; pinned to one core, ABBA-alternated, 31 pairs, outputs verified lossless before timing.
claimed_speedup: Encode 672 ms vs 813 ms (0.83x FFmpeg CPU time, 17.3% faster); decode 266 ms vs 344 ms (0.77x, 22.7% faster); 31/31 wins on both, z = 5.57. Output files smaller than FFmpeg's on 20 of 20 gate-matrix combinations (for example stereo guitar s24 level 8: 539,087 vs 565,122 bytes).
hardware: Not stated ('single core, this machine'); four AVX2 kernels are runtime-detected
stars_or_usage: 1 star; README says 321 active installs via one named downstream app
tradeoffs: Pure Rust (no_std plus alloc capable, unsafe only in four AVX2 kernels with scalar twins), no C API, so C++ use needs an FFI shim. FLAC subset with LPC orders up to 12. Part of the Remade With Rust ecosystem, which also ships remade_ffmpeg_rs.
caveats: First-party claim: CPU model, compiler and rustc flags are not stated and the harness outputs are not published as raw data, so it falls short of tier A. The baseline is FFmpeg's native flac encoder, not the reference libFLAC; libFLAC was not tested. Single 180 s clip for the speed numbers; the smaller-file claim is on the gate matrix, not on the timed clip. Project is young and its commit history shows rapid release churn (v0.2.0 merged 2026-09-30).

name: SampleRateTap (async engine)
baseline: libsamplerate 0.2.2 (Secret Rabbit Code, MEDIUM and BEST converters)
workload: Asynchronous near-unity sample rate conversion (two clock domains) measured as million output frames per second for mono, stereo and 8-channel streams at a matched ~120 dB and ~140 dB stopband tier, plus algorithmic latency and embedded instruction counts.
claimed_speedup: Doc states SampleRateTap is 3.1-3.9x (stereo/mono; 1.5x at 8 channels) faster than libsamplerate at the matched ~120 dB tier and 6.1x at ~140 dB, with 2-3.6x less latency. Table: stereo 14.6 vs 4.8 Mframes/s (balanced vs libsamplerate MEDIUM), mono 20.3 vs 5.2, 8-ch 3.0 vs 1.9; ~140 dB stereo 9.6 vs 1.6 (BEST). The same table shows soxr HQ at 52.9 and r8brain-free-src at 16.5 stereo, i.e. it is SLOWER than soxr and r8brain on x86 host throughput.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3 -O3 (CMake Release); libsamplerate 0.2.2 and soxr 0.1.3 Ubuntu 24.04 packages; r8brain at pinned commit 7.5 with Ooura FFT
hardware: shared Xeon @ 2.10 GHz (exact model not stated), run 2026-09-25; embedded rows use QEMU instruction counting for Cortex-M33 and Hexagon
tradeoffs: Specialised: near-unity asynchronous ratio (+-1000 ppm default) for clock-domain bridging, not a general-ratio resampler. Header-only C++20. Fixed-point Q15/Q31 paths for FPU-less DSPs. Very low latency (0.5 ms filter, 1.5 ms default).
caveats: Only beats libsamplerate; the same page shows soxr HQ (52.9 stereo) and r8brain (16.5 stereo) faster on x86 host throughput, which the author states openly. Measured on a shared Xeon with exact CPU model missing and ratios said to be the meaningful figures; libsamplerate latency rows were measured on 2026-06-12. Benchmark code is in the repo behind TAP_SR_BUILD_COMPARE_BENCH (off by default). Very young repo (commits Sep 30 to Oct 3 2026 visible, 225 commits), 5 stars; the benchmark page was written by the project author (first-party).

stars_or_usage: 17 stars; described in its README as the bottom of the stack of the Surge libraries
tradeoffs: Small-window Lanczos (A=4, 8 taps) with a 8192-entry interpolated coefficient table and SSE intrinsics, built for 48 kHz to variable-rate use; the header needs sst simd setup and a sum_ps_to_float reduction (or hadd) when copied. Filter quality versus long sinc kernels is not measured in the evidence. Only the three listed headers are MIT; everything else needs GPL-3.0.
caveats: Only evidence is an unanswered user question in another repository: no CPU, compiler, flags, timings or baseline version, and it is not clear whether the compared 'Sinc' was libsamplerate or the Holters-Parker resampler. NonIntegerSRC vendors an older copy of the Surge resampler class (src_utils/LanczosResampler.h), not the sst-basic-blocks header; its libsamplerate wrapper runs one channel; its CMakeLists sets no build type or optimization flags (README builds with plain cmake -Bbuild, and --config Release only matters for multi-config generators), so a Linux default build may be unoptimized. The same README claims its Holters-Parker resampler is about 17-40x faster than libsamplerate (chart: 39.81x for 48k to 96k, 16.92x for 96k to 48k, 21.17x for 44.1k to 48k, 21.85x for 48k to 44.1k), which is far above the Lanczos 2x. No libsamplerate or r8brain comparison and no benchmark exist in sst-basic-blocks itself (README, tree and header read). A search snippet from another source ('Lanczos 4.5x slower than sinc_best, 2x faster than sinc_fastest') was not traced to a page I opened and is not used.

name: SuperFast Codecs (fre:ac multi-threaded codec drivers)
baseline: fre:ac's regular single-threaded codec drivers: libopus (Opus), FAAC and Core Audio AAC in the initial release; FDK-AAC, LAME and Speex drivers added later
workload: Converting a single input file to a single output file with 4 worker threads, each running its own codec instance on overlapping 128-frame blocks (8-frame overlap).
claimed_speedup: 'Using four threads, the conversion is already three times faster than with the regular drivers, which use only a single thread in this mode' (single file mode). In multi file mode the SuperFast drivers are only slightly faster. The measured chart is an image in the PDF; the text gives no per-codec table.
hardware: Not stated (the text mentions a 6 core CPU)
stars_or_usage: 65 stars; code merged into mainline fre:ac (BoCA)
tradeoffs: Chunked parallelism over several codec instances, so output is not bit-identical to a single-threaded encode and the 8/128 overlap caps speedup at 16x. Works for Opus, AAC, Speex and MP3 drivers; the author says Vorbis, FLAC and WMA do not fit. Needs the fre:ac BoCA and smooth class libraries to build. It speeds up a driver, not the codec library itself.
caveats: First-party blog post (PDF) whose numbers are only in a chart image; CPU, thread counts per test and codec versions are not given in text, so tier C. The comparison is multi-threaded drivers against the same codec run single-threaded, not a faster codec implementation. Repo is archived since 2020-12-11 (code lives on in enzo1982/BoCA). The Opus resampler in the pipeline stays single-threaded, which limits gains for non-48 kHz input.

name: SuperLAME
baseline: LAME (stock single-threaded libmp3lame 3.101 beta)
workload: Encoding a 44-minute album to CBR 320 kb/s MP3, 2 to 16 threads, in-RAM benchmark mode.
claimed_speedup: 'Roughly 8x faster than stock single-threaded LAME at the same quality'; Ryzen 7 5800X3D, v1.1.0: 13.8 s at 2 threads down to 3.9 s at 16 threads (about 680x realtime); parallel efficiency about 93% at 2 workers and about 61% at 16.
compiler_and_flags: clang++ -std=c++17 -O2 -march=x86-64 for the frontend, clang -O2 for dr_flac, plus four libmp3lame engine builds (znver5, znver4, znver3, SSE2) in one binary; Windows executable
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 5800X3D
tradeoffs: Runs many libmp3lame instances in parallel on chunks and repairs the bit reservoir, so the gain is thread parallelism. Single-thread output is bit-identical to stock LAME; multi-thread output differs by an inaudible (below -45 dB) reconciliation at chunk seams. Whole input and output are held in RAM (about 1-2 GB input limit). Needs clang to build the SIMD paths; GPL because it combines LGPL LAME and mpg123 with GPL code ported from fre:ac/BoCA.
caveats: First-party README numbers; the stock-LAME timing that the 8x is measured against is not shown on the page, and the 8x applies to multi-threaded use on a many-core desktop. A --bench mode and tests/scaling.ps1 are described (not opened or run). Very new repo (July 2026) with 3 stars. Windows-oriented.

caveats: Tier D because the repository has no speed numbers. name: rav1e
baseline: libaom (AV1 reference encoder)
workload: AV1 video encoding speed; the README positions rav1e for cases where libaom is too slow, with speed presets 0-10.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. README: 'The fastest and safest AV1 encoder.' and 'in its current form it is most suitable for cases where libaom (the reference encoder) is too slow.'
tradeoffs: Written in Rust with hand-written x86_64 NASM and NEON assembly; needs NASM 2.14.02 or newer and Rust 1.85 or newer. A C API can be built (README section 'Building the C-API'), so it is callable from C++. 11 speed settings from exhaustive to near real-time.
caveats: The README gives no benchmark. The HN thread snippet 'The fastest and safest AV1 encoder but it's also 62.1% assembly?' questions the claim, and other AV1 encoders such as SVT-AV1 are commonly reported as faster; I did not verify that here. Report as tier D only because the project is notable. A verifier should find a public benchmark (for example Phoronix or AOM Codec Working Group tests) or retier it.
